sentences.text: The water came up on a Tuesday, which Wren thought was an unremarkable day for something so large to happen.
She had gone to bed with the river where the river belonged, down past the allotments, behind the willows, making the noise it always made.
She woke to a different noise.
It was softer and much closer, and it was coming from the stairs.
By morning the lane was a river and the river had no idea it was in the wrong place.

It went about its business between the houses exactly as it had gone about its business between the banks, carrying a fence panel, a plastic crate, and one green welly boot, all at the same unhurried speed.
Her grandmother had already moved the chairs upstairs.
She had done it in the dark, alone, without waking anybody, and she was drinking tea on the landing when Wren came out in her socks.
"Don't go down past the fifth step," her grandmother said.
"The carpet's ruined and I don't want you slipping on it." That was all.
No panic, no explanation.
That was how Wren knew it had happened before.
From the landing window she could see the tops of the fence posts, each one wearing a little collar of foam.
The Hendersons' shed had come loose and turned itself round to face the wrong way, which struck her as somehow ruder than the flood itself.
Beyond that, where the road should have been, there was a wide brown sheet of water going quietly out towards the fields.
The town had become an archipelago overnight.
Every house was an island.
The people in them stood at their upstairs windows and waved, and after a while stopped waving, because there is only so long you can wave at somebody you cannot reach.
That was when she saw the bird.
It stood on the ridge of the roof of the house opposite, with its neck folded down into its shoulders the way herons do when they have decided to wait.
It was very still.
She thought at first that it was one of those plastic ones people put on ponds to frighten the fish.
Then the light moved, and went through it.
It was clear all the way through, like a bottle held up to a window.
The grey morning went into it at the top and came out at the bottom the colour of the river, a soft moving brown-green, as if something were being stirred inside it very slowly.
Wren did not call anyone.
She had the strong feeling, the way you sometimes do about a wild thing that has come close, that a creature like that should be allowed to arrive without a fuss.
If she shouted, her grandmother would come, and then her grandmother would explain it, and then it would be a thing that had been explained.

So she stood at the window in her socks and watched it, and it did not look at her once, and after twenty minutes it lifted, and its wings when they opened were the thinnest thing she had ever seen, and it went across the water to the roof of number eleven and folded itself down again.
Her grandmother came and stood beside her, eventually, with a second cup of tea.
"Ah," she said.
"It's back, then." And she went downstairs to see about the carpet, which was, Wren thought, an extraordinary thing to say and then simply leave lying there.
By the second day the shouting had stopped.
It had been fun on the first day, in a grim way.

Mr Adeyemi at number nine had a good carrying voice and had shouted news across the water like a town crier: the electricity was off at the bottom end, the shop had moved its stock to the upper shelf, somebody had seen a pike swimming past the postbox.
People had leaned out and laughed.
But shouting all day makes a person hoarse, and it makes them tired, and by Wednesday afternoon the windows had gone quiet and everybody was alone in their own house being sensible.
Wren wrote a note.
She did it mostly to have something to do.
She tore a page out of the back of an exercise book, and she wrote *are you all right over there*, and she did not put a name on it because she did not know which house she was writing to.
She folded it small, and she put it on the outside sill under a stone.
She did it the way you throw a coin in a well.
Not really expecting anything.
Just doing it.
In the morning it was gone.
In its place was a different piece of paper, damp at one corner, folded the same way.
It said: *yes, and we have too much bread.* Wren stood at the window with it in both hands for a long time.
After that, nobody needed to explain anything to anybody.
That was the strange part, the part she thought about for years afterwards — how quickly a thing becomes normal when it is useful.
By Thursday there were notes on four sills.
By Friday there were notes on twelve.
The heron went from roof to roof with its long careful step, and it never hurried, and it never went to a house that had not put something out.
Where its feet touched the water at the edge of a roof, the water rang, very faintly, like a wine glass tapped with a spoon.
If you were listening for it you could tell where in the town it was.
The notes were not dramatic.
That was what Wren liked about them.
*We have too much bread.
Mrs Pryor has a cough and no honey.
Can anyone reach the Kellys, nobody has seen a light at the Kellys.
There is honey at number four, tell Mrs Pryor.

The Kellys went to their daughter's on Sunday, they are fine, please stop worrying about the Kellys.* And later, when it had gone on for five days and everybody was bored and frightened in equal measure: *Tomas is eight today and there is no cake.* A dozen houses put something on their sills that night.
Wren saw the heron cross the water nine times before it got dark, going slower each time, and once it came so close to her window that she could see the river turning over inside its chest.

In the morning Tomas at number six had a paper crown, a chocolate bar, a drawing of a dog signed by somebody called Iris, a book about submarines with the first page torn, and four separate notes that said *happy birthday* in four different handwritings.
Her grandmother watched all of this from the landing chair without much comment.
"Doesn't it want anything?" Wren asked.
"For doing it?" Her grandmother thought about that with the seriousness the question deserved.
"Some helpers," she said, "don't care to be thanked.
It isn't rudeness.
It's just that thanking makes it into a favour, and it was never a favour.
It was only ever the thing that needed doing."
On the sixth night the heron did not come.
Wren put her note out at the usual time, under the usual stone, and she watched the sill from the landing until her grandmother made her go to bed, and in the morning the note was still there.
Damp, and curling at the corner, and unread.
She thought at first that she had done something wrong.
She read her own note back four times looking for the mistake in it.
It said: *Mrs Pryor's cough is worse, does anyone have a thermometer.* She put it out again the next morning with a stone on top and went to the window every twenty minutes.
By eleven o'clock the sills along the lane had started to fill up.
She could see them from the landing: white squares appearing at number four, at number nine, at the Hendersons', at number eleven.
Everybody had written something.
Everybody was waiting.
Nothing came.
It is difficult to describe what that day was like without making it sound worse than it was.
Nobody was in danger.
The water had not risen; there was food in every house; the electricity was on at the top end of the lane and people were charging their phones at the Adeyemis' by passing them across on a boat hook.
Nothing had actually changed except that thirteen notes were sitting on fourteen windowsills getting wet, and everybody could see everybody else's note not being collected.
The town had got used to it in five days.
That was the thing.
Five days is nothing — it is less than a school week — and it had been long enough for a whole way of living to establish itself and start to feel permanent.
Wren's grandmother made lunch and did not mention the notes.
At four o'clock Mr Adeyemi shouted across the water.

It was the first shouting in three days and it sounded rusty and much too loud, and he asked whether anybody had a thermometer, and somebody at number four shouted back that they did, and there followed a slow, difficult, forty-minute business involving a bucket, a length of washing line, and a great deal of instruction being shouted from three directions at once.
The thermometer arrived at Mrs Pryor's dry.

The whole thing had taken forty minutes and twelve people, and it had worked, and Wren stood at the landing window watching the bucket go back across the brown water on the line and understood something that she did not have the words for until much later.
The heron had not been doing something they could not do.
It had been doing something they had stopped doing.
She said so to her grandmother, more or less, in worse words, over tea.
Her grandmother listened to the end without interrupting, which she always did, and then said: "It came the year I was nine, as well.
Four days that time.
And when it stopped coming, the lane put a line across from the Hendersons' gatepost to ours and left it up for six years." She stirred her tea.
"It was still up when your mother was born.
Somebody took it down in the end because it had gone green." "Why did it stop?" "I've had sixty years to think about that and I've only got the one answer, and you won't like it." Wren waited.
"Because we were managing," her grandmother said.
The heron came back on the eighth night.

Wren saw it from the landing at about six in the morning, working its way along the roofline of the odd-numbered houses in the grey light, unhurried, exactly as before, collecting six wet notes that by then said things like *the line worked, use the line* and *Mrs Pryor is better* and, from number six, in a child's writing, *where did you go.* It took them all.
It did not, as far as anybody could tell, bring anything back that morning.
And the line stayed up between the gateposts, because by then people had got used to that too.
The river left the way it had come — without apology, over four slow days.
First the fence posts came back, then the tops of the gates, then the gates.
The lane reappeared under a layer of silt the colour of milky tea, and it smelled of cold pennies and something older underneath.
There was a fish in the Hendersons' garden and nobody could agree on what to do about it.
Wren went up to the landing on the last morning, before school, in the grey part of the day when everything looks unfinished.
The heron was still there.
But it had stopped being clear.
It stood on the ridge of the roof opposite in exactly the place it had stood on the first morning, and the light did not go through it any more.
It was green at the edges and cloudy in the middle, the way glass is when the sea has finished with it.
There was nothing moving inside its chest.

She went across the lane in her wellies through six inches of silt and got the ladder from the Hendersons' shed, which was still facing the wrong way, and she climbed up, which she was not supposed to do, and she put her hand on it.
It was cold, and it was heavier than it looked, and it did not move.
She carried it down under one arm with the ladder wobbling and set it on the corner fence post at the end of the lane, where the light comes along the road in the late afternoon.
It is still there.
Somebody put a stone slab under it eventually so it would not sink when the ground softened.
People walking past assume it is an ornament, and it is, now, but it is also a heron.
The notes went into a biscuit tin under Wren's bed.
There were thirty-one of them, from twelve different houses, including one that said *there is honey at number four* and one that just said *yes*.
Her grandmother said they ought to keep the tin somewhere sensible.
They kept it under the bed.
The attic light had been left on for as long as anyone could remember, and nobody could say who had done it.
It bothered Ines more than it bothered anybody else.
She had asked her uncle about it twice.
The first time he had said it was cheaper than arguing about it, which was not an answer.
The second time he had said that some things in a house are older than the people in it, which was less of an answer than the first one but sounded more like one.
She could see it at night from the garden — a thin orange line around the edge of the trapdoor, hanging in the dark of the landing ceiling like a picture of a door rather than a door.
She went up on the first warm night of the year, because the trapdoor had begun to hum.
That was new.
It was a low sound, not electrical, more like the noise a bee makes inside a jam jar three rooms away.
It had started on the Tuesday and by the Friday she could feel it in the ladder rungs.
She waited until her uncle had gone out to lock the greenhouse, and then she went up.
The attic was full of moths.
Not fluttering.
Not knocking themselves stupid against the bulb, which is what moths do and the only thing Ines had ever seen them do.
These were resting.
Hundreds of them, folded flat against the rafters and the underside of the roof slates, wings closed, absolutely still, arranged the way pages are arranged in a book.
They were the colour of old paper — some almost white, some the yellow of a page that has been in a window, a few nearly brown.
They did not startle when her head came up through the hatch.
One near her hand adjusted itself very slightly, the way a person shifts in a chair.
She sat on the edge of the hatch with her legs down through it, because the floor did not look trustworthy, and she looked at the one nearest to her.
There was something on its wings.
Not a pattern.
She knew what moth patterns looked like: eyes and speckles and the little false faces.
This was a picture.
A very small one, painted in the way a stamp is printed, right across both wings so that the join ran through the middle of it.
It was a kitchen.
A yellow kitchen with a window over the sink and a chair pulled out from the table.
She looked at the next one.
A boat, on a grey sea, seen from behind.
She looked at the next one, and it was a face she almost knew, and then did not, and the almost stayed with her all the way down the ladder.
She went up again the next night, and the night after that.
By the fourth night she had worked out how to pick one up.
You do not catch a moth; you put your finger against the wall beside it and wait, and eventually it walks onto you, unhurried, like somebody stepping onto a bus.
The one that came onto her finger on the fourth night had a hallway painted across its wings.
A long hallway with a runner carpet, and at the end of it, a green door.
She held it under the bulb and looked at it for a long time.
The longer she looked, the more certain she became that she had walked down that hallway.
She knew what the light was like at the far end in the afternoon.
She knew the carpet had a worn patch two thirds of the way along and that you could feel it through socks.
And at exactly the same time, with exactly the same certainty, she knew that she had never been there in her life.
Her uncle came up the ladder behind her with two mugs of tea, which is a difficult thing to do and suggested practice.
He did not seem surprised by any of it.
He handed her a mug, sat down on an upturned crate that had clearly been sat on many times before, and looked at the moth on her finger.
"Green door," he said.
"That's a good one.
Somebody misses that." Ines said nothing, because she could not think of a question small enough to start with.
"People drop dreams," her uncle said.
"All the time.
The way you drop a glove out of a pocket — you don't feel it go, you just find later that you've only got the one.
Wake up too fast, somebody says your name, the alarm goes off in the wrong part of it.
And the dream falls out." He drank some tea.
"They have to go somewhere.
Everything has to go somewhere.

This house has been collecting them since before it was mine, and before it was my mother's, and I've never worked out why this house and not the one next door." "How many are there?" "I stopped counting in about nineteen ninety." Ines turned her hand slowly so the moth stayed level.

On the wall above her, a hundred pale wings held a hundred small pictures: a bicycle, a hospital corridor, a hillside with a wall across it, a wedding, a dog, a shop she was almost sure was the shop on Bridge Street but with different windows.
"Can they go back?" she said.
"Can you give one back to someone?" Her uncle looked at his tea for a while.
"That," he said, "is the difficult part."
The one she wanted was the face.
She had found it on the first night — third along the rafter, near the chimney breast — and she had gone back to it every night since, and every night the same thing happened.
She would look at it and think *oh, that's* — and then the name would not arrive.
It was a man.
Middle-aged, or getting there.
Dark hair going back at the front.
He was looking slightly to the left of whoever was dreaming him, and he was in the middle of saying something, and his eyebrows were up.
It was painted better than the others.
That was the strange part.
The kitchen and the boat and the green door were all painted the way a thing is painted from memory — the important bits sharp, everything else vague.

This one had a collar on his shirt with a button missing at the point, and a small scar through one eyebrow, and the sort of detail you only get when somebody has looked at a face for years and years and years.
She asked her uncle who it was.
He came up and looked at it for a while with his hands in his pockets and said he had no idea, and that he had been wondering about that one himself since about 2003.
She did the sensible thing, which took her three weeks.
She drew it — badly, then less badly, then on the fourth attempt well enough to be recognisable — and she carried the drawing round the town in her coat pocket and showed it to people.
The woman at the bakery said no.
The man at the bicycle shop said no, and then held the drawing at arm's length and said no again, more slowly.
The librarian said he looked like somebody's brother, which was not useful.
Father Costa said he looked like everybody's brother, which was less useful still.
A man at the bus stop said it was a very good drawing, which she appreciated but could not do anything with.
At the end of three weeks she had shown it to thirty-one people and none of them knew him.
She sat on the wall outside the chemist with the drawing on her knee and worked it out, and she did not enjoy working it out.
There were only two ways it went.
Either the person who had dropped that dream had moved away — in which case the moth would sit on that rafter until the house fell down.

Or the person who had dropped it was dead, and the dream had come loose the way the last of anything comes loose, and it had come up the hill and in under the slates and folded itself against a beam, and there was nobody left in the world who could be given it.
She went home and up the ladder and sat on the edge of the hatch for a long time.
Her uncle came up eventually with the tea.
He did not ask how it had gone; he had clearly worked out how it had gone from the fact that she was sitting in the dark.
"There are about four hundred like that," he said.
"That I know of.
Ones nobody claims.
They don't go anywhere.

They don't die, as far as I can tell — I've got one up there with a horse and cart on it and there hasn't been a cart on this hill since before the war." "So what are they for?" "They're not *for* anything," he said.
"That's the bit that took me longest.
I spent about fifteen years trying to make this place useful and I got nowhere, because I was asking the wrong question." He nodded up at the rafters.
"It's not a lost property office.
Nobody's coming to the desk.
It's just where they end up." Ines looked at the man with his eyebrows up, in the middle of saying something, to somebody who had loved him enough to keep the missing button.
"That's sad," she said.
"It is," her uncle agreed.
"But look at the state of him.
Somebody was extremely fond of that man.
That's still true.
It's true right now, on that rafter, whether or not anybody comes for it." He drank his tea.
"There are worse things to have a house full of."
It took most of the summer to work out, and the working out was not magical in the least.
It was mostly asking people awkward questions and being wrong.
The rules, as far as Ines ever established them, were these.
A moth would not go to just anyone.
You could carry one out in your cupped hands to a person and open your hands and it would sit there like a scrap of paper, entirely uninterested, and eventually walk back up your sleeve.
It had to be dusk.
Not dark, not evening — dusk, the twenty minutes when the streetlights are on but you can still see the colour of things.
And you had to be standing near where the person had been when they lost it.
That was the part that made it hard, because it meant working out who, which meant asking, and there is no good way to ask an adult whether they have recently mislaid a dream about a boat.
She got round it by asking about the pictures instead.

The woman at the bakery, when Ines described a grey sea seen from the back of a boat, stopped counting change and said, "My father had a boat like that," and then, "Why?" — and Ines said she had seen a painting, which was a lie, but only a small one.
She let the boat moth go outside the bakery at dusk on a Thursday.
It went in through the top window, which was open for the heat, and did not come out.
The man who fixed bicycles had lost the hallway with the green door.

She was almost sure before she asked him and completely sure afterwards, from the way he said "that was my grandmother's house" and then stopped talking and went back to truing the wheel he had been truing.
She let it go outside his shop the following evening.
He was still there, working late, and he did not see her do it.
She watched from across the road as the moth went in under the shutter.
He came out about a minute later and stood on the pavement, looking at nothing in particular, for quite a long time.
Then he went back in and got on with the wheel.
He never mentioned it to her, and she never mentioned it to him, and for about a year afterwards he did her brake cables for nothing and neither of them ever said why.
She did nineteen that summer.
Nineteen out of hundreds, and it took her from June to the middle of September, and she got four of them wrong and had to bring them home again.
At the end of it she went up the ladder one last night before school started, expecting — she was not sure what.
Some visible dent.
Some gap in the rafters where nineteen used to be.
The attic looked exactly the same.
"It always does," her uncle said, from the crate.

"That's not a reason not to." And he left the light on, the way it had always been left on, and they went down and shut the trapdoor, and the humming went on very quietly above them all night, the way it had for years, the way it presumably still does.
Spring was four weeks late and everyone in the valley had a theory.
Mr Varga at the garage said it was the jet stream, and said it in the tone of a man who had recently learned what a jet stream was.
The women who came up from Brod on the Thursday bus said it was because the winter had been mild and the year was making up for it.
Father Emil said it was not for us to know, which Tolek noticed was the answer Father Emil gave to almost everything, and which had the advantage of always being technically correct.
Tolek's mother said the weather owed nobody an explanation, and told him to bring the washing in.
But the almond tree by the church had put out buds in February and then thought better of it.
That was the part nobody had a theory for.
The buds had come, small and pink at the tips, in a warm week at the end of winter.
And then they had stopped.
They had not opened and they had not fallen.
They had simply shut, and gone hard, and stayed like that on the branches for nine weeks — hundreds of little closed fists, waiting.
Old trees do not do that.
Old trees commit.
And the snow on the high field was not melting.
It was not falling either.
That was the other thing.
There had been no new snow since the second week of March, and there had been sun, real sun, enough to warm the stones on the south wall.
But the white line across the top of the mountain had not moved down by so much as a metre.
It sat where it was, exactly where it was, with an edge as clean as a page.
Tolek walked up to it after school on a Tuesday, with his hands pulled inside his sleeves.
He was not being brave.
He wanted to know, and the wanting had got bigger than the not-wanting over about fourteen days, which is how most brave things actually happen.
At the edge of the snow he stopped and looked at the ground.
There were tracks going up.
They were enormous — deep, round, with the claw marks well out in front of the pad — and there were no tracks coming down.
Not old ones filled in with new snow, because there had been no new snow.
None at all.

He stood there for a while doing the arithmetic that everybody does at that moment, which is: *if it went up, and it has not come down, then it is up there.* Then he followed the tracks, because he was twelve, and because some questions will not wait until you are older.
The tracks went up through the thin birch and across the shoulder of the hill and stopped at a hollow under a leaning rock, and the bear was in it.
She was asleep.
Tolek's first thought, which he was not proud of afterwards, was that she was much too big.
Everything he had been told about bears had been told to him by people describing bears, and describing is not the same as seeing.
She filled the hollow the way water fills a cup.
His second thought was that he was not frightened, and that this was strange, and that he should probably examine it later when he was somewhere else.
The cold was coming off her.
He could see it.
That is the part he could never explain properly, not to his mother and not to anyone since.
You know how heat comes off a road in August — that shiver in the air, that wobble?
It was that, but backwards, and going down instead of up.
It poured off her shoulders and pooled in the hollow and ran out over the lip of it, and where it ran, frost stood up on the grass in little white fences.
She was breathing.
Very slowly.
He counted, and it was nine seconds in and thirteen out, which is slower than seemed reasonable for something that size.
There was snow in her fur.
Not on it — in it, down between the hairs, right against the skin, and it was not melting even there.
When he finally came close enough to look properly he could see individual flakes, whole and six-sided and perfect, months old, held there as if the calendar had not been told.
He sat down at what he judged to be a polite distance, which was about four metres, on a stone that turned out to be very cold.
And sitting there, in the quiet, with the frost fences growing at his feet, he understood the thing that had brought him up the mountain, and it arrived complete, without anybody telling him.
She was not causing the winter.
She was holding it.
Somebody had to carry the cold from one year to the next.
It could not simply stop; it had to be taken somewhere and kept until it was needed again.
And the carrying was heavy — you only had to look at her to see how heavy — and she had been carrying it since October and she had not been able to put it down.
He did not know why she could not put it down.
He thought about it a great deal and never worked it out.
Some things are heavy for reasons that are nobody's business.
He went down before dark.
The tracks he made going down were the only tracks going down.
He made the mistake of telling his brother.

Marek was fifteen and had recently become impossible in the specific way that fifteen-year-olds become impossible, which is that he had stopped being interested in anything and had started being interested in not being interested in things.
Tolek told him because he had to tell somebody.
He had been up the mountain three times by then and the knowledge had got too big to carry alone; it kept coming up in his throat at the dinner table.
Marek listened to the whole thing.
Then he said: "It's a bear." "I know it's a bear." "Bears sleep.
That's what they do.
It's the entire thing bears are known for." He was not being cruel.
That was somehow worse.
He was being reasonable, patiently, the way you are reasonable with somebody who is quite young.

"It'll wake up when it's hungry and go and eat something and you won't want to be sitting four metres away when it does." "The snow isn't melting round her." "The snow isn't melting because it's a north face and it's in shadow until half past two." Tolek had no answer to that, because it was true.
It was a north face and it was in shadow until half past two, and that fact had been sitting there the whole time being an excellent explanation for something that was not what was happening.
That is the trouble with a good reason.
It does not have to be the right one to be difficult to argue with.
Marek came up with him on the Saturday.
He came up in the way older brothers come, complaining about the walk and going too fast and stopping to wait with his hands on his hips.
At the edge of the snow he stopped complaining.

Tolek watched him look at the line — that clean straight edge running across the mountain like the top of a page — and then look down at the frost fences standing up in the grass, in April, at two in the afternoon, in the sun.
They went up to the hollow together and Marek looked at the bear for about ninety seconds and then turned round and went back down the mountain without saying anything at all.
He did not speak to Tolek for two days.

On the third day he came into the room where Tolek was doing his homework and stood in the doorway and said: "Don't tell Mum." "I wasn't going to." "Don't tell anybody." He was holding the door frame with one hand.
"You know what happens if you tell people.
Somebody rings the forestry office and they come up with a truck, and they'll be right to, because it's a bear and there's a school in the valley.
And they'll do it properly and humanely and everything and it will still be a truck coming up the mountain." Tolek had not thought that far.

He thought about it for a long time afterwards — that his brother, who was impossible, who had not been interested in anything for a year and a half, had gone up the mountain, looked at a sleeping animal for ninety seconds, and immediately understood the whole shape of the danger while Tolek was still working out how to describe the frost.
"Are you coming up again?" Marek asked.
"Yes." His brother nodded slowly, and looked at the floor, and said, "Take the red coat, not that one.
That one's too thin and Mum'll notice you shivering." And he went out and shut the door.
They never discussed it again.
Not that spring, not that summer, not in the thirteen years afterwards while their mother was alive, and not at the funeral, and not since.
But Marek asked him one thing, at the funeral, standing at the back with a paper cup of coffee, out of nowhere, after a silence of about four minutes.
"That thing on the mountain," he said.
"Did it ever wake up?" And Tolek said: "No.
Not while I was there." And Marek said, "Right," and they went back in.
He came back the next day.
And the day after that.
He did not do anything clever.
That is the part he told his own children, years later, when they asked, and they were always disappointed by it.
He did not sing to her.
He did not bring her anything, because what do you bring.
He did not try to wake her, because it seemed to him that waking somebody who is carrying something heavy is a good way to make them drop it on their foot.
He sat on the cold stone at four metres, and he stayed for an hour, and then he went home.
Sometimes he read out loud, because the silence up there had a quality that made him want to put something into it.
He read a book about a shipwreck, which he had read twice already, and he skipped the boring middle both times.

Once he told her, at length and with considerable feeling, about a disagreement he had had with his brother — a disagreement which had seemed enormous at eight in the morning and which had somehow got smaller and smaller as he described it, until by the end of the telling it had shrunk to roughly the size of a misunderstanding about a bicycle pump, which is what it had actually been all along.
He talked to her for fourteen days.
On the eleventh day the snow around the hollow had gone soft at the edges.
He noticed it on the way up: the clean line had lost its cleanness.
It had begun to fray.
On the twelfth day there was water running under the snow.

He could hear it before he could see it — a thin sound, very cold, like a wire being drawn — and when he knelt down and pushed the crust with his thumb it came away and there were threads of water underneath, going down the mountain in a hurry, as though they had been waiting a long time and had somewhere to be.
The bear did not wake while he was there.
Not once, in twelve days.
He went up on the thirteenth day and the hollow was empty.
It was warm.

That was the thing that stopped him at the edge of it — the hollow was warm, and it smelled of wet stone and crushed grass and, faintly, of animal, and there was a shallow dish pressed into the ground where something very large had lain for a very long time.
There were no tracks leading away.
He looked.
He looked for most of an hour, in widening circles, and the ground was soft enough that there should have been tracks, and there were none.
He went down the mountain with his coat over his arm because he did not need it.
In the valley the almond tree by the church had opened.
All of it.
Every bud on every branch, all at once, in a single afternoon, as though the tree had been standing there for nine weeks with its arms folded waiting for somebody to give it permission.

The petals were coming off it already in the warm air and going along the road in drifts, and two of the Sokol children were running through them, and the smell of it reached him before he got to the gate.
His mother was in the doorway with a basket on her hip.
"There you are," she said.
"Spring, at last.
About time." "Did you see the tree?" "I saw it.
Sixty years I've been looking at that tree." She shifted the basket.
"The weather owes nobody an explanation." Tolek considered telling her.
He thought about it the whole way across the yard, and he decided — for reasons he could not have given you at the time and could give you perfectly well now — that it was not his to tell.
"No," he agreed.
"It doesn't." And he went to wash his hands.
The hare kept an office in the root of a beech, which Marisol found by walking into it.

She had been going along the top edge of the wood where the bracken thins out, not paying attention, thinking about something else entirely, and her boot went into a gap between two roots and stopped against something that was not earth.
It made a sound.
Wood on wood.
A small hollow knock, like knuckles on a door, which in a sense it was.
She got down on her knees and put her eye to the gap.
There was a room in there.
It was about the size of a bread oven and it had been fitted out with considerable care.
There was a desk made from a slate roof tile balanced on two flints.
There was a lamp that was not a lamp but a piece of foxfire in a nutshell, giving off that cold green light that rotten wood gives off in autumn.
And there were papers — a great many papers, rolled and stacked in the corners and held down against the draught with acorns.
The hare was at the desk, drawing.
It was an ordinary hare in every respect that Marisol could see.
Brown, long, with the black tips on the ears and the eye set high in the side of the head the way a hare's eye is, so that it can see behind itself without turning.
It was holding something in one forepaw and moving it across the paper in short strokes.
It went on drawing for some time after she put her eye to the gap.
Then it said, without looking up: "You're standing in the light." Marisol moved.
"Thank you." She waited.
It kept drawing.
She was aware that she was kneeling in wet bracken and that her knees were getting cold and that she did not want to be anywhere else.
Eventually the hare put the stylus down and turned the paper round with both paws so that she could see it through the gap.
It was a map of her wood.
She knew it immediately, and it was a good map.
There was the stream, with the two kinks in it near the bottom where it goes round the boulder.
There was the fallen oak that had come down in the storm three winters ago and had been lying across the bottom path ever since, forcing everyone into a detour through the nettles.
There was the fence, and the place where the fence gives up and just stops, halfway along, for no reason anyone has ever explained.
And there was a path.
It ran from the stile at the bottom corner, up along the flank of the hill, and over the top to the ridge.
It was drawn firmly, as a path is drawn, with a dashed line and a little scale bar beside it: eight hundred metres.
Marisol had lived at the bottom of that wood her whole life.
"There isn't a path there," she said.
"No," the hare agreed.
"I've been here twelve years.
There's no path there.
There's bracken up to here and then a bank and then more bracken." "Yes," said the hare.
"It's a matter of timing."
It explained with the particular patience of somebody who has explained the same thing many times and has stopped being irritated by it, which Marisol thought was probably a considerable achievement.
Most mapmakers, it said, draw what is there.
This is useful.
Nobody is saying it is not useful.
If you want to know where the stream is, a map of where the stream is will tell you where the stream is, and you can go and put your hand in it and confirm the matter.
But it is not interesting.

"I draw," said the hare, "what is going to be there." Marisol asked how that was possible, which she was slightly ashamed of afterwards, because it was the obvious question and the hare had clearly been asked it a great many times.
The answer was not what she expected.
"Paths are not built," it said.
"Almost nobody understands this.
People think somebody decides — a council, a landowner, somebody with a plan — and then men come with gravel.
That is a road.
A road is built.
A path is worn." It got down off the stack of paper it had been sitting on and went to the wall of the office, where a larger map was pinned up with thorns.
"Somebody goes first," it said.
"One person.
And they go through the wrong part of the bracken, at the wrong time of year, usually for a bad reason.
They have left something at the top.
They are avoiding somebody on the road.
They are twelve and they are in a temper.
The reason is nearly always small and nearly always private." "And then?" "And then the bracken is bent.
Only a little.

But the next person who comes along that way — and there is always a next person, that is the whole trick of it — the next person finds that going where the bracken is bent is very slightly easier than going where it is not.
And they are not deciding anything.
They are not thinking about it at all.
They are simply taking the easier of two options, which is what everything alive does, always." It turned round.
"Do that four hundred times and you have a path.
Do it four thousand times and somebody puts up a sign with the mileage on it and a little picture of a boot.
And by then everyone has completely forgotten that there was a first person, and that the first person went that way by mistake." Marisol sat back on her heels.
"So how do you know which way the first person will go?" There was a pause.
"I don't," said the hare.
"I guess." "You guess?" "I guess extremely well.
I have been doing it for a long time and I understand where people are likely to leave a jumper.
But it is a guess, and I have been wrong four hundred and six times, and I do not enjoy discussing it."
She should not have asked about the four hundred and six.
She knew it at the time.

The hare had said, very clearly, that it did not enjoy discussing them, and Marisol had heard that and had waited nearly a week, and then had asked anyway, because she was twelve and because a locked drawer is a locked drawer.
The hare did not refuse.

It went to the corner of the office where the oldest papers were — the ones gone soft and furred at the edges, held down with a flint instead of an acorn — and it pulled one out with its teeth and unrolled it across the slate with a paw at each corner.
"Nineteen forty-six," it said.
The map showed a stretch of country Marisol half recognised: the valley on the other side of the ridge, before the reservoir, when the reservoir was still a river and three farms.
And there was a path on it, drawn firmly, dashed, with a scale bar.
It went from a farm gate up over the shoulder of the hill to a chapel.
"That's a good path," said the hare.
"That is one of the best I ever did.
The gradient is right, it avoids the wet ground in February, it comes out at the chapel from the south so you get the light on the door.
A person walking that path would have enjoyed it every single time." "What happened?" "Nothing happened.
That is precisely the difficulty." It sat back.
"The first person did not go.
I had them — a woman at the farm, thirty-one, walked to the chapel on a Sunday and back, every week, and the road went round the long way and she resented it.
Everything was in place.
She had the reason and the temper and the legs." The hare's ears went flat and then came up again.
"And in the March her sister got ill in Tarragona, and she went down to nurse her, and she did not come back.
That is all.
There is no more to it than that." Marisol looked at the dashed line going up over the shoulder of the hill to the chapel with the light on the door.
"Couldn't somebody else have gone?" "Somebody else did not have her reason.
That is what people never understand about this." It turned the map round to look at it the right way up, which Marisol thought it probably did not need to do.
"A path is not a good idea.
A path is one person's bad afternoon, repeated by strangers who never knew about the afternoon.
If you take away the afternoon, there is nothing left to repeat." "So it's just — gone." "It is under a dozen metres of water now, along with the farm and the chapel.
But it was gone long before the reservoir.
It was gone in the March of nineteen forty-six." It rolled the map up.
"I keep them because somebody should.
That is the entire reason and I have stopped looking for a better one." Marisol sat back on her heels in the wet bracken.
"Doesn't that make you want to stop?" The hare put the flint back on the roll.
"Four hundred and six," it said.
"In two hundred and twelve years.
Which means the other ones are out there being walked on, right now, this minute, by people who think the ground has always been like that." It went back to the desk.
"You are standing in the light again." She moved.
She thought about that conversation for a long time afterwards, and the part she came back to was not the woman who went to Tarragona.
It was the arithmetic.
Two hundred and twelve years, and it had counted the failures precisely and had not, as far as she could tell, counted the others at all.
She walked it that afternoon.
Stile to ridge, the way the map had it, and it was awful.
The bracken came up past her shoulders in the middle stretch and it did not want her there.
It closed behind her.
It got down her collar.

There was a bank two thirds of the way up that was not marked on the map at all and that she had to go up on her hands, and there was a wet patch in a dip near the middle where her boot went in to the ankle and came out with a noise like a kiss.
It took her an hour and ten minutes.
The bottom path takes twenty.
She did it again on the Thursday, because she had left her jumper at the top.
That was all.
That was the entire reason.

She was cross about the jumper and she went back up the way she knew rather than the way that was sensible, and the second time it took fifty minutes because the bracken in the middle stretch was already bent.
In August her cousins came from the coast, three of them, and she took them up that way because she said it was the fastest route to the view.
That was a lie.
She knew it was a lie when she said it.
She has never entirely worked out why she said it — some part of her wanted them to go that way, and the reason was small and private, exactly as the hare had said it would be.
By the following spring there was a line of flattened green from the stile to the ridge, visible from the road if you knew to look.
By the spring after that there was bare earth showing in it in three places.
The year after that somebody put a plank across the wet part near the middle.
Nobody knows who.
Marisol asked four people and they all assumed it had been there for years.
She is grown up now, and she went back once, in her thirties, on a cold bright day in February when the bracken was down and everything was visible.
The path is a path.
It has a sign at the bottom, on the stile, a small green one with the mileage and a little picture of a boot.
It says 800m, which she thought was a nice touch, or would have been if anyone else had been there to say it to.
She went along the top edge of the wood afterwards, where the bracken thins, and she looked for a long time for a beech with a gap between two roots.
She found several beeches.
She found several gaps.
She was not, in the end, entirely surprised, and she did not stay long, because the light was going and she had a train.
The kite was good.
That was the frustrating part.
If the kite had been bad, Dai would have known what to do.
He would have taken it apart and started again and the whole thing would have been simple.
But it was good, and he knew it was good, and it still would not fly.
He had made it in April from his father's instructions, which were written on the back of an envelope in his father's small square handwriting and which had been in the kitchen drawer for six years.
The spars were bamboo out of the old window blind that had been in the shed since before they moved in.
The sail was paper the colour of weak tea, glued along the folds and then glued again where the first glue had gone brittle.
The bridle knots were the ones on the envelope, tied four times each until he got them right.
Every measurement was correct.
He had checked them against the envelope twice and against a metre rule once.
It went up eight feet and came down like a dropped coat.
It did it thirteen times.
Not a spin, not a dive — nothing dramatic enough to be interesting.
It went up, it hesitated, the nose came round, and it settled onto the grass with a small papery sound that Dai came to hate more than he had ever hated a sound.
The crows on the telephone wire watched all six.
There were seven of them.
He noticed the number on about the fourth attempt, because they were in a row and evenly spaced, which crows are not usually, and because they had not moved.
Crows on a wire shuffle.
They open a wing and shut it.
They shout at each other.
They leave and come back.
These sat.
They watched the way a builder watches somebody else's wall — not unkindly, but with a professional attention that made Dai's ears go hot.
On the twelfth attempt, when the kite came down again in exactly the same way, the smallest of them made a sound.
It was not a caw.
It was short and flat and came out of the side of its beak, and Dai understood it immediately and completely, with no evidence whatsoever, to be a criticism of his tail.

He stood in the middle of the field with the string in his hand and looked up at the wire and said, out loud, to seven birds: "It's the length on the envelope." The smallest one turned its head so that one eye was pointing at him, and said nothing at all, which was somehow much worse.
He lengthened the tail that evening.

He did it in the kitchen with the envelope in front of him, feeling as though he were doing something slightly disloyal, and he added forty centimetres of torn sheet in bows, and he went out again the next day.
It went up thirty feet and stalled.
Thirty feet is better than eight.
Thirty feet is a real height; at thirty feet the kite was above the hedge and you had to tip your head back.
But it hung there and would not go higher and then it came down, tiredly, the way a thing comes down when it has been trying.
The crows watched.
The small one said nothing.

He lengthened it again — another sixty, which made the tail longer than the kite by a distance he found embarrassing — and this time when he got to the field the small crow made no sound at all, which he decided, after some thought, to take as approval.
The trouble that afternoon was the wind.
It was the kind that arrives in gusts and then apologises.

It would come across the field in a rush and flatten the grass in a moving line and the kite would leap, and then it would go, and there would be nothing at all for five or twelve seconds, and the kite would find itself standing on nothing.
That is not a thing you can fix with a tail.
Dai ran with it.
He ran the length of the field four times, which is what you do, and which never works as well as it does in your head.
By the fourth run the string had cut a line across his fingers and he was breathing in a way that would have embarrassed him if there had been anyone there.
There was, of course.
There were seven of them.
They came off the wire together.
Not in a scatter.
That was the thing he remembered longest — that they did not burst upward the way birds do when something startles them, all in different directions at once.
They dropped off the wire in order, from the left, at intervals, like a sentence being read.
They came out across the field low and fast and rose under the kite, and they took the line.
Seven crows, at seven points along the string, each one closing its feet on it and beating steadily.
They did not go to the kite.
They went to the *string*, spaced along it like beads, and they held the whole length of it up out of the dead air.
And they did not lift the kite.
He was certain of this afterwards and he was certain of it at the time.
They were not carrying it.
They were showing it where the wind was — holding the line at the height where the moving air was, so that the kite could find it and lean on it.
It found it.
The kite went up so fast that the string burned through his fingers before he thought to let it.

It went past the chimneys and past the church weathervane and kept going, and became a small brown shape against a very large white sky, and the crows fell away from the line one at a time and went back to the wire and sat down in a row.
Dai stood in the middle of the field with both arms shaking and the whole sky on the end of a piece of string.
He asked his mother about the envelope that night.

He had been holding the question for a week and he asked it badly, over the washing up, in the way you ask a thing you have rehearsed too much: "Did Dad fly kites on the field, or somewhere else?" She did not answer straight away.
She finished the pan she was doing.
"The field," she said.
"Every Sunday for about two years.
He was insufferable about it." "Was he any good?" "He was terrible." She put the pan on the rack.
"He was terrible for a very long time and then he was suddenly extremely good, and he could never explain what had changed, and it drove him mad.

He used to say he'd had help." She said this lightly, and then, hearing herself, more carefully: "Why?" "No reason." She looked at him for slightly too long and then let it go, which he was grateful for.
He went out to the shed afterwards and got the envelope out of his coat and read it again under the light, and this time he read it properly instead of reading it for measurements.
The instructions were in his father's small square handwriting, and they were exactly what he had thought they were: spar lengths, bridle knots, the angle of the bow, the weight of paper.
Numbers, mostly.
But at the bottom, under the last line, in the same hand but written faster, at a slight angle, as though added later and in a hurry, there was this: *Tail is longer than the envelope says.
Trust the wire.* Dai stood in the shed with the door open and the moths coming in and read it five or twelve times.
*Trust the wire.* He went out to the field the next afternoon at the same hour and they were there, all seven, evenly spaced, doing nothing.
He stood underneath them with his hands in his pockets and looked up, and one by one they looked back at him with one eye each, which is how crows look at anything they are taking seriously.
"He was my dad," he said.
Nothing at all happened.
A car went past on the top road.
The smallest one shifted its feet on the wire and settled again.
He had not expected anything to happen.
He had expected exactly this.

And yet he stood there for a good while feeling foolish and then, gradually, less foolish, because the thing he had actually come to find out had already been answered before he opened his mouth — they were still here.

Whoever they were and whatever they did, they had been on that wire for at least six years and probably a great deal longer, doing this, for whoever turned up on the field with a bad kite and a stubborn streak.
"He said you helped him," Dai said.
The smallest one made the short flat sound out of the side of its beak.
It was not, this time, a criticism of anything.
He was almost sure of that.
It was the sound you make when somebody says something obvious and you cannot be bothered to agree with it out loud.

He went home and put the envelope back in the kitchen drawer where it had lived for six years, and he did not tell his mother, and he has still not told her, although he thinks now that she probably knows, because she has never once asked him what happened to the ticket.
His grandmother had told him, once, that you could send a note up a kite string.

She had told him in the front room in the winter, when he was small enough to be on the floor, and she had described it exactly: you write it on a scrap, you make a ring of it round the string, and you let it go, and the wind walks it up.
All the way to the top.
She said her brother had done it in Aberdaron in about 1951 and that it had taken most of an afternoon.
He had never had a kite that stayed up long enough to try.
He had the pen in his pocket already, which tells you something about what he had been hoping for.
He wrote it on the back of a bus ticket, holding the string under his arm, with the paper against his knee.
It was not a wish.
He wants that understood, because people always assume it was a wish, and there is something a bit cheap about a wish.
It was four words about his grandmother.
They are his, and he has never told anyone what they were, including the two people who have asked properly.
He curled the ticket into a ring and hooked it over the string and let go.
It went up in little hops.
That was the part nobody had described to him.
It did not travel smoothly; it caught, and stuck, and shivered, and then a gust would come along the line and it would run four or five metres and catch again.
He stood with his head back and his neck aching and watched a bus ticket climb a piece of string for thirteen minutes.
He lost sight of it twice and found it again both times.
When it reached the kite — when it finally got up to where the string met the bridle, so far away that it was only a change in the shape of the thing — the crows let go.
All seven, at once, from the wire, and they did not fly.
They simply dropped forward off the line and opened out and were gone in seven directions, low, over the hedge and the church and the allotments.
And the kite went on flying.
For about four seconds, with nothing holding the line and nobody pulling, in air that had gone completely still, the kite stayed exactly where it was.
Then it came down.

It came down slowly and in a long slant, across the field, over the wall, into the long grass by the water trough where the nettles are, and Dai walked the whole length of the field to get it with the slack string looping along the ground behind him.
It was not damaged.
One spar had come out of its pocket, which took a minute to fix.
The ticket was gone.
He looked for it.
He looked properly, for about half an hour, on his hands and knees in the long grass, and it was not there, and the string was unbroken from his hand to the bridle with nothing on it.
He flew that kite for four more summers.
It is in his loft now, in a bag, with the envelope.
He never sent another one.
Under the pier the water went black at two metres, and everyone in the town agreed that this was simply how it was.
They had reasons, and the reasons were good.
The pier had been built on the silt side of the bay, and silt comes up when the tide turns, and where silt hangs in the water the light does not get through.
Any of the fishermen would tell you this.
Nuria's father had told her, twice, in the voice adults use when they are explaining something for the last time.
Nuria did not disagree with the reason.
She disagreed with the tone.
She was of the opinion — and she held this opinion at fourteen and holds it still — that a thing being always true is not the same as a thing being explained.
The water had gone black under the pier for as long as anyone remembered.
That was a fact.
It did not stop being a question just because everybody had got used to it.
So she lay on the boards at low tide with her face in the gap between two planks.
This was not comfortable.
The planks were rough and salted and there was a splinter situation on the left one that she learned about the hard way.
But if you got your eye right down into the gap and let it adjust — five minutes, more on a bright day — the dark under there stopped being a flat black surface and became a *space*.
You could see the near pillar going down.
You could see the crust of barnacles and, below that, the green weed lying along the current all in one direction like brushed hair.
And then, about two metres down, everything stopped, and there was nothing, and the nothing had no bottom to it.
She saw the light for the first time in April.
She assumed, immediately and sensibly, that it was a reflection.
Something behind her — a car windscreen up on the front, a window, the sun off somebody's phone.
She turned round to check.
Behind her was the beach, and the beach was empty, and beyond the beach was the ice cream shop, which was shut and had been shut since October and had a board across the window.
She turned back and it was gone.
The second time was three weeks later, in May, on a flat grey afternoon with no sun at all to reflect off anything.
That time she did not turn round.
It was small.
It was warm — properly warm, the orange of a lit room seen from a garden, not the blue-white of anything electric.
And it was moving.
That was what settled it for her.
Reflections do not move like that.
Reflections slide when you move, or they stay put, or they shiver with the water.
This went sideways, behind the second pillar, paused, and came back, and then went down and away until it was the size of a full stop and then was not there.
It was moving with purpose.

Nuria lay on the boards with her cheek on the wood for a long time after it had gone, working out what she was going to do about it, and knowing, in the way you sometimes know, that she had already decided.
Between the second time she saw the light and the Sunday it came up, there were six weeks.
Nobody ever believes this part.
When she tells it, people want the light and then the otter, one after the other, the way it goes in a story.
But there were six weeks, and they were mostly boring, and she has come to think that the six weeks were the actual point.
She learned the tides first.

She got the table from the harbourmaster's board and copied it into the back of her maths book, and then she discovered that a printed tide table tells you when the water is high and low and tells you nothing whatsoever about when the silt lifts, which is the thing that actually matters.
So she watched instead.
She sat on the steps at different hours with a notebook and wrote down, in a column, what she could see and how far down she could see it.
*Tues 4pm — nothing, brown.
Weds 7am — two pillars, weed moving.
Weds 4pm — nothing.

Thurs 7am — two pillars.* It took her nine days to see it, which she was annoyed about afterwards, because it is obvious: mornings were clear and afternoons were not, and it had nothing to do with the tide at all.
It was the boats.
The bay had six working boats and they all went out and came back through the same channel, and they stirred the bottom, and the silt took about six hours to lie down again.
Nobody had told her that.

She is fairly sure that every fisherman in the town knew it, in the way you know the shape of your own kitchen, and that not one of them had ever said it out loud, because why would you say a thing everybody knows.
Then she learned the hours.
Sunday between one and two was the only window when the front was empty *and* the water was still.
She got there by elimination and a certain amount of lying to her mother about where she was going.
And then she waited.
That was the six weeks.
Nine days of the notebook, and then five Sundays of sitting on cold steps with her feet in the water from one until two, and nothing, and nothing, and nothing, and once a plastic bottle, and nothing.
She thought about giving up on the fourth Sunday.
She wants that on the record.

She sat there in the wind with her jeans wet to the knee and thought, with total clarity, *this is stupid and I have made it up and I am going to keep coming here until September and nothing is going to happen.* She came back on the fifth.

Her father found the notebook once, years later, doing something else entirely, and read the tide column all the way through without comment and then said, "You worked out the boats." "It took nine days." "It took me until I was twenty," he said, "and somebody had to tell me." That is the only compliment she ever got out of him about the whole business, and she has decided it was a large one.
It surfaced near the third pillar on a Sunday.
She had been coming down every day for six weeks by then and she had worked out the hours.
Sunday between one and two is when the town is at lunch, when the front is empty and the beach belongs to nobody and even the gulls have gone up to the car park where the bins are.
She was sitting on the steps with her feet in the water when it came up.
There was no drama about it.
The water opened and closed and there was a head, round and slick and dark, with the water beading and running off it, and two eyes set close together looking at her from about four metres away.
An otter.
From the neck back, an entirely ordinary otter — she could see the shape of it under the water, the flat tail, the way it hung upright with its paws tucked, the way they do.
In its front paws it held a lamp.
It was about the size of a jam jar and it was made of something that was not glass, or was glass but very old glass, thick and slightly green and full of tiny bubbles like the good marbles.
The light inside it was not a flame.
It did not flicker.
It was slower than a flame — it moved, but the way honey moves, and it was the colour of the inside of a peach.
Water ran off it and the light did not care.
The otter looked at her.
It looked at her for a long time, and Nuria understood, with complete clarity, that she was being decided about.
She sat very still on the steps with her feet in the cold and did not say anything, because whatever she said was going to be the wrong thing.
Then it went under.
It did not go away.
It went down about a metre and stopped, and hung there in the green murk with the lamp held out in front of it in both paws, and waited.
She could see it perfectly.
That was the worst part.
It was a metre down and it was looking up at her and it was *plainly waiting*, and there was nothing ambiguous about it at all.
Nuria was not a strong swimmer.
This is a fact she has never dressed up.

She could swim — she had done her badges at the pool in Torreblanca like everyone else — but she was not strong, and the water under the pier was cold in a way that pool water never is, and it was the last week of May.
She went in anyway.
She has thought about that afternoon many times since, and she thinks about it with an uncomfortable mixture of pride and alarm, because both are correct.
It was the bravest thing she has ever done and it was also, by any reasonable measure, extremely stupid, and she has never worked out how to hold both of those at once.
She has stopped trying.
There were steps.
That is the whole of it, and it was enough.

She followed the lamp down along the third pillar with her ears aching and her eyes stinging, and the light went ahead of her into the dark, and about four metres down the silt came up out of the murk to meet her and it was not silt.
It was stone.
A flight of stone steps, wide ones, going down and away from her at a shallow angle.
Nine of them, or ten — she counted nine on the way down and ten on the way up and has never resolved this.
They were worn in the middle.
That was what she understood immediately, and it was the thing that went through her properly, colder than the water.
Steps worn by water wear at the edges; water takes the corners off.

These were worn in a dish in the centre of each tread, deepest in the middle, exactly the way the steps of the church on the hill are worn, exactly the way any step is worn by five hundred years of feet going up and down in the middle where feet go.
At the bottom the steps stopped at a wall.
It had been a doorway.
The arch was still there, filled in with different stone, rougher, done in a hurry by somebody who wanted it shut.
Over the arch there was a carving, and the otter went up close to it and held the lamp against it so that the light came across it sideways and she could see it.
It was a boat.
A small one, with a high curved bow, and something above it that might have been a star or might have been a bird and that she could not make out because her chest had begun to insist.
She went up.
She came out under the pier making a noise she was not proud of, and got to the steps, and sat on them shaking for about a quarter of an hour before she could be trusted to walk.
She told her father that evening.
He listened all the way through, which she had not expected, and did not laugh, which she had expected even less.
When she got to the steps he put his cup down.
"The town was further out," he said.
"Everybody knows that.
Before the sea came in.
There are maps of it in the museum in Cadaqués — my father took me.

Half of it's under the bay." "You knew?" "Everybody knows, Nuria." And she said the thing that she had been carrying up from the water all afternoon without knowing she was carrying it: "Everybody knowing a thing is not the same as anybody having seen it." Her father sat with that for a moment.
He was a fisherman's son and a practical man and he was not in the habit of losing arguments to eleven-year-olds, and Nuria watched him decide, quite visibly, not to win this one.
"No," he said.
"It isn't." Then he asked her not to swim under the pier alone again.
She agreed to the part about alone.
The boar came through the hedge at the same place every night, and there was no place in the hedge.
Sabela had checked.

She had checked in daylight with her hands, working along the bottom of it from the gatepost to the corner, pushing her arm in up to the shoulder where the blackthorn allowed and taking it out again scratched.
The hedge at that point was two hundred years of blackthorn grown into itself, laid twice by somebody who knew how, and packed at the base with bramble that would have stopped a dog.
At about ten past nine, most nights, the boar came through it as though it were a doorway.
She had seen him first in April, from the bathroom window, and had assumed he had come round the end.
In May she watched properly, with the light off, and he did not come round the end.

He came out of the hedge at the third fence post, walked diagonally across the top of the vegetable garden without touching a single thing in it, went along the wall, and left through the far hedge at a point where there was also no gap.
He was enormous and he was old.
The bristles along his back had gone grey at the tips and there was a notch out of his left ear the size of a coin.
He never hurried and he never looked at the house.
What bothered her was the diagonal.
If you are an animal crossing a garden, you cross it.
You go where it is easy and you leave where you can.
He did not do that.

He walked a line — a specific line, the same line, so exactly the same that by June there was a faint pale track worn across the top bed where nothing would grow — and the line did not correspond to anything.
It went past the shed at a distance of about a metre and a half.
It went between the two apple trees and not around them.
It crossed the wall at a place where the wall was highest, and he went over it there, heavily, when there was a low bit twelve metres to the left.
Sabela was eleven and she was extremely interested in things that did not make sense, which her mother described as a phase and her grandfather described, more accurately, as a personality.
The interest had a shape, and the shape was always the same.
She did not want an explanation.

She wanted the thing to go on being odd for as long as possible while she found out more about it, and she had learned by about nine that if you take a strange thing to an adult too early they hand you back an ordinary one and are pleased with themselves.
So she did not tell anybody about the boar for two months.
She started marking the line.
She put a stone at the fence post, a stone at the shed, a stone between the apple trees, a stone at the wall.
When she had four stones down she stood at the gatepost and looked along them, and they made a road.
Not a path.
A road: straight, purposeful, wide enough for a cart, going from somewhere behind the hedge to somewhere over the wall.
It went through the vegetable garden the way a road goes through a field, which is to say without any interest in the field at all.
She went in and asked her grandfather whether there had ever been a road across the top garden.
He was doing the crossword and he did not look up for a while.
Then he said: "Which way was it going?" Which was, she thought afterwards, an extraordinary way to answer a question about whether something exists.
He told her about the mill over three evenings, in pieces, in the order he felt like telling it, which was not the order it had happened.
There had been a mill up the valley.
It had ground for a dozen villages.

There had been a road to it — a proper one, stone-based, wide enough for two carts to pass at the wide places — and it had come down off the hill, through what was now their top garden, and out over the wall towards the ford.
The mill closed in 1888.

The road was formally stopped up in 1890, which is a phrase that means somebody wrote it down somewhere, and after that the hedges were planted across it and the fields were rearranged and within a generation there was no road and within two there was no memory of a road.

"So how do you know about it?" "Because my grandmother's grandmother carried flour along it," her grandfather said, "and she told my grandmother, and my grandmother told me, and I am telling you, and that is the entire mechanism.
There is nothing clever about it." Sabela followed the boar in July, on a warm night when it did not get properly dark until after a dozen.
She did not follow him closely.
She had been told about boars, at length, by three different adults, and she had believed all of them.
She went behind at about forty metres, in trainers, on grass, with a torch she did not turn on.
He went through the hedge.
She could not.

She had to go round by the gate and along the lane and back up the far side, which took her four minutes, and she was certain she had lost him, and when she came over the rise he was standing in the middle of the Oteros' hayfield waiting.
Not for her.
She wants to be clear about that; he never once acknowledged her in the whole business.
He was waiting the way a person waits at a level crossing, facing forward, for something to be over.
Then he walked on, and she followed, and this is where it got strange.
He walked across the hayfield in a line.
Through the crop, which was standing, which he did not eat.
Out through the far hedge, where there was — she checked afterwards, in daylight, with her hands — no gap.
Along the edge of a plantation of young pines that had been planted in 2004 and that he went through as though the trees were somewhere else.
Down a bank so steep that she had to sit and slide, at a point where the bank had clearly, once, been cut into steps.
By the time they came out at the river she had stopped being frightened and started being something else that she did not have a word for at eleven and has never quite found since.
She was walking on a road.
It was not there.
There was bramble and bracken and a wire fence and a plantation and somebody's hayfield.
But her feet knew, in the way your feet know a stair in the dark, that the ground she was putting them on had been made.
The mill was less than she expected and much more.
She had imagined a building.

What was there, at the bottom of the slope where the river turned, was a rectangle of walls about waist high, full of elder, with one gable end standing to about her shoulder and a doorway in it with the lintel still across the top.
The river went past it fast and shallow and busy, as though it had been let off.
The boar walked into the rectangle through the doorway.
That was the thing that undid her.
Not the road, not the hedges, not the walking through pines that were not there when the road was.
It was that he had the whole of a wall-less ruin available to him on three sides, and he went in through the door.
He stood in the middle of the floor for a while.
Sabela sat down on the wall about six metres away, because her legs had decided.
She had the sense, sitting there in the smell of elder and cold water at half past eleven at night, that she had understood something and would spend a while catching up to it.
He was not lost.
That was the first part.
Everybody who had ever half-seen him crossing a field at dusk had assumed he was wandering, because that is what a big animal in the wrong place looks like from a car.
He was not wandering.
He was commuting.
And the second part, which took her longer, and which she only got hold of properly on the walk home in the dark: the road was still there.
It had never gone anywhere.
Roads are not made of the surface; the surface is just the part people maintain.
The cut into the bank was still cut.
The gradient was still graded.

Somebody in about 1740 had chosen that line down that hill because it was the line that worked, and the choosing was still true, and the hedges and the pine plantation and the wire fence were all things that had been laid on top of a fact.
The boar was not remembering the road.
The boar was just using it, the way you use a thing that is there, and everybody else had stopped being able to see it.
She got home at ten past one.
Her grandfather was in the kitchen with the light on, not making a fuss about it, doing the crossword he had already finished.
"Well?" he said.
"It goes in through the door," said Sabela.
Her grandfather put the pen down and looked at her for a moment, and then he laughed — one short surprised laugh, not at her — and he said, "Does it.
Does it now."
The archive in the town was open on Tuesdays and Thursdays between ten and one, which she found out by walking there four times.
The woman behind the desk was called Dona Amparo and was not, at first, encouraging.
She said the tithe maps were not for handling.
She said there was an index.
She said what exactly was it that Sabela wanted.
Sabela said she wanted to know if there had been a road across her garden before 1890.
Dona Amparo looked at her for a second and then got up and went into the back room without another word, and came out seven minutes later with a flat grey box.
The map was enormous and the colours in it were still bright.
It was dated 1871.
It took them a while to find the house, because the house was smaller on the map than Sabela expected and because the field boundaries were all wrong, which was the point.
Dona Amparo found it in the end by working out from the church.
And there it was.

A double line, ruled, going down off the hill from the top left, through the plot that was now their garden, over the corner of what was now the Oteros' hayfield, along the edge of nothing in particular, down the bank at the place with the steps, and along the river to a small black rectangle labelled, in beautiful sloping brown ink, *Muíño*.
Sabela put her finger about a centimetre above the paper and traced it, and it was the line.
Every turn.
The distance-and-a-half past where the shed would be built in 1963.
The high part of the wall, which on the map was not a wall at all but the road's own edge.
"You knew where to look," said Dona Amparo.
"I followed a pig," said Sabela.
There was a pause of the particular kind that happens when an adult decides how to take something.
"Mm," said Dona Amparo, and turned the map round so it faced Sabela properly, and left her with it for the best part of an hour.
The boar still comes through the hedge.

He is older now — the notch in his ear has a second notch above it and he takes the bank at the river in two goes instead of one — but he comes at about ten past nine, most nights, and he walks the diagonal.
Sabela has photocopies of the 1871 sheet on her wall and a stone at each of the four points, which her mother has twice tidied away and twice put back after being told.
She has not told anyone at school.
She has thought about it and decided that it does not come out well when you say it, and that this is fine, and that the road is not less there for nobody looking at it.
That is, after all, exactly the situation it has been in since 1890.
The rule about the seal was not written down anywhere and everybody in the bay knew it exactly.
You saw her once.
Not once a year, not once a season — once, in a life, and then never again, and the once was not at a time of your choosing.
And you did not go looking, because looking did not work, and everybody had an uncle who had spent a summer proving it.
Maeve knew the rule the way she knew that the harbour steps were slippy on the fourth one from the bottom.
She had never been told it in a single sitting.
It had assembled itself out of twelve years of overheard sentences at the co-op and on the pier and in the back of the van.
What she had noticed, and what nobody talked about, was the shape of when it happened.
Mr Nolan had seen her the winter he lost the *Bright Star*, three days before the insurance came through.
The Coyle brothers had both seen her, separately, in the same week, which was the week their mother was in Sligo hospital.
The woman who ran the chandlery had seen her on the morning she had decided to sell the chandlery, and had not sold it.
