Maeve made a list once, in a maths copybook, of the thirteen sightings she could get people to be specific about.
Then she wrote what had been going on for that person at the time, which took longer and involved asking questions that made two adults change the subject.
She looked at the list for a while.
Then she wrote, at the bottom, in small letters: *she comes when you are about to stop.* She did not show it to anyone.
It is still in the copybook and the copybook is still in the drawer under the stairs.
There were two things about the list that she did not write down.
The first was that in every single case, the person had carried on.
Mr Nolan had bought the second boat, which everyone agreed was a worse boat.
The Coyles had kept fishing through the whole of their mother's illness and after it.
The chandlery was still there, with the same woman in it, still complaining about the same suppliers.
That could have meant that the seal changed something.

It could also have meant that she only came to people who were going to carry on anyway, and that the ones who really stopped never saw her, and that nobody had ever thought to count those because a person who leaves a place stops appearing in the conversations of that place.
There was no list of the people who had gone.
There could not be.
That was the whole difficulty with it.
Maeve turned this over for most of a winter and could not find a way to test it, and it bothered her in a way she has never entirely got rid of.
The second thing was smaller and worse.
Her father had seen the seal.
Everybody knew he had.
It was said about him the way you say a man is left-handed — a settled fact, mentioned in passing, of no particular weight.
And in twelve years nobody had ever once said when.
Her father had seen the seal and would not discuss it.
This was unusual, because her father discussed everything.
He was a man who could take twenty minutes to explain a decision about diesel.

But if the seal came up — and it came up, because it came up in that bay the way the weather comes up — he would go quiet and busy, and find something that needed doing with his hands, and the conversation would move on without him.
Maeve worked out the year from other people.
It had been the year before she was born.

The boat he had then had gone on the rocks at the north end in a February gale, with nobody aboard, because he had not gone out that morning, and the not going out was the part nobody explained properly.
He had lost the boat and the gear and, for nine months, the licence.
She asked her grandmother about it once, in the kitchen, when they were podding peas.
Her grandmother did not look up.
"He'd made his mind up," she said.
"To do what?" "To go to Liverpool.
He had a cousin there and a job at the end of it.

He'd told me and he'd told your mother and he'd gone down to the pier that evening to look at the water and say goodbye to it, which is a thing men here do and pretend they don't." She pushed a pod open with her thumb.
"He was twenty-four and he'd been on the water since he was younger than you and there was nothing left in this bay for him.
That's not a mood, love.
That's a sum.
He did the sum and the sum came out Liverpool." She was quiet for a moment.
Peas went into the bowl.
"I'd have gone with him.
I want you to know that, because you'll hear it told differently by people who weren't in the house.
I had the case down off the wardrobe.
It was not a bad decision and I'll not sit at this table and have anyone call it one." "So what changed it?" "I've told you.
He went down to look at the water." "That's not an answer, Avoa." Her grandmother looked at her then, properly, over the bowl.
"No," she agreed.
"It isn't." "And he came back up an hour later and he never mentioned Liverpool again." Maeve waited.
"That's the whole of it, love.
I've never had another word out of him about that evening and I've stopped asking.
Some things a person needs to keep whole."
Her grandmother had thirteen creels in the water off the point, and had had them there for forty years, and in April she had a stroke.
It was a small one, as those things go.
She came home after nine days and she could walk with a stick and she was extremely irritated about the stick.
But her hands did not do what she asked them to any more, and there was no version of the situation in which she was going out to the point in a punt.
So Maeve went.

She was eleven, which everyone had opinions about, and the arrangement was that she went with her father when he was in and with Mr Nolan when he was not, and that she never, under any circumstances, went alone.
She hauled thirteen creels twice a week from April to July.
It was heavier than she had understood.
That was the thing that surprised her — not the cold and not the early mornings, which she had been warned about, but the sheer physical arithmetic of a creel full of water coming up over a gunwale.
She got better at it.
She got a system.
She got a place on her right palm that stopped being a blister and started being something else.
The system was this.
You came at the creel from downtide, so the punt held still against the rope instead of swinging off it.
You took the buoy with the hook and never with your hand, because your hand would be wet and cold and would not close properly by the fourth one.

You brought the creel up in three pulls with a rest between, and on the rest you put your forearm along the gunwale and let the wood take the weight instead of your back — which her grandmother had taught her without a single word, by putting one hand on her shoulder and pressing down until Maeve moved her arm to the right place herself.
And you did not look into the creel until it was aboard.
That was the important one.
Looking early made you hurry, and hurrying was how a rope went over the side, and a rope over the side in April water was how a girl of eleven became a thing that happened in that bay.
Thirteen creels took about two and a half hours with Mr Nolan, who talked the entire time about a dispute over a mooring that had begun in 1998.
It took about ninety minutes with her father, who did not talk at all, and who watched her do the third pull on every single creel without ever once offering to take it.
Her grandmother asked about them every evening, in the same words, from the chair by the window.

*What were they like.* And Maeve would go through them in order — this one heavy, this one empty, weed on the north two, a crab in the fifth that was undersized and went back — and her grandmother would listen with her eyes shut and say *mm* in the places where *mm* went.
Sometimes she would say *that's the ground there* or *she'll fill next week*, and once she said *your grandfather lost that one twice*, about a creel that was in fact new.

That quarter of an hour was the part of the day that Maeve did not mind at all, and she understood at the time that she was going to remember it, which almost never happens while a thing is still going on.
And in the second week of July she decided she was going to stop.
She decided it on a Tuesday, rowing back in, with an empty box and a low sky and her hands hurting in a new way.
It was not dramatic.
She was not crying.

She had simply run the numbers, the way you do at eleven when nobody is watching, and the numbers said: her grandmother was not going to be able to do this again, and her father could not do this and his own boat, and Mr Nolan was seventy-one, and she could not do it alone for the rest of her life, and every week she kept it going was a week that made the ending harder for everybody.
The kindest thing, she thought, was to stop now while it was still her doing it.
She was going to say it that evening at the table.
She had the sentence ready.
She had been building it since the point.
She rowed in past the black buoy with the sentence in her mouth.
The seal came up six feet off the port bow and looked at her.
Maeve stopped rowing.
She was grey and she was enormous — much bigger than Maeve had pictured, and she had pictured her often — and she had a scar across the bridge of her nose that had gone pale.
The water ran off the top of her head.

She was low in the water, only the head and a little of the shoulder, and she was completely still, and she looked at Maeve with round black eyes that were not kind and not unkind and not anything, and were paying complete attention.
They stayed like that for a length of time that Maeve has never been able to estimate.
She has said thirty seconds.
She has said four minutes.
She does not know.
Nothing happened.
That is the part she has never been able to explain to anybody, including herself.
There was no sign.
Nothing was communicated.
The seal did not nod, or gesture, or swim in a meaningful direction, or do any of the things that would have made it a story with a shape.

She looked at Maeve, in the flat grey light, with the oars up and the water ticking under the hull, until Maeve understood that she was being looked at properly — the way almost nobody looks at an eleven year old — and then she went down without a splash and did not come up again.
Maeve sat in the punt for a while.
Then she rowed in, and tied up, and carried the empty box up the steps, and went home, and had her dinner, and did not say the sentence.
She has never worked out what happened.
She has considered every version of it.
That the seal comes to stop you.
That the seal comes because you are about to stop and the stopping is the thing that calls her, and she has no opinion about it whatsoever, and just comes to look, the way you look at a fire.
That there is no seal and there is only an ordinary grey seal in an ordinary bay and seven people over sixty years happening to be at the end of their rope on the day they saw her.
She thinks the last one is probably true and she does not think it makes any difference.

Because the thing that actually happened, the thing she can point to, was this: for four minutes on a Tuesday in July, at the exact moment when she had decided that what she was doing did not count, something came up out of the water and gave her its whole attention.
She kept the creels going until September, when the season ended, which was always when it was going to end.
Her grandmother died the following March.
The creels went to the Coyles, which is what her grandmother had arranged in February without telling anybody, because she was that sort of woman.
Maeve is twenty-six now and she has not seen the seal again, and she does not expect to, and she has never once gone looking.
She did tell her father, in the end.
Not that summer — years later, in the van, going to Sligo for something else.
He drove for about a mile without saying anything.
Then he said: "Where was she?" "Just off the black buoy." "Mm," her father said.
"That's where she was for me." And he put the radio on, and they went on to Sligo, and that is the only conversation the two of them have ever had about it.
Ada noticed it because of the wires.
There were four wires across the yard behind the flats, and everything sat on them.
Pigeons sat on them in a row like a badly made fence.
Starlings sat on them and shouted.
A collared dove sat on the middle one every afternoon in the same spot and did nothing whatsoever for an hour at a time, which Ada respected.
The swifts never sat on them.

They came in May and they were gone in August and for those three months they went over the yard at eleven o'clock at night still screaming, in loops, four and five together, at a speed that made the pigeons look like furniture.
And in all of it — she watched properly, from the fire escape, for two summers — not one of them ever landed on anything.
Not the wires.
Not the gutters.
Not the aerial, not the flat roof of the bin store, not the one tree.
She mentioned it to her mother, who said they must land somewhere, everything lands somewhere.
She mentioned it to her teacher, who said it was a good observation and moved on.
She mentioned it to Mr Iqbal on the ground floor, who had been a merchant seaman and now had a telescope pointed permanently at nothing in particular, and Mr Iqbal put down his tea and said, "Ah.
Well.
Now you've asked the right person the right question, which almost never happens, so I'm going to enjoy this."
What Mr Iqbal told her, over about six weeks, in the wrong order and with a great many diversions, was this.
A swift lands to nest.
That is the only reason.
It builds under an eave or in a gap in a wall, it raises its young, and then it goes, and it does not come down again until the next nest.
A young swift leaves the nest and goes into the air and *does not land at all* until it is two, or three, or in some cases four years old.
It flies to Africa and it flies back and it does it again, and in between it never once stops.
It feeds in the air.
It drinks in the air, off the surface of a lake, without stopping.
It gathers material for the nest out of the air — bits of seed-fluff and feather that happen to be up there — because it cannot pick anything off the ground.
And it sleeps in the air.
It goes up at dusk, very high, two thousand metres, and it sleeps up there in the dark going round and round, and it comes down in the morning.
"That's not true," said Ada.

"It's extremely true," said Mr Iqbal, "and it took people a very long time to believe it, and if you'd like I'll show you where to check, because you should never take a fact off an old man who is enjoying himself." She checked.
It was true.
It was true in a way that made her cross.
She had been alive for eleven years on a planet where this was going on, and nobody had mentioned it.
It was not a secret.
It was not even difficult.
It was in a library book on the second shelf of a public library in a town with a retail park in it, and every adult she had ever met had been walking around not saying anything about it.
She put this to Mr Iqbal, with some heat.
"Yes," he said, delighted.

"Now you have found the actual problem, and the actual problem is not swifts." "What is it, then?" "People are given a small number of facts at school and they assume, quite reasonably, that if there had been better ones, those would have been included." He picked his tea back up.
"Nobody hid this from you, Ada.
It is simply that the world is a great deal stranger than the timetable has room for.
Most people never find that out.

The ones who do generally find it out by becoming annoyed about a bird, or a rock, or a number, and it is always an accident, and it is always small." She sat on the fire escape that evening in the warm and did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what got her.
A swift that has not nested has not landed.

If a bird had hatched under an eave the year Ada was born, and had gone into the air that August, and had not yet nested — and some of them do not, for three or four years — then that bird had been flying, continuously, without ever once putting its feet on anything, for as long as Ada had been alive.
Every night she had ever slept, it had been awake or asleep in the air.
Every single thing she had ever done, it had been flying.
She tried to make the thought hold still and it would not.
Every meal.
Every argument.
The whole of Year Three.
The fortnight her mother spent in hospital and the fortnight after it.
The night the boiler went and they all slept in the front room.

Every one of those had happened inside a stretch of time in which something weighing about as much as a bar of chocolate had been continuously airborne, over nine countries and two seas, without once stopping.
She could not decide whether that made her feel small or whether it made her feel slightly accompanied, and after about a week she stopped trying to decide and let it be both.
It became, that summer, a slightly unreasonable interest.
Her mother's word for it was *fixation*, said fondly in June and less fondly by the third week of July.
Ada is prepared to admit this now.
She kept a notebook.
She wrote down times: first bird of the evening, last bird, direction of the loops.
She got a library book that was too old for her and read the parts she could.
She annoyed her mother by explaining swift digestion at dinner on four separate occasions.
The question that would not leave her alone was the sleeping.
She could accept the flying.
Flying is what wings are for.

But the idea that a creature could be asleep — properly asleep, off, gone — two kilometres up in the dark, and continue to fly, seemed to her to be a much bigger claim than anybody was treating it as.
She asked Mr Iqbal how it worked.
He was in the yard when she asked, in the deckchair he kept behind the bin store, with the telescope pointed at the same nothing as always.
"Nobody entirely knows," he said, with enormous satisfaction.
"The current thinking is that half the brain sleeps and the other half keeps an eye on things, and then they swap.
Dolphins do something similar.
But if you are asking me whether anyone has been up there at two in the morning and watched — no.
They have not.

There are radar traces and there is a French pilot in 1914 who flew into a lot of them at two thousand metres at night and never got over it, and that is roughly the state of human knowledge." "So it might be something else." "It might be anything at all," said Mr Iqbal.
"That is the good news." Ada started going out on the fire escape at eleven, which was permitted, and at two, which was not.
She thought about the French pilot for weeks.
She looked him up in the end, at the library, on a computer with a sticky keyboard.
There was not much.
A few lines, repeated in several places, all of them obviously copied from each other.
A reconnaissance flight at night in 1914.
Two thousand metres over the lines.
He had cut the engine to glide, and come down through an enormous number of birds, and in the silence he could hear them all round him, and they were not visible and were not disturbed by him.
What got her was the detail about cutting the engine.
He had not been looking for anything.

He had switched off for some ordinary practical reason, in a war, at night, and in the quiet that followed he had found out something true about the world that nobody on the ground knew — and then had had to land, and had had nobody to tell, and had written it down anyway.
She wrote *1914* on the inside cover of the notebook and did not explain it to anybody.
She never saw one at two.
Of course she didn't; they were two thousand metres up.
But she went out anyway and stood in the cold with her head back, and there was the orange sky over the retail park, and the aerial, and the one tree, and nothing.
And she knew that they were up there.
Directly up there.
Above the flats, above the retail park, above the whole ridiculous orange glow of it, going round in slow circles in the actual dark with half of themselves asleep.

She has said since that this was the first time in her life she understood that something can be completely true and completely invisible at the same time, and that the two facts have nothing to do with each other.
She tested the idea on other things for about a month, which is what you do when you are eleven and have got hold of a good one.
The water in the pipes in the wall of her bedroom, going somewhere, all night.
The tectonic plate under the retail park, moving at the speed a fingernail grows.
Whatever was in the sealed flat on the third floor that nobody had opened since Mrs Kaur died.
The fact that on the other side of the world it was Wednesday afternoon and a very large number of people were having an ordinary day she would never hear a single detail of.
Some of these worked better than others.
Mr Iqbal was given all of them and rated them.
In the third summer they came back on the eleventh of May, and on the fourteenth one of them landed.
Ada was on the fire escape.

It came in off the loop, fast and flat the way they do, and instead of pulling up it went straight at the wall of the flats — at the point where the render had come away above her bedroom window, leaving a gap about the width of two fingers — and folded, and went in.
She did not move for a long time.
There had been a swift nest above her bedroom window and she had not known, and the reason she had not known was that a swift going into a hole does not slow down first.
There is no landing.
There is a bird at forty miles an hour and then there is no bird.
She told Mr Iqbal the next morning and he came up the stairs, which he did not do, and stood in the yard with his head back for a quarter of an hour.
"Above the window," he said.
"Yes." "Above your window." "Yes." He put his hands in his pockets.
"You understand what that means," he said.
"That bird has been coming back to that hole every May since before that render came off, probably.
They use the same hole.
They use it for years.

Which means for the whole time you were lying in that bed noticing that they never land — that one was landing about a metre and a half above your head, six times a day, for three months a year." Ada thought about that for the rest of the summer and has thought about it, on and off, for twenty years since.
She is at university now, doing something entirely unrelated, and she goes home in May.
The render has still not been fixed.
She has asked, twice, in writing, that it not be fixed, and has had one letter back from the housing office that did not really engage with the question.
She sits on the fire escape at eleven at night when she is home, and the loops go over, and she cannot tell one from another and never could.

Somewhere in that noise is a bird that has not touched the ground since April, and will not until next April, and is going to sleep tonight two kilometres above the retail park with half its head switched off.
She finds that she thinks about it whenever she is having a difficult week.
Not as a comfort exactly.
More as a fact she likes having available: that while she is doing whatever she is doing, badly, in a small room, something is up there going round.
The street light outside number forty had been out since February and the council had a reference number for it.

Bruno knew the reference number by heart because his mother had said it into the phone thirteen times, and each time she had said it a little more slowly, and each time a different person had told her it was logged.
What the reference number meant, in practice, was that the last sixty metres of Rua da Cordoaria were dark.
It was not frightening in October.
In October you came up from the bus at half four and it was only just going.
By the end of November it was properly dark at five and the sixty metres had become a thing Bruno thought about on the bus, from about three stops out.
There was nothing in it.
He knew that.
He knew it the way you know things that make no difference at all: there was a wall on one side, and the back of the tile warehouse on the other, and a doorway, and the corner.
Nobody was in it.
Nothing had ever happened in it.
It was just dark, and dark that you walk into alone at eleven years old is a specific substance, heavier than the other kind.
He had worked several things out about it by the end of November.
The first was that running made it worse.
He had tried running in the first week and had arrived at the corner with his heart going and his bag banging against his hip and the very strong sense that he had confirmed something.
Walking was better.
Walking was a statement.
The second was that the doorway was the difficult part.
It was set back about a metre from the pavement, and it was the one place in the whole sixty metres where something could be that you would not see until you were level with it.
He had developed, without ever deciding to, a habit of walking on the far side of the road and turning his head into it at the last moment.
It took about half a second.
He did it every single evening for four months.
The third thing was that none of this was reasonable, and he knew it was not reasonable, and knowing made not the slightest difference.
He would like that on the record.
He was not a small child.
He had walked past that doorway in daylight perhaps four hundred times with no thought at all.
The knowing sat in one place and the walking happened somewhere else, and the two of them did not talk.
He saw the cat for the first time on a Thursday at the start of December.
He had come round the bend by the pharmacy and stopped, the way he had started stopping, to do the small private business of deciding to walk.
And there, at the far end, right at the corner where the light came back, something was sitting.
It was grey and it was ordinary and it was facing him.
He walked.
It stayed.

He got to about the halfway point and it stood up, unhurried, and turned, and walked round the corner ahead of him — not away, exactly, more at the pace of somebody who assumes you are coming — and when he came round the corner into the light it was sitting again, ten metres on, waiting.
He said, "Hello." It looked at him.
He put his hand out, in the way you do, and made the noise, and it stood up and walked off along the wall and was gone between two parked cars.
He mentioned it at school and discovered, over about a week, that this was not a new phenomenon and that everybody had a slightly different version of it.
Inês had one on the steps behind the market.
Hers was black and she called it Senhor and it had walked her up the steps every night in January when her father was working late.
Teodoro said his was ginger and lived by the football ground and only turned up when it was raining, which he had a theory about.

The twins from the year above said they had never seen a cat but that their mother had, when she was small, on the road out to the quarry, and that in her version it had come out from under a car and gone with her the whole way to the junction and had not been there when she turned round.
The only rule that was in every version, and Bruno checked, was this: it never came when you called it.
He collected twelve accounts by the end of January and wrote them in the back of his Portuguese copybook, under a heading he later scribbled out because it looked childish.
Grey, black, ginger, tabby, and one that Rita would not be moved on: white, with a grey face.
Different streets.
Different years.
The twins' mother's was from about 1994, which made it either a very old cat or, as Teodoro observed at some volume in the corridor, not one cat.
Nobody had ever touched one.
He checked that specifically, because he had put his hand out on the first night and had felt stupid about it for a week afterwards.
Nobody had.
They came to about two metres and stayed at two metres and were gone once you were in the light.
Nobody had ever seen one arrive, either.
That took him longer to notice, because it is a difficult thing to notice the absence of.
In all twelve accounts the cat was simply already there, sitting, at the far end, facing you.
Not walking up.
Not coming out from under something.
Sitting, at the place where the dark stopped, already looking at you before you looked at it.
You could stand at the top of the street at eight in the evening when you were perfectly fine and say *here, here, here* until you felt stupid, and nothing would happen.
Teodoro had tried it with food.
Inês had tried it for a week straight in February out of pure scientific curiosity and got nothing but a cold.
And then on a night when you were frightened, it would be there.
Bruno's grandmother, who was the only adult he told, listened all the way through with her hands in the sink and then said something he did not understand for about four years.
She said: "It isn't the cat that changes." He asked her what that was supposed to mean.
She dried a glass and put it on the rack and did not answer for long enough that he assumed she was not going to.
"When I was a girl," she said, "there was a woman on this street who could not go out after dark at all.
Not would not — could not.
Something had happened to her, before, somewhere else, and nobody in the street ever knew what, and it was not our business.
And for about twenty years, whenever she had to go anywhere in the evening, one of the men would happen to be standing at the top of the steps having a cigarette.
Different men.
Never the same one twice in a row.
Never arranged, as far as I could ever tell." "That's not the same thing." "No," his grandmother agreed.
"It's not." And she gave him the cloth to dry with, which was how conversations ended in that kitchen.
In March the days got longer and the sixty metres went back to being sixty metres.
Bruno noticed this only in the way you notice that a tooth has stopped hurting, which is to say, late, and by accident.
He was coming up from the bus on a Tuesday and he was thinking about a thing that had happened in maths, and he came round the bend by the pharmacy and did not stop.
He was most of the way down before he realised he had not looked at the corner.
He stopped then, in the middle of the dark bit, and turned round, and looked properly at where he had come from and where he was going, and there was nothing in either direction.
The tile warehouse.
The wall.
The doorway.
The bins.
The cat was not there.
He stood there for a while, and he felt — and he has never been able to make this sound sensible — a bit rejected.
He went back the next night on purpose.
He walked down the middle of the road slowly, looking at every part of it in turn: the wall, the back of the warehouse, the bins, the doorway.

He stood in the doorway for a full minute, which he had never once done in his life, and found that it was a doorway with a worn step and some leaves in the corner and a dead bolt painted over about nine times.
He said *here*, twice, quietly, feeling ridiculous.
There was a car somewhere up on the main road, and somebody's television through a window, and that was the entire contents of Rua da Cordoaria at ten past six on a Wednesday in March.
He tried again in April, with a piece of chouriço, which he is still embarrassed about.
He said, to the empty street, "I'm still here, you know." Nothing happened, which is what happens.
He went home and had his dinner and did not mention it, and it took him until about April to work out that the cat had not stopped coming.
He had stopped needing it.
Those were two entirely different events that had looked, from inside, like the same one.
The following winter the light outside number forty was still out and there was a new reference number.

Bruno was twelve by then and had stopped thinking about the sixty metres entirely, and the reason he remembered any of this at all is a girl called Cátia who moved into the flats above the pharmacy in October and who was nine.
He noticed her because she stopped.

He came round the bend one evening at about half five and there was a small person standing at the top of the dark part with her bag held against her front in both arms, doing the private business of deciding, and not deciding.
He knew exactly what she was doing.
He had done it for four months.
He did not say anything about it, because he was twelve and knew that would be the wrong thing.
He walked past her and said "Boa noite" and kept going at a normal speed, and she came after him, about four metres back, all the way down and round the corner into the light.
She did that every evening for about three weeks, at four metres, and neither of them ever mentioned it.

And then one evening at the start of December he was late — he had stayed for the football and come on the later bus — and he came round the bend at nearly seven, and the dark bit was properly dark, and there was nobody in it at all.
And at the far end, at the corner where the light came back, something grey was sitting facing him.
Bruno stopped.
He stood there at the top of Rua da Cordoaria for a while, a good deal longer than he needed to, looking down sixty metres of dark at a cat he had not seen for a year and a half.
Then he walked.
It stood up when he was halfway, unhurried, and went round the corner ahead of him at the pace of something that assumes you are coming, and when he came into the light it was sitting ten metres on.
He did not put his hand out this time.
He had learned that much.
He said, "I know.
I'm going." And it looked at him, and stood up, and walked off along the wall and was gone between two parked cars.
He told his grandmother that night, because she was still the only adult he told, and she was doing the same thing at the same sink.
"It came back," he said.
"I'm twelve." "Mm," his grandmother said.
"But I wasn't frightened.
I was late, that's all.
I was just late." His grandmother turned the tap off and dried her hands and looked at him for a moment with an expression he could not read at all.
"Bruno," she said.
"You were on your own, in the dark, and you're twelve, and you stood at the top of that street for a full minute before you moved.
I watched you from the window." She hung the cloth on the rail.
"It isn't the cat that changes."
The hare turned white seven days before the snow, every year, and had done for longer than anybody could account for.
This was not a story in Bjørnstad.
It was not told at parties or written on anything.

It was the sort of fact that a place keeps in the same drawer as the date the water gets turned off and which side of the church the ice comes in on — dull, useful, and known by everybody in a way that meant nobody explained it.
The hare lived on the slope above the last houses.
There was only ever one.
When one died another was there the following spring, which people accepted without much comment, in the way you accept that there is always a robin in the churchyard.

And in October or November — it moved about, which was the whole point of the thing — the hare would come down onto the lower ground one morning with its coat gone from brown to white, and everybody in the village would look at it and go home and do the seven days' work.
The seven days' work was specific.
You brought the outside animals down.
You lifted whatever was still in the ground, potatoes especially, because potatoes in frozen ground are potatoes you have lost.
You got the winter wood stacked under the eave and not merely stacked.
You put the boards over the pump.

You did the thing with the pipe under the Hansens' bridge that nobody could explain the reason for but which had been done every year since 1938 and which the year it was not done, in 1971, had cost the village a great deal of money.
Seven days was exactly enough time if you started on the first day.
Marit's grandfather had done the sums once, on the back of a feed bag, in about 1980, and the feed bag had been kept.
Two people, seven days, working evenings and the whole of a weekend, came out at just over the total.
Not comfortably over.
Over by about half a day, which meant that a broken pump or a sick cow or somebody's back going ate the margin entirely.
That was why the seven days was a village thing and not a household thing.
Nobody in Bjørnstad got their own potatoes up.

Everybody got everybody's potatoes up, in a rolling order that had been settled some time before the war and that was never discussed, and if you were new you were told the order once and then never again.
The Hansens went first because they were oldest.
The top houses went last because they had the pump and the pump had to be done anyway.
You did not thank anyone.
Marit had once, at nine, thanked Kristian's mother for coming, and had been looked at in a way that stopped her doing it again.
It was not enough time if you started on the third.
The year they started on the third was 1971, and it is the only year anybody in Bjørnstad ever refers to by its number.
What happened in 1971 was not dramatic and that is exactly why it is remembered.
The hare turned on the ninth of November.

A man called Sverre, who had come from Bergen two years earlier and who was by all accounts perfectly capable, was at that time renting the mill house and had responsibility for the stretch of pipe under the Hansens' bridge.
He did not do the thing with the pipe.
He did not refuse to do it.

He simply did not know it was his, because the man who had told him the order had told him once, at a wedding, and had not mentioned the pipe, because the pipe was not part of the order — the pipe was just a thing the mill house did.

The pipe froze and split on the second night of the snow and the water went under the Hansens' bridge instead of through it, and the bridge came off its abutment in the January thaw, and the village was seventeen months and a great deal of money getting a new one.
Nobody blamed Sverre.
Marit has checked this with three separate people who were adults at the time and they all say the same thing with some force: nobody blamed Sverre, Sverre was fine, Sverre was told wrong.
What the village blamed was the telling.
And from 1972 there was a list, typed, on the wall of the co-op, with everything on it including the pipe, and it is still there, and it has been retyped twice.
Marit was twelve the year the hare turned in the second week of October, which was three weeks early and which nobody at all had been expecting.
She saw it first, from the school bus, which she was extremely pleased about for approximately four hours.
By the evening she understood that being first to see it had put her in the middle of the only argument the village had had in seventeen years.
Because the hare, that year, was wrong.
Everybody could see it was wrong.
The birches still had most of their leaves and the leaves were still half green.
There had not been a frost.

The forecast — and Bjørnstad had had a proper forecast on a phone for about a decade by then, which is important to this — the forecast said mild and wet for the whole of the following fortnight, and then more mild and wet, and the long-range said a late winter.
Her father said the hare had got it wrong and that was all there was to it.
Her mother said the hare had never once got it wrong.

Her father said that a thing that has not got something wrong yet has still only not got it wrong yet, and that he was not lifting two hundred kilos of potatoes in the second week of October on the say-so of a rabbit.
Her mother said it was a hare.
Marit went out to the woodpile, which is what you did in that house when the kitchen got like that.
She split wood for forty minutes, badly, and thought about it.
The thing that bothered her was not that her father might be wrong.
Her father was wrong about plenty of things and said so, eventually, in his own time.
What bothered her was that he had a reason and her mother did not.
Her father could say: here is the forecast, here is where it comes from, here are the satellites, here is a man on the television with a map.
Her mother could say: the hare has never been wrong.

And Marit could see, standing in the cold with the axe, that those two sentences were not the same kind of sentence at all, and that everybody in the village was about to have to choose between them, and that the choosing was going to be based on something other than which one was true.
She went in at nine and her parents were being polite to each other, which was worse.
What happened over the next three days was, Marit thinks now, the most interesting thing she has ever watched, and at the time she mostly found it embarrassing.
The village split, and it did not split the way you would expect.
It did not split old against young.
That was the thing that surprised her.
The Hansens, who were both over seventy, looked at the forecast and did nothing.

Kristian at the garage, who was twenty-six and had a tattoo of a wolf and who nobody would have picked, brought his mother's sheep down on the first afternoon and said, when asked, that his grandfather had been very clear with him about the hare and that he was not going to be the one who tested it.
It did not split by belief either.
Nobody in the village believed the hare was magic.

Marit asked several people directly, in the blunt way you can at twelve, and got six versions of the same answer: it is a hare, it goes white when it goes white, there is presumably a reason, the reason is presumably to do with light or cold or something in the ground.
The split was about something else, and it took her until she was much older to put a name on it.
She watched it happen over three days at the co-op, which was the only shop and therefore the whole of public life.
People came in and bought things, and what they bought told you where they stood.
Sacks.
Twine.
The particular blue tarpaulin.
Batteries, which was the tell, because batteries in the second week of October means somebody is expecting the power to go.
Nobody argued in the shop.
That was not how it was done.

What happened instead was that two people would meet at the till and one of them would have twine and the other would not, and there would be a fractional pause, and then they would talk about something else with great warmth for four minutes.
By the Wednesday the shop had run out of twine and had not run out of anything else, which told you the proportion better than any conversation.
Marit's mother did the seven days' work alone, in the evenings, without ever once asking Marit's father to help.
Marit helped.

She wants that recorded too, because at the time she told herself she was helping her mother and she has since worked out that she was hedging, and that hedging is the most common position in any argument of this kind and the one nobody ever admits to.
It was between the people who trusted a thing they could not explain because it had never failed, and the people who trusted a thing they could explain because they could explain it.
Her father was firmly in the second group and made an excellent case at every meal.
About half the village did the seven days' work.
The other half looked at the sky, which was mild, and at the leaves, which were on the trees, and got on with October.
The snow came on the night of the twenty-second, which was nine days after the hare turned, and it did not stop for four days.
It was not a normal fall.
That has to be said, because otherwise the story sounds smug and it was not smug at the time; it was frightening.

Two metres came down onto ground that was not frozen, which meant the whole lot sat there wet and enormously heavy, and the power went at some point on the second night, and the road out was not cleared until the twenty-eighth.
Nobody was hurt.
Marit wants that first.
Nobody in Bjørnstad was hurt, that year or any year, and the village is still there and so is most of what happened to it.
But the Hansens lost their long greenhouse, which went in under the weight on the second night with a noise she heard from her bedroom.
Four houses at the top lost water for fourteen days because the pump was not boarded.
The Iversens' potatoes were still in the ground and stayed in the ground and came up in April as a smell.

And on the third morning, in a whiteout, with the power off, Kristian from the garage went out on the tractor and got as far as the top houses, because his tractor had a blade on it, because he had put the blade on it on the fourteenth of October when the forecast said mild.
Marit's father did not say anything about the hare that winter.

He did not admit anything either — that is not how he was made — and the two of them never had a conversation where he said *you were right* or *the hare was right*, because that was not available in that house.
What he did was this.

The following autumn, on the morning the hare turned, which that year was the fourth of November and entirely reasonable, Marit came downstairs at half past six and her father was already dressed and had the box of potato sacks out on the table.
He said, "It's turned, then." And she said, "Yes." And he said, "Right," and went out.
She has thought about that a great deal since, because she works in meteorology now, which several people in the village find extremely funny.
She has run the numbers on it.

She has the records — the parish kept the date of the turning and the date of the first snow going back to 1911, in a ledger, because of course they did — and she has done the arithmetic properly, with error bars, twice, as an adult who is paid to do exactly this.
The gap is seven days, plus or minus two, for a hundred and fourteen years.
She has no explanation.
There are three or four candidates and none of them survives contact with the data, and she has written about it once, carefully, in a journal that six people read.
What she says, when people ask her at conferences, is that she does not know how the hare does it and that this has never once been the interesting part.

The interesting part is that her village had a hundred and fourteen years of a signal that worked, and a mild October, and a forecast on a phone, and that half of them looked at all three of those things and picked the one that came with an explanation.
Her grandmother read the stag the way other people read a barometer, which is to say quickly, without ceremony, and while doing something else.

They would be walking the top field in April and the stag would be at the far edge of the birches — he was always at the far edge of something, never in the open, never hidden — and her grandmother would glance over, and keep walking, and say something like *wet June* or *the pears will do nothing* and not mention it again.
Petra spent two summers assuming this was a joke that adults did.

She stopped assuming that in the August she was ten, when her grandmother looked at him across the stream in the second week of the month and stopped walking, which she never did, and stood there for a while.
"What?" "He's put on a fourth on the left." "So?" Her grandmother started walking again.

"So bring the ladder round on Thursday and we'll get the apples." They got the apples on the Thursday and Friday, all of them, three weeks earlier than any year Petra could remember, and everybody in the house complained about the work and about the apples being hard.
Her mother complained the loudest and complained for two days, and the complaint had a specific shape to it that Petra only understood later: it was not about the apples.
It was about being the household that did the strange thing, again, in a village where everybody could see the ladders from the road.
On the Sunday night the wind came in off the sea and took a dozen trees down along the river and stripped every orchard in the valley that had not been picked.
Petra asked to be taught and her grandmother said no.
Not unkindly.
She said: "I can't teach it because nobody taught me.
I watched, and I got it wrong for about nine years, and then one year I got it right and I couldn't tell you what changed." "That's not helpful." "It isn't.
I know." Her grandmother was doing something at the sink.
"But if I make you a chart you'll read the chart and not the stag, and the chart will be wrong in a year that matters.
So no." What she did instead was better and much slower.
It was also, Petra realised at about thirty, the only way anybody has ever taught anybody anything difficult, and it is the method that no school has time for.
She started taking Petra with her.
That was all.
Three or four times a week, from April, they went up the top field or along the birches or down to the stream, and if the stag was there they looked at him, and Petra was asked one question.
*What's changed.* Not what does it mean.
Just what has changed.
For the first month Petra could not answer at all.
A stag is a stag; the antlers are complicated and they are also moving because he is moving, and they are usually a hundred metres away against a background of branches which are also complicated.
By June she could say *he's grown*.
This was received without comment, which was the system.
There was never any praise and there was never any correction.
Her grandmother would hear the answer, and nod, or not nod, and they would keep walking, and Petra would spend the next four days working out which it had been.
She learned things in a strange order.

She learned the light before she learned the antlers — that he was easiest to see in the hour before the sun went behind the ridge, and almost impossible at noon, and that this was not about brightness but about which way the shadows ran in the birches.
She learned that he had a place he stood and three places he might stand and that if he was in none of the four you would not find him that day and should go home.
She learned, in July, that he knew perfectly well they were there.
That was the one that took her a while.

He never fled and never approached and never fed while they were watching, and once, in the second week of July, he turned his head and looked directly at her grandmother for a period that Petra found extremely uncomfortable and that her grandmother met without any reaction at all.

"Does he know you?" "He knows there's two of us and there used to be one." By the end of July she could say *the right one's gone out and the left one's gone up*, which her grandmother received with a nod and no comment whatsoever.

By the following March — because it takes a year, and the antlers drop in the spring and grow again from nothing between April and August, and you cannot learn this thing in a season for the simple reason that there is only one of them per year — by the following March, Petra could look at a stag at ninety metres in poor light and say what was different from the week before.
The winter in between had been the hard part, and nobody had warned her about it.
The antlers come off in the spring.
She had known this in the way you know a fact.

She had not understood that it meant the stag she had spent five months learning would, in April, simply stop being the same object — that the whole structure she had been watching grow would drop off in a wood somewhere and a new one would start from two bare stumps.
She took it badly.
She said something at the kitchen table about all of it having been a waste, and her grandmother let her finish and then said: "You didn't learn the antlers.
You learnt to look." "That's a thing adults say." "It is," her grandmother agreed.
"It's also true, which is why they say it.
Go up on Thursday and tell me you can't find him against those birches in nine seconds flat.
You couldn't do that in April." Petra went up on the Thursday partly to prove her wrong.
She found him in about four seconds, in flat grey light, at over a hundred metres, standing in the third of his four places, and she stood there in the cold feeling extremely annoyed about it.
She still could not say what any of it meant.
"That's fine," said her grandmother.
"That's the whole of the first part and it takes most people three years."
The trouble started when Petra tried to make it make sense.
She was thirteen by then and had discovered graphs, and she did what any reasonable person does, which was to write everything down.
She kept a book.
Date, sketch, number of points on each side, and then, at the end of the season, what the weather had actually done.
She sketched him every week from April to August for three years and she had a system of measurement involving a pencil held at arm's length that she was very pleased with.
At the end of the third year she had thirty-nine pages and she sat down to find the rule.
There was no rule.
She checked it four times over the fortnight, each time convinced she had made an arithmetic error, and each time she had not.

Or rather — and this took her a bad fortnight to accept — there were about nine rules, each of which worked for two years out of three, and none of which worked together, and several of which contradicted each other in ways that were not resolvable.
A fourth point on the left had meant an early hard autumn in the year of the apples.
It had also appeared in a year when the autumn was long and soft and nothing happened at all.
She took the book to her grandmother in a temper.
The temper had been building for a fortnight and it was not really about the book.
It was about the fact that she had done everything properly.
She had been rigorous.
She had measured, and dated, and controlled for what you control for, and she had not fudged a single entry even when she badly wanted to.
She had done, as far as she could tell, exactly what a person is supposed to do with a phenomenon.
And it had produced nothing.
Not a partial rule, not a rule with exceptions — nothing at all.
Three years of Thursdays.
Her grandmother read it properly, front to back, which took her most of an evening, and she was complimentary about the drawings.
Then she said: "You've written down the points." "Yes." "I've never once counted the points." Petra said that the points were the only thing there was to count.
"I know," said her grandmother.
"That's why you counted them." She turned a page of the book, back near the start, to the second summer.
"Look at this one.
April, you've got him at eight points and you've written *nothing yet*.
And here's the same week the year after, eight points again, and you've written *nothing yet*." She tapped it.
"Two identical entries.
Do you remember those two springs?" Petra did, faintly.
One had been the year of the late frost that took the blossom.
The other had been the year of nothing at all.
"So they weren't the same," said her grandmother.
"They were the same number.
Those are different words." "Counting," her grandmother said, "is what you do when you can't see the shape yet.
That's not a criticism.
I counted for nine years." She closed the book and gave it back.
"What I look at now is whether he looks like he's expecting something.
And I can't draw that and I can't measure it and if I say it out loud in the village they'll think I've gone, so I don't."
The stag died in the November Petra was sixteen, of being old, on the far side of the birches, and there was another one by the following spring, which is how it goes.
Her grandmother died in the February after that.

Petra did not go up the top field at all that April, or in May, and by June she had convinced herself that she had lost the thing entirely — that whatever it was had been her grandmother's, and had been the sort of knowledge that is really a relationship, and that it had gone where she went.
She went up in the last week of July because her mother made her, on an errand about a gate.
The new stag was at the far edge of the birches.
He was smaller, and darker, and he was standing with his head slightly turned, and he had a fourth on the left.
Petra stopped, exactly the way her grandmother had stopped in the second week of August six years earlier, and stood there in the top field and looked at him for a very long time.
She has never been able to say what she saw.
Not the fourth point; the fourth point was just the thing her eyes landed on.
What she saw, and what she has never been able to put into a sentence that survives being said out loud, was that he looked like something was coming.
She went down and told her mother to get the apples in.
Her mother, who was not sentimental and who had spent thirty years mildly embarrassed about her own mother and the stag, looked at Petra for a second and then went and got the ladder.
The wind came in on the eighth of August.
Petra is forty-one now and she keeps the top field.
The field is not worth keeping, agriculturally.
Three people have told her so, one of them with a spreadsheet.

She has never written another thing down and she has never taught anybody, and she has an eleven-year-old nephew who comes up with her three or four times a week from April, and who is asked one question, and who has been getting more and more annoyed about it since Easter.
He asked her last Thursday what the point of the question was and she said that she could not tell him, and he said that was not an answer, and Petra said no, it was not, and kept walking.
The gull put things on the third bollard from the steps, and only on the third.
Nobody knew why the third.
It was not the biggest or the nearest or the one that got the sun.
It was a bollard exactly like the four on either side of it, cast iron, painted white about nine times, with a chip out of the top where somebody's rope had been.
Things appeared on it.
Not often — four or five times a year, no more — and always overnight, and always after weather.
A green plastic torch.
A single earring, gold, bent.
A tobacco tin with somebody's initials scratched in it that turned out to be nobody's initials anybody recognised.
A watch that did not go.
A folding knife with the blade rusted open.
A hair slide with two of the four stones missing.
And, since before Nél was born, the small blue shoe.
There was a book, as well, though nobody called it a book.
It was a school exercise book in the harbourmaster's office with a list in four or five different handwritings: the date, what had appeared, and whether it had gone.
It started in 1974, which was when somebody had finally thought to start it, and it had five pages used.
Nél had read the whole thing in an afternoon when she was ten, standing up, because she had not been exactly given permission.
*14.xi.81 — spectacles, one arm missing.
Claimed 19.xi by Sr.
Bento.* *3.iii.86 — small anchor, brass, ornamental.
Not claimed.* *22.ix.94 — mobile telephone.
Not claimed (obviously).* The *(obviously)* had been added in different ink, later, by somebody with a sense of humour.
The shoe was the only one that had ever stayed.
Everything else got claimed, usually within a week, usually by somebody who came down and stood in front of the bollard for a while first.
The standing in front of it was not a formality and nobody had ever decided it should happen.
It simply did.
A thing appeared, word went round the harbour by lunchtime, and over the following days people came down and looked at it, one at a time, and most of them went away again.
Nél watched four claimings before she was twelve and they were all the same shape.
The person would come down the steps and along the wall and stop, and they would not touch it at first.
There would be a pause of about a minute in which they did not touch it.
Then they would pick it up and turn it over once and put it in a pocket and walk back up the steps, and that would be the whole of it.
Nobody ever announced anything.
Nobody ever said *that's mine*.
Somebody would ask Dona Lurdes the next day and she would say *the earring's gone*, and that was how the harbour found out.
The tobacco tin went to a man from Cabo who did not explain himself.
The torch went back to a boy in Nél's own class who had dropped it off the ferry and had been shouted at about it.
The shoe had been on that bollard, more or less, for seventy years.
There were three photographs of it that Nél knew about.
One from a newspaper in 1979, in an article about the town that got almost everything else wrong.
One taken by a Dutch couple in about 2004 and put on the internet, where it had attracted thirteen comments, all of them from people inventing worse versions of the story.
And one on the wall of the café, black and white, from some time in the sixties, in which the shoe is on the bollard and there is a boy in the background who is now a man who runs the chandlery.
It was not always on the bollard.
People had moved it.
It had been in the harbourmaster's office, in a drawer, for a while in the nineteen-eighties.
It had been on a shelf in the café.
It had been, for one summer, in a small glass box which everybody agreed afterwards had been a mistake.
Every time, within a year or two, somebody had quietly put it back out on the third bollard, because that was where it went.
Nél was eleven and had recently become the sort of person who wanted the rule stated properly.
She got a lot of different answers.
The clearest came from Dona Lurdes at the café, who had been in that harbour since 1961 and who set it out for her over a cup of milky coffee that Nél had not asked for and drank anyway.
The rule, said Dona Lurdes, was this.
The gull does not bring you things.
The gull brings back things.
There is an enormous difference and half the town gets it wrong.
Everything on that bollard, ever, has been something the sea took off somebody.
Not something lost inland and washed down the river.
Not something dropped on the beach.
Something the water took: off a boat, off the wall, out of a pocket in a swell.
"And she brings it back?" "She puts it where a person can find it.
That's all I'll say she does.
What you make of that is your affair." Nél asked how long the gull had been doing it, expecting an answer in years.
Dona Lurdes said that was the wrong question and that Nél was clever enough to work out why, which took Nél about four seconds and then made her sit back in her chair.
Gulls live for twenty or thirty years.
Some go longer.
Not seventy.
"So it's not the same gull." "No." "Then who taught it?" Dona Lurdes drank her coffee.
"That," she said, "is the question I have been not answering for sixty years, and I am not going to spoil my record for you."
Nél took the shoe seriously in the way that only somebody eleven can take a thing seriously.
She measured it.
It was fourteen centimetres, which she looked up, which made it roughly a size five, which made it a child of about eighteen months to two years.
It was leather, and it had been blue, and it was now the colour of a blue thing that has spent a long time somewhere.
It had a strap and a small button and the button was still on.
Somebody, at some point, had put a stitch into the strap by hand with a thread that did not match, which Nél found harder to look at than anything else about it.
She thought about that stitch a great deal.
It was not a repair the shoe needed.
She looked at it closely, several times, and the strap was not torn and had never been torn.
Somebody had put a stitch into a strap that was perfectly fine, in the wrong colour, by hand.
Which meant somebody had done it after.

On the wall, or in a kitchen, or in the harbourmaster's drawer — somebody at some point in seventy years had picked this thing up and sat down with a needle and put one stitch into it for no practical reason whatsoever.
Nél asked four adults and none of them knew, and two of them looked at her differently for asking.
She was, at first, entirely certain of what it meant.
She was eleven and she had read books.
She took this theory to her father, who put down what he was doing, which he did not usually do.
"No," he said.
"No.
Nobody drowned.
Not a child, not ever, not in this harbour.
I want you to hear that properly." "How do you know?" "Because it's a harbour town and that is precisely the kind of thing a harbour town knows to the exact date." He picked his work back up.
"There's a list in the church with every soul this water has taken since 1804 and it is not a long list and there is not a child on it.
You can go and read it.
I did, when I was about your age, for the same reason." Nél went and read it.
It took her forty minutes and she was quiet for two days afterwards, but not the kind of quiet she had been expecting.
The list was cut into two slate panels on the north wall inside the door, and it ran from 1804 to 1998, and there were sixty-one names on it.
She had expected to be frightened by it.

What she actually felt, working down it with her finger, was something more complicated and a great deal more useful: that all sixty-one had been men, and all sixty-one had been at work, and that the water in that harbour had never once taken anybody who was not being paid to be on it.
She recognised nineteen of the surnames.
Four of them were in her class.
She came out and sat on the church steps for a while.
Then she went down to the harbour and looked at the shoe again, and it had completely changed, and she has never been able to explain to anybody how a thing changes when nothing about it has moved.
The woman came in the second week of September, on the ferry, with a stick.
Nél noticed her because she came down the harbour steps very slowly and then went and stood in front of the third bollard, which is what people did, and which meant something.
She stood there a long time.
Longer than anybody Nél had ever watched.
Then she picked up the shoe.
Nél was up on the wall by the ice machine and she got down and went along, which she would not normally have done, and stopped about four metres off, which was as close as she could make herself go.
The woman said, without turning round: "You'll be wanting to know." "Sorry." "Don't be.
If I were eleven and lived here I'd have been over quicker than that." She turned the shoe over in her hands.
She was perhaps eighty, and she was extremely well dressed, and she was not crying at all.
"It's mine," she said.
"I was twenty-two months old.

My mother had me on the wall in that pram there — well, not that one, but there — and she turned round for a matter of seconds and the pram went over the edge, brake and all." Nél did not say anything.
"They got me out.
Two men off a boat that shouldn't have been in that day.
My mother could not tell the story without stopping in the middle, so she stopped telling it, and I grew up knowing it the way you know a thing that is never described." She held up the shoe.
"One of these came off in the water.
She looked for it, apparently.
For years.
She used to say it as a joke and it was not a joke." "When was this?" "Nineteen forty-eight." The woman put the shoe back down on the third bollard.
Nél said, "Aren't you taking it?" And the woman looked at her, and looked at the shoe, and said something that Nél has repeated to people ever since and has never once had come out right.

She said: "It's been doing a job." Then she said that her mother had died in 1991 and had never known it had come back, and that she herself had only found out about the harbour and the bollard four months ago, from a cousin, at a funeral, in a conversation about something else entirely.
She stayed two nights and went back on the Thursday ferry.
Nél saw her once more, on the Wednesday evening, sitting outside the café with a coffee she was not drinking, looking at the water.
She did not go over.
She has wondered since whether she should have, and has concluded, most days, that she should not.
The shoe is still on the third bollard.
It has been moved twice since — once into the café and once, briefly and outrageously, into a display at the tourist office — and both times somebody put it back.

Nél is grown now and she works at the harbour, and about four times a year, after weather, there is something on the third bollard, and she is one of the three or four people who quietly makes sure the right person gets told.
She has never seen the gull do it.
Nobody has.
She has asked everybody.
She has stopped thinking that this is the interesting part.
A kestrel hunting hangs in the air.

That is the thing about them that everybody notices first and that Tomás's father had explained to him when he was about six, on the way to somewhere, in the way of a man filling four minutes in a car.
She faces the wind and she flies forward at exactly the speed the wind is coming at her, and the two cancel, and she stops.
Not gliding, not soaring — actively flying, hard, and staying in one place.
Her head does not move at all.
The body shifts and the wings work and the tail spreads and closes, and the head hangs there in the air as though it has been nailed to a point in the sky.
Then she moves a dozen metres and does it again over the next patch.
That is the whole method.
She holds still, she looks, she moves on.
A field is searched in about forty minutes.

The reason she has to hang there, his father had said, is that she is looking for something that is trying not to be seen, in grass, from twelve metres up, and the only way to do that is to hold your eye absolutely still over one patch until the patch gives something away.
Everything about the bird is built round that one requirement.
The wings are doing enormous work.
The tail is doing continuous small corrections.
The head is doing nothing at all, and the doing-nothing is the entire point of the rest of it.
Tomás had thought that was the best thing he had ever heard and had told several people at school, who had not agreed.
Which is why, when she stopped moving on, Tomás noticed.

He was thirteen and he went past the Vasco field twice a day on the bike, and on the Monday she was hanging over the near corner, and on the Tuesday she was hanging over the near corner, and on the Wednesday morning she was over the near corner and he stopped the bike and put his foot down and watched her for twelve minutes.
She was working.
That was what was wrong.
She was not perched somewhere with a good view, saving her energy, which is what a bird does when it is not hunting.
She was hovering — which is expensive, which is the most expensive thing a small bird can do — over one patch of ground about the size of a garage, for a third day.
There was nothing there.
He could see the whole of it from the road.
Stubble, a bit of thistle, the concrete pad where a shed had been.
He asked at home and got the answer people give.
His mother said there was probably a nest of something.
His father said the same and added that the field had been left three years and was full of voles and that a bird over a field was not news.

His sister, who was nineteen and studying something with animals in it and who was therefore insufferable that year, said that kestrels absolutely do repeat productive patches and that Tomás had discovered nothing.
She was right, as it happens, about the general case.
That is what makes the argument worth reporting.
Kestrels do repeat productive patches.
They will work a good verge for weeks.

Everything his sister said at that table was correct as a statement about kestrels, and it was delivered with the total confidence of somebody in the second year of a degree, and it was very nearly the reason Tomás dropped the whole thing.
He has thought about that more than about any other part of it.
She had better information than he did.
She had actual training.

And what she did with the better information was use it to explain away an observation she had not made, about a field she had not looked at, because the observation had come from her thirteen-year-old brother.
He went back on the Thursday mostly out of spite.
He would like to be able to claim a better reason and there was not one.
He went back on the Thursday.
She was there.
Same corner.
Same height, which he had started estimating and had settled at about twelve metres.
He watched her for half an hour this time and counted.
He had brought a watch and a notebook, having decided overnight to be serious about it, and he sat on the verge with the bike laid over in the grass and did the thing properly.
In thirty-one minutes she came down twice — properly stooped, dropped feet-first into the stubble — and came up twice with nothing, and went straight back to the same place and hung again.
That was the part that undid the vole theory.
A kestrel that misses moves.
It is not sentimental about a patch.
Two misses in half an hour on the fourth day and she was still there.
He worked out the rest of it on the way home, standing on the pedals up the hill.
Hovering costs.

He did not have the number, but he did not need the number; he had watched her do it for thirty-one minutes without a break longer than a few seconds, and anything that looks that much like hard work is hard work.
A bird does not spend four days doing the most expensive thing it can do over a patch of stubble the size of a garage because it is fond of the view.
Either there was something there worth four days, or she was broken.
And she was plainly not broken.
She was hovering beautifully — better, if anything, than the ones he saw over the motorway, holding position in a crosswind that was pushing the thistles about.
So there was something there.
He had been looking at the wrong part of the field for three days.
He had been looking at the grass, because the grass is where a vole is.
He had not once looked at the concrete.
He said this at dinner, with numbers, and his sister said that was actually interesting, in the tone of somebody surprised to be saying it.
His father put his fork down.
"Fourth day." "Fourth." "Which corner?" "The one by the road.
Where the shed was." His father looked at the table for a moment and then said, "Ask Old Vasco."
Vasco was ninety-one and lived in the house at the top of the lane and had not farmed the field in a dozen years.
He was hard to talk to.
Not unfriendly — he simply took a long time to arrive at a conversation, and if you filled the silences he would let you, and then you would have said everything and he would have said nothing.
Tomás had been coached on this by his father in the car and did the difficult thing, which was to state the situation in four sentences and then stop talking.
Vasco sat in his chair for what felt like a year.
Then he said: "By the concrete." "Yes." "How high." "About twelve metres.

Same place, four days." Vasco nodded slowly, twice, and then said something that Tomás did not follow at all, which was: "Then it's not a vole, and I'm too old to go down there, and you'd better take a spade." He would not explain further.
Tomás asked twice.
What he said, on the way out, at the door, in the tone of a man deciding to give away one thing and not two, was this: "My father used to say you don't look for a lost thing.
You look for what's paying attention to it."
It was not treasure and Tomás would like that stated at the top, because when he tells this story people always lean forward at exactly this point and he always has to take it away from them.
It was a dog.

The concrete pad was the floor of a shed that had come down in about 2009, and along the road edge of it the slab had cracked and settled and left a gap about the width of a fist between the concrete and the earth, and under the slab there was a void perhaps a metre across where the ground had washed out.
A dog had gone in after something and could not get back out.
She had been in there four days.
Four days.
Tomás did that arithmetic standing on the concrete with his father's jacket in his hands and it is the only part of the whole business that still gets him.
She had been under there on the Monday, when he cycled past twice and looked at a bird.
She had been under there on the Tuesday and the Wednesday, when he stopped and watched for twelve minutes and decided there was nothing in that corner.
She had been under there on the Thursday morning while he sat on the verge with a notebook and a watch, being pleased with himself about method.

She was a small brown mongrel with a collar and no tag and she was extremely thin and completely silent, which was why nobody walking the road had heard a thing — she had gone past barking days ago and was doing the other thing, the quiet thing, that animals do at the end of it.
It took Tomás, his father, and a neighbour with a crowbar about ninety minutes to get the slab up enough to reach in.
The first twenty minutes were spent establishing that there was anything there at all, because the gap was a fist wide and dark and Tomás's father would not let him put his arm in it.
They got a torch on it.
Then they got a longer torch on it.

Then Tomás lay flat on the concrete with his cheek against it and his eye at the gap for about a minute, in silence, with the two men standing over him, and said, in a voice he did not entirely recognise, "There's a dog." After that it was a matter of levers and swearing.

The slab was thicker than it looked and had reinforcing in it, and they could not lift it, and in the end they did not lift it — they broke the corner off it with a sledge, in stages, going carefully because nobody knew exactly where under there she was.
She did not make a sound the entire time.
Not when the sledge went in.
Not when the corner came away and the light got to her.
Tomás's father put his jacket over her and got her out with both hands, and she weighed, he said afterwards, about as much as a bag of sugar, and she was still trying to wag.
The kestrel was overhead for the first half of it and then was not, and Tomás did not see her go.
He has thought about the bird every so often for twenty years and he has arrived at a position that satisfies him about eighty per cent of the time.
There were flies.

There must have been flies, and there were probably beetles, and there was something dying in a hole in a field, and a kestrel is an opportunist and will take an insect and will absolutely notice a smell and a movement and a change in a patch of ground.
That is almost certainly all it was.
She was not standing guard.
She was not signalling.
She was a small falcon economically monitoring an anomaly, for four days, at considerable metabolic cost, because there was something in that corner and she had noticed and she is built to notice.
Which is, when he says it out loud, not actually a smaller thing than the version people want.
The dog belonged to a family in Almeirim who had lost her from a car five days earlier and had put up posters in the wrong town.
She lived another nine years.
Tomás is thirty-three.
He does not have a job that has anything to do with birds.

But he has never in his life been able to walk past a hovering kestrel without stopping, and he has twice made himself late for things by standing in a road counting the minutes she stays in one place, and once — only once, in a lay-by on the way to Beja in 2019, over a drainage ditch — it was four days again, and he went and looked, and there was nothing there at all, and he sat back in the car feeling foolish and then, on the whole, not.
Rui found out about it because of a maths test.

The test was on a Friday and he had meant to work on the Thursday evening, and on the Friday morning he had not worked on it, and the reason he had not worked on it was that he could not account for the Thursday evening at all.
He could account for the afternoon.
He had come in at twenty past four, and there had been the business with the bicycle chain in the yard, and his aunt had rung and been on the phone about the wedding for a while.
He could account for the night: he had been in bed at half nine and had read for a bit and had heard the ten o'clock news through the floor.
Between those two there was nothing.
Not a blur.
Not the ordinary vagueness of an evening where you did not do much.
Nothing at all, in the way that there is nothing before you were born.
He sat in the maths test working out what he could do about the four questions he had not revised, and underneath that he was thinking: *where did Thursday go.* It happened again on the Sunday.

He noticed it the moment it happened, or rather the moment after — he was at the kitchen table with the light on and it was properly dark outside and the last thing he was certain of was standing at the back door looking at the sky going orange behind the depot.
He got up and went to the door and opened it and stood there.
It was cold.
It was black.
The depot lights were on.
There was no orange anywhere.

He went and asked his mother what time it was and she said quarter past seven without looking up, and Rui stood in the kitchen doorway holding on to the frame and doing arithmetic that would not come out.
He had lost an hour and ten minutes and he had lost it while awake, standing up, at a back door.
Over the following fortnight he kept a record, which is what he did with things.
