He wrote down the last moment he was sure of and the first moment after, and by the end of November he had nine entries and they had a shape.
It was always the same hour.
Not the same clock time — the clock time moved, earlier and earlier as the month went on.
It was the hour when the light goes.
The last of it, the part where the sky has colour in it and the streetlights come on and everything outdoors turns the colour of a photograph of itself.
That hour, a dozen times, had not happened to him.
He asked his mother, carefully, whether he had been strange on the Sunday.

She said he had been perfectly normal, that he had helped with the potatoes and had been quite chatty about a boy at school called Duarte, and that she did not know why he was asking, and could he not stand in the doorway with the cold coming in.
He found the box on the eleventh of December, under the hedge at the bottom of the yard, and he found it by putting his hand somewhere he should not have put his hand.
The hedge at the bottom was thick at the base and full of the things hedges are full of.
He was after a ball that had gone under, and he was flat on the wet ground with his arm in up to the shoulder, and his fingers came down on a corner that was flat and dry and cardboard.
It took him a long time to get it out.
It was further in than his arm went and he had to fetch the rake and work it sideways.

While he was working it out he found four other things, which is what happens under a hedge: half a tennis ball, a fork, a plastic dinosaur that had been his when he was about six, and a great quantity of leaves that had been leaves for a very long time.
None of them were dry.
It was a shoebox.
Green, with a brand on the side that had not existed for twenty years, and it was not damp, which under a hedge in December is not a thing a shoebox can be.
He sat back on his heels in the wet and took the lid off.
The box was full of evenings.

He has never worked out how to describe this and he has stopped trying, so what he says now is simply what he saw, which is that the box contained nine flat pieces of light about the size of a postcard, lying on top of each other like slides, and every one of them was the last hour of a day.
You could see into them.
Not a picture — a picture is flat and this was not flat, it had a distance in it.
He looked into the top one and there was the back yard from the height of his own eyes and the sky going orange behind the depot and the sound, faintly, of his aunt on the telephone in another room.
The second one down was a different evening.
There was rain on it.
He went through all nine, kneeling in the mud with the lid beside him, holding each one up to what was left of the daylight.
Three of them had rain.
One had the smell of somebody burning garden waste two gardens over, which he remembered and had not thought about since.
One was almost entirely dark and had a single lit window in the top corner, which he worked out after a while was the Ferreiras' landing.
And every one of them was the yard.
Every single one was that view, from that height, from the back door — as though somebody had stood in exactly his place on fourteen separate evenings and had not moved.
He put the lid back on because his hands had started to shake, and he sat in the mud at the bottom of the yard with a shoebox on his knees for a while, and then he heard the noise.

It was a snuffling, industrious, entirely un-mysterious noise, coming from under the hedge about a metre to his left, and it was the noise of a hedgehog who has been interrupted and is deciding whether to be bothered about it.
She was not enormous and she was not small and she did not, when he finally got a proper look at her, seem in the least surprised.
She had come out and stopped about half a metre from his knee and turned herself broadside on, which he later learned is what they do when they are considering the situation rather than fleeing it.
She was not what he had pictured, which was a Christmas card.

She was bigger than a Christmas card and much dirtier, and there was a patch on her left side where the spines were thin, and she smelled — this is the detail he always includes and people never like — she smelled strongly of a hedge.
They looked at each other for a while.
A dog barked over towards the depot and neither of them reacted to it.

Rui said, "This is mine." The hedgehog did not say anything, because hedgehogs do not, and Rui would like that understood at the outset because people always assume this story has a talking animal in it and it does not.
What she did was go back under the hedge and come out again with something in her mouth.
It was another one.
Flat, about postcard size, with a dark blue evening in it and a smell of frost coming off it that he could feel on his face from where he sat.
It was not from the box.
That was the thing he understood immediately and could not have explained.
The box was on his knees with the lid on.

She had gone back under the hedge and had come out with a twelfth one from somewhere else, and he never found out where, and he did ask, later, in the only way available to him, which was to look under the hedge with a torch for about an hour.
She put it down on the ground in front of him, and then pushed it towards him with her nose, twice, in a way that could not have meant anything else.
He picked it up.
And that is how Rui found out what the last hour of a day feels like when it is handed back to you all at once instead of being lived through a minute at a time.
It was the eighth of October.
He knew it was the eighth of October because he was in it.

He was standing at the back door — the same back door — and the sky was that colour, and inside the house behind him his grandmother's carers were in the hall talking to his mother in the low voices that adults use when they think they are being quiet.

And Rui, standing at the back door on the eighth of October, was eleven years old and was not going to cry, and had gone out into the cold specifically so that he would not, and was doing the thing where you press your thumbnail hard into your finger.
The hour ran through him and finished and he was back in the mud in December with a piece of cardboard in his hand that was no longer anything at all.
It had lasted, by the clock, no time whatsoever.
He checked.
He had gone in and it had been twenty to five and he came out of it and it was twenty to five, and the light at the bottom of the yard had not changed.
It had also lasted an hour and ten minutes, all of it, in order, including the part in the middle where nothing happened and he had just stood there being cold.
He looked at the hedgehog.
The hedgehog looked back at him with the total lack of embarrassment of a creature that has done nothing wrong.
His grandmother had been ill from the middle of September to the middle of November and had then, slowly and grumpily, got better, and was at that time upstairs complaining about the television.
There were nine evenings in the box and there had been nine entries in his notebook, and the dates were the dates.
Rui did the sum in about four seconds and then sat with it for most of a week.
She had not taken his afternoons.
She had not taken the nights, or the mornings, or the two whole days in October when it had been bad and he had known it was bad.
She had taken exactly the hour when the light goes — the hour when you are eleven, and there are people in the hall, and nobody has told you anything, and it is not yet time for bed.
That hour, a dozen times.
He thought for a while that he should be angry, and tried it, and it did not fit.

What he settled on instead — and he was eleven, and it took him until about February to put it in these words — was that somebody had looked at him standing at a back door pressing his thumbnail into his finger and had decided that he did not have to carry that particular hour on that particular night, and had taken it, and had not thrown it away.
That was the part.
She had not thrown it away.
She had put it in a box under a hedge four metres from his own back door and kept it dry for three months.
He took them back one at a time.
He did it over the winter, out at the bottom of the yard in the cold, roughly one a week, and he chose which one by looking into it first, which she permitted.
Some of them were nothing much.
Two of them were extremely bad.
The one from the twenty-ninth of October he put back in the box three times before he took it, and when he did take it he sat under the hedge afterwards for twenty minutes.
He finished the last one in March.
He put the empty box back under the hedge, because it was hers and not his, and it is still there as far as he knows.
Rui is nineteen now.
His grandmother lived another five years and was extremely rude about the television for all of them.

He has not lost an hour since, and he is not sure whether that is because nothing has been bad enough, or because you only get that arrangement once, or because it is not an arrangement at all and there is simply a hedgehog at the bottom of a yard in a town in the north who notices things and does what she can with them.
He leaves food out.
He has read the guidance and he leaves the correct food and not the food people used to leave.
He has never once seen her take it, which he finds entirely in character.
The ermine came down the scree in November and went up again in March and in between she was somewhere on the mountain with her mouth full.
Everybody in the valley had seen her at least once.
She was not shy and she was not hiding; she went along the top of the dry-stone walls in broad daylight with the confidence of something that has never been caught.
In summer she was brown with a white front.

From the first snow she was white all over except the tip of the tail, which stayed black, and which was the only part of her you could actually see against a drift — a small black comma travelling along a wall at speed with nothing attached to it.
And from November she carried the thaw.
You could see it if she stopped, which she did about once a minute, sitting up on her back legs the way they do to look at you.
There was something in her jaws.

It was not large — the size of a hen's egg, perhaps — and it was not any colour, which is the difficulty; Lise had looked at it four times at close range over three winters and could only ever say that it was the same colour as the day after tomorrow.
It was warm.
You could tell from a distance of two metres.

On the coldest morning of the year, standing at the wall with the frost cracking in the grass, you could feel it on your face like an open oven door, coming off a thing the size of an egg being carried by an animal that weighed less than a cup of coffee.

Lise had tried, once, at nine, to work out how she could carry something that warm in her mouth all winter without it doing her any harm, and had been told by her father to stop asking questions of that kind about that particular animal.
She had not stopped.
She had simply stopped asking him.
She would not put it down.
That was the whole of the arrangement and everybody in the valley knew it.

She would carry it all winter, up and down the scree, through the snow and under it, without ever setting it down for a second — not to eat, not to sleep, not for anything — until somebody came up and asked her, properly, to let it go.
And then it would be spring.
Not in a week.
Not gradually.

There were photographs in the parish office, four of them, taken by a man called Anton in the 1960s who had been a serious person about photography: the same view of the same slope on four consecutive days, and on the third one there is snow to the wall-top and on the fourth one there is grass, and everybody who sees them for the first time says the same thing, which is that the man had obviously cheated.
He had not cheated.

The four negatives are in the same strip, in order, with the frame numbers on them, and they have been looked at by two people from a university who came up in 2003 and were extremely polite and went away again.
What happens is not that the snow melts.

Melting takes days and leaves the ground wet and the drifts hollowed out and grey at the edges, and everybody in that valley has watched melting happen every spring of their lives and knows exactly what it looks like.
The snow goes.
There is no water.
That is the part that nobody from outside believes and that nobody inside bothers arguing about.
The ground under it is dry.
Nikolai Braun had done the asking for forty-one years and he was not going to be doing it a forty-second.
He had had a stroke in the September.
He was alive and he was at home and he was, by all accounts, entirely himself in the head, and he could not walk to the end of the lane, let alone up the scree.

The valley discussed the problem for most of October in the way that valley discussed everything, which was by not discussing it in front of children and then discussing it at length in front of children who were pretending to read.
Lise, who was twelve, learned the following.
That the asking was not a ceremony.
There were no words.
Nobody wore anything.
If you went up there expecting to say a formula, Nikolai had told the last three people who asked him, you would come down again with nothing having happened and you would feel extremely silly.
That you went alone, and in the last week of February or the first of March, and you went up to wherever she was, and you asked, and either she put it down or she did not.
That it had not always been Nikolai.
Before him it had been a woman called Frau Ebner for a very long time, and before her a man whose name was on the war memorial, and before that the records got vague.
And that in 1934, and again in 1968, the person who went up had come back down without it, and both of those springs had come in the second week of May and both of those years had been hard.
1968 was in living memory when Lise was small.

Frau Hofer, who was ninety and who had been a young woman that year, would talk about it if you got her going: the hay running out in March, the road shut until the twenty-first of April, the two families who left the valley that summer and did not come back.

She never once said who had gone up that year and failed, and nobody else ever said it either, and Lise worked out at about ten that this was deliberate and that the name was known to everyone over sixty.
What nobody could tell Lise, because nobody knew, was what *properly* meant.
She asked her mother, who said she supposed it meant being sincere.
She asked Herr Vogel at the shop, who said it meant you had to mean it, which was the same answer with fewer syllables.
She asked Nikolai Braun himself, in the front room of his house, in November, with his daughter listening from the kitchen and pretending not to.
He took a long time to get the sentence out.
That was one of the things the stroke had left him.
He said: "It means you have to know what you're asking for." Lise said that everybody knew what they were asking for.
They were asking for spring.
And Nikolai Braun laughed, which was alarming, and then took another long time, and said: "That's what I said in 1962.
And I came down that day and it was still there in her mouth and I was up that mountain three more times before the ninth of March."
She went up on the twenty-sixth of February.

It had been agreed, in the way things were agreed there — which is to say that nobody had ever said to Lise *you are doing it*, and yet by the end of January there was no other candidate and everyone had stopped mentioning alternatives.
She was not the obvious person.
She was twelve.

But the valley had seven households left in it and four of those were people over seventy, and of the rest there was Lise, her brother who was six, and the Marek boys who were nineteen and twenty-two and who had both said no in a way that closed the subject.
It took her two hours and forty minutes to get up to the shoulder, in good weather, with a flask.
Her father walked with her as far as the second gate, which was as far as anybody was allowed to come, and stood there while she went on up.
She did not look back until the bend, and when she did he was still there, and she was extremely annoyed with herself for looking.
Above the second gate the path stops being a path.

It is a line of slightly-less-bad ground across a slope of loose grey stone, and in February it has snow on it in the hollows and ice under the snow, and Lise went up it in her brother's crampons, which were too big, taking the long zigzag her father had made her promise to take.

The ermine was on the wall by the ruined byre, which is where Nikolai had said she would be, and she sat up when Lise came round the corner and looked at her with the egg-sized nothing glowing in her jaws.
Lise had thought about it for four months and had prepared nothing, on purpose, because everyone had told her that preparing was the mistake.
She said: "Please can you put it down." Nothing happened.
She said it again, and then she said it a third time in dialect rather than in school German, in case that was the thing.
The ermine sat on the wall and looked at her and did not put it down.
Lise stayed up there for about an hour.
She sat on the wall herself, at a distance, and she talked.
She said all the reasonable things: that the valley needed the grass, that the Hofers had run out of hay, that her father's back would not stand another month of it.
She said, at one point, feeling humiliated, that she was sorry she was not Nikolai.
The ermine washed her face with one front paw, which is a thing they can do while holding something, and which Lise found extremely rude.
Then she went along the wall and off into the rocks.
Lise came down the mountain in the dark, badly, having stayed too long, and was met halfway by her father with a torch who did not ask her anything at all until they were inside.
When they were inside, and she had her boots off, he asked her whether she was cold, and she said no, and he said good, and that was the entire conversation about it.

She heard him on the telephone to Nikolai's daughter later, through the floor, saying it had not worked, in a voice that was not disappointed at all — and she lay in bed working out that he had never expected it to, and that he had not said so, and that both of those had probably been kindnesses.
She went up twice more in the following week and got nothing, and on the third of March she went to see Nikolai Braun and told him she was finished.
She said it in a temper.
She said that she had asked, and had meant it, and that if he had a magic word he ought to hand it over, and that she was not going up there again to be looked at.
Nikolai listened all the way through.
His daughter brought coffee and left.
Then he said, in his slow way, with a great many pauses: "What do you want the spring for." Lise said, for the grass.
He shook his head, slightly.
She said, for the hay, for the Hofers, for the road.
He shook his head again and did not say anything, and the silence went on long enough to be a question.
And Lise sat in that front room in a bad temper and heard herself say something she had not known she was going to say, which was: "Because I can't do another one." Nikolai did not move.
"I can't do another winter here," she said.
"There's seven houses and my brother's six and there's nobody.

I've got two more years of the bus and then I'm going to Innsbruck and I'm not coming back, and everybody knows it and nobody will say it, and I'm going to be the one who leaves and Papa is going to be here on his own with the wall." She stopped.
"That's what I want the spring for," she said.
"I want it to be March so it's April so it's June so I can get out." There was a very long pause.
"Yes," said Nikolai Braun.
"That's it.
That's the asking." She went up on the fifth.
She found the ermine on the same wall.
She did not make a speech.
She sat down about three metres away with her hands in her sleeves and she said the true thing, out loud, in the cold, to a weasel.

The ermine listened — she is prepared to be argued with about the word *listened* and will not move on it — and then came four metres along the wall towards her, which she had never done, and opened her mouth, and put it down in the snow.
Then she went off into the rocks with her tail up.
The snow was gone from the lower slope on the eighth.
Lise has the date because she wrote it in the back of a school exercise book, next to a sum she had got wrong.
She did go to Innsbruck, at eighteen, and she did not come back, in the sense that she does not live there.
She goes up every February.
She has done it for nineteen years.
She takes the train and then the bus and then she walks, and she asks, and it has worked every time, and the true thing she says has been different every single year.
The rule was explained to Tam in the first week, at the bus stop, by a girl called Effie who had appointed herself to the job of explaining things and who was not always accurate.
The rule was that there was a fox in Fernaig wood, and that you only saw it when you were lost.
"Lost how?" "Lost lost.
Off the path, don't know where the road is, that kind." Effie was eating something out of a bag and did not appear to consider any of this remarkable.
"My cousin saw it when he went in after a ball and came out the wrong side by the quarry.
My mum saw it once.

Everybody's seen it once." "Have you?" "No," said Effie, with some annoyance, "because I've lived here my whole life and I can't get lost in it, can I." Tam had moved to Fernaig in the August from a town with a one-way system, and he had not been in the wood, and he filed the fox with the other information he had been given that week: that the shop shut at four on Wednesdays, that you did not sit in the third row on the bus, and that Mr Ross would let you off homework if you asked about the war.
Fernaig had a shop, a school with eighty-one pupils in it, a hall, and a wood that went up the back of everything and did not stop until the forestry track seventeen kilometres north.
It had one bus in the morning and one at half three and a third on Fridays that people spoke about with some ceremony.
It had, as far as Tam could establish in his first fortnight, no way at all of arriving in it.
Everybody there had always been there.
He asked Effie who else had moved in recently and she thought about it seriously for some time and said the Polish family at the sawmill, in 2011.
He saw the fox for the first time on the twelfth of September, in the car park behind the school, at half past three in the afternoon.
It was sitting by the bins, in daylight, in the middle of a village, about five metres from the door he had just come out of.
It was not doing anything.
It was sitting the way a dog sits when it has been told to wait, front legs straight, looking at him.
Tam looked around the car park.

There were two teachers by the minibus and a group from the year above on the wall and Effie's brother locking up a bike, and not one of them had noticed a fox sitting by the bins in the middle of the afternoon.
He looked back and it was still there.
He walked to the bus with his heart going and did not tell anybody, because he had been in that school for four weeks and knew exactly how that conversation would go.
He looked it up that night, which is what you do.

He found that foxes in villages are entirely normal and increasingly common and often bold in daylight, and that this is well documented, and that there was nothing whatsoever remarkable about a fox sitting by some bins.
He read four pages of that and felt better and went to sleep, and in the morning it was on the wall outside the shop.
By the middle of October he had seen it thirty-one times and he had started counting because the counting made it feel like a project rather than a problem.
It was in the car park.
It was on the wall outside the shop.
It was on the road out to the caravan site at seven in the morning, and again at four, and once at both ends of the same day.
It was in his own garden.
That was on the eighteenth, and it was the one that stopped him sleeping.
He got up for water at about one and looked out of the landing window because he always looked out of the landing window, and it was on the grass by the shed, sitting, facing the house.
It never came closer than about ten metres and it never went further than about thirty.
It never ran.
Twice he walked directly at it, in daylight, in a temper, and it stood up and moved off at a walk and stopped again when he stopped.
He tried, twice, to get somebody else to see it.

The first time was on the road by the caravan site with his mother in the car, and he said *there's a fox* in the most ordinary voice he could manage, and she said *oh yes* — and he spent the rest of the journey working out from what she said next that she had been agreeing with him rather than looking.
The second time was worse.
It was on the school wall at lunch and he said it to Effie, and pointed, and she looked exactly where he was pointing for a good four seconds and said, "Where?" He said he'd been mistaken.
She was decent about it, which he minded.
He went into the wood in the end, in the last week of October, on a Saturday, on purpose, because he had worked out what was bothering him and could not make it stop bothering him any other way.
The rule was that you saw the fox when you were lost.
He was not lost.
That was the point.
He was not lost in Fernaig wood or anywhere else; he was in a car park, and a shop doorway, and his own garden, four metres from a back door he could have found blindfolded.

So either the rule was wrong, or Effie was wrong, or — He went in at the top gate and walked for two hours, deliberately, badly, taking every wrong turn he could identify, and got himself thoroughly and genuinely lost somewhere in the middle by about half two.
He stood there in the wet bracken, properly disoriented, no idea which way the road was.
And there was no fox.

He came out an hour later at the quarry side, scratched and extremely cold, having established the one thing he had least wanted to establish, which was that the rule worked fine and that the problem was him.
He sat on the wall at the quarry for a while before going home, working it through.
If the rule was about woods, he was fine and the fox was a coincidence and foxes are common.

If the rule was not about woods, then something in Fernaig had decided he was lost — had been deciding it, daily, since the twelfth of September, in car parks and shop doorways and his own back garden — and had gone to the trouble of sitting down in his eyeline about thirty-one times to say so.
And the second one was ridiculous, and he believed it, and he could not think of a single person in that village he could say it to.
He told his mother in November and it went about as well as these things go, which is to say she was kind and completely missed it.
She said everybody found moving hard.
She said it took a year.

She said she had been miserable too when she was thirteen and Granny had moved them to Aberdeen, and that it had come good, and that he was doing so well and that Miss Cameron had said he was settling in beautifully.
All of which was true, and none of which was the thing.
He tried Mr Ross, obliquely, at the end of a Thursday, on the pretext of asking about local stories for a project he had not been set.
Mr Ross was about sixty and had been at that school for twenty-eight years and was not in a hurry.
He taught history to three year groups and ran the minibus and had a way of answering a question about forty seconds after you had given up on him.

He listened to the whole of Tam's very careful question about the fox — a question that mentioned folklore twice and did not mention Tam at all — and then he sat back and said, "How often are you seeing it?" Tam looked at the desk.
"Most days," he said.
"Aye," said Mr Ross, and did not seem surprised, and did not say anything for a bit.
"The rule's about the wood," Tam said.
"That's what everybody says.
In the wood, off the path, don't know where the road is." "That's what everybody says because that's where everybody's seen it, once, when they were eleven and daft." Mr Ross took his glasses off.
"It's not a rule about woods, son.
It's a rule about not knowing where you are." Tam said nothing for a moment.

"That's the same thing." "It is not remotely the same thing," said Mr Ross, "and you know fine it isn't, or you wouldn't have come in here with a project you've not been set." "I know where I am." "Do you." Tam did not answer that.

"I've been here twenty-eight years," said Mr Ross, "and I came from Glasgow, and I saw that animal roughly every second day for the whole of my first winter, and I have not seen it since about 1999." Tam sat there.
"Nobody else says that," he said.
"Everybody says once.
Everybody says they saw it once, off the path, when they were wee." "Aye.
Because everybody here got lost in a wood once when they were wee and found their way out by teatime." Mr Ross put his glasses back on.
"You cannot be lost in a place you were born in.
It is not available to you.
Which is why the folk in this village think it's a story about a wood — because for them, it is." He started stacking papers, which meant the conversation had about ninety seconds left.
"There's maybe four people in Fernaig it's not a story about a wood for.
I'm one.

You're one." "Who are the other two?" "That," said Mr Ross, "would be their business." "What changed?" "I stopped pretending I was fine," said Mr Ross, "which took me thirteen months and a very bad Christmas, and I would not particularly recommend the method."
He said it on the eighth of December, in the kitchen, at about nine at night, and he said it badly.
What he said was that he hated it.
He had not planned to.
He had come down for a glass of milk.
His mother had asked him a completely ordinary question about a form for a trip, and he had heard himself start talking and had been, for about the first thirty seconds, as surprised as she was.
He said he hated the bus and the shop shutting at four and that there was nothing, there was actually nothing, there was one shop.
He said everybody had known each other since they were three and that they were not unkind about it and that was somehow worse.
He said he had been at that school for four months and had not once been to anybody's house.
He said that when they had left he had told everyone at his old school he'd be back at Christmas and that he had known when he said it that it was not true.
He said that everyone kept telling him he was settling in beautifully and that he had no idea who had told them that, because it had not been him.
His mother did not say it would come good.

She sat at the table and let him finish and then she said, "I know," and then, after a while, "I don't know what to do about most of that." Which was, Tam thought later, the first accurate sentence anybody had said to him since August.
They talked for about two hours.
Nothing was solved.
The shop still shut at four.
He did not see the fox in December at all.
He noticed the absence about ten days in, on the way home on the bus, going past the wall by the turning where it had been every second Tuesday since October.
It was an odd feeling and not a good one at first.
He had spent three months wanting it to stop and it had stopped, and the stopping did not feel like winning.
It felt like the end of something he had been having a conversation with.
He looked.

He is not going to pretend he did not look — he checked the garden from the landing window every night for three weeks like an idiot, and there was the shed and the grass and the wheelie bin and nothing else.
He saw it once more, in the following June, on a Tuesday, from the bus.

It was on the wall by the turning to the caravan site, sitting, front legs straight, and by then he was fourteen and had been to Effie's house fourteen times and was in the football, and he was not in the least lost, and he looked at it all the way past and it looked back.
He has thought about that one for years.
The version he has settled on is that it was not there for him at all.
There were about thirty people on that bus.

But he is not certain, and the other possibility has never entirely gone away, which is that you do not stop being somebody who arrived from somewhere else, and that the fox knows this, and that once in a while it sits on a wall in the sunshine to remind you.
He is twenty-six now and he lives in Fernaig, which nobody who knew him at thirteen would have predicted, including him.
The reservoir went down in the drought and the church tower came out of it in the second week of August, and by the Friday there were cars parked all the way along the dam road.
Vera watched it happen from the caravan site with a mixture of feelings she has never entirely sorted out.
The tower was not much to look at.

It was six metres of grey stone with no roof, standing in a plain of cracked mud the colour of a paper bag, and it had a tide mark round it at about the height of a person which was the mark of a normal year.
People walked out to it across the mud, which they were not supposed to do, and stood next to it, and took photographs of themselves next to it, and drove home.
Vera worked at the caravan site in the holidays, cleaning the shower block and handing out the wristbands, and she heard the same four conversations every day for a month.
That it was sad.
That it was fascinating.
That they had seen a programme about one in Spain.

And, from a man on the Thursday who was very pleased with himself, that it was a reminder that nothing lasts, which Vera thought was an odd thing to take from a village that had been deliberately drowned by people who filled in a form.
The newspaper called it *the ghost village*, which Vera's grandmother heard on the radio in the kitchen and responded to with a single syllable.
Her grandmother had been eleven when they flooded it.
That was 1963.

She had been eleven, and had left the house on the twelfth of March with a case and a bird in a cage, and had gone up the hill to the new houses at Aldeia Nova with everybody else, and had never gone back down because there was no back down to go to.
The new houses were fine.
Vera had grown up in one of them.

They had bathrooms and they had been built in a straight line facing the road, and every single one of them was identical, and her grandmother had lived in the same one for sixty-two years and had never once called it anything but *the new houses*.
She was seventy-four now and she lived with them and she had not been out to the dam road all week.
"They're calling it a ghost village," Vera said.
"Mm," said her grandmother.

"Have you been down?" "No." "Are you going to?" Her grandmother put the pan down and looked out of the window at the hill for a moment, and Vera thought she was going to get an answer of some kind, and what she got instead was: "There's four hundred cars on that road and a man selling water out of a van.
No." "It's not, is it." "It's a village," her grandmother said, "with a lot of water on it." She was doing something with beans.
"Ghosts is what you say when you'd rather not say drowned, and drowned is what you say when you'd rather not say we did it on purpose for the electricity."

Vera found the eel in the third week, in one of the pools that were left in the mud, and she found it because she was doing the thing everybody at the caravan site was doing, which was walking about out there when the light went and it got cool enough.
The pool was maybe four metres across and knee-deep and warm as soup, and there were sticklebacks in it, and there was, along the bottom, an eel about as long as her arm.
She thought it was stuck.

That was her first thought and it was a reasonable one — there were fish stranded all over that mud in August, dying in shrinking puddles, and she had already carried two carp to the main channel and been extremely pleased with herself.
The carp had been horrible to carry.

They were enormous and they had gone quiet in the way a fish goes quiet, and one of them had come back to life halfway and nearly gone out of her arms, and she had walked the last thirty metres holding it against her chest like a baby with the mud sucking at her feet.
She had told nobody about the carp either.
It was that sort of August.
She got down on her knees and put her hands in.
The water was the temperature of a bath that has been left.

There was mud in it that came up in clouds the moment she moved, so that she had to wait between attempts for it to clear, kneeling in the warm with her sleeves pushed up and the sun going down behind the dam.
The eel did not want to be carried.
It went round her wrists twice and got out the other side and came back to almost exactly the place it had started, and settled, and looked at her, which eels can do more than people expect.
She tried again and the same thing happened.
The third time she stopped and sat back on her heels in the mud and looked at where the pool was.
She was not thinking anything clever.
She was thinking that she had been beaten by a fish and that her knees hurt.
It was in a straight line.
She had not noticed it because she had come at it from the side.

But standing up, in the low sun, with the shadows long, she could see that the pool she was kneeling in was one of about nine, in a row, running away from her towards the tower — and that the row was not a row of pools at all.
It was a street.
The pools were the low bits.
Between them, under a skin of dried mud, was the crown of a road, cambered, running from somewhere behind her all the way to the church.

She walked the length of it in the last of the light, out and back, four hundred paces one way, and where the crust was thin she could put her heel through it and there was stone underneath, laid stone, set on edge the way they used to set it.
She went out at the same time every evening for a fortnight and the eel was always in a pool on the street, and never the same pool.
That was the whole of the phenomenon and it does not sound like much written down.
Vera would like to insist that it did not feel like not-much at the time.
She started marking.

She used stones at first and then, when she worked out that people kicked stones, she used a stick to draw a line in the crust from pool to pool, and she extended it each evening from wherever the eel was.
The rule she gave herself, which she took extremely seriously, was that she was only allowed to draw as far as the eel had been.
Not as far as she could see the low ground going.
As far as the eel had actually been on an evening she had witnessed.
She has thought since that this was the only genuinely good decision she made that summer, and that she made it for no reason at all except that it felt like cheating otherwise.
By the end of the fortnight she had a line four hundred metres long, and it did not go where she expected.
She had assumed the road went from the dam road to the church, because that is the way people were walking.
It did not.

It came in from the north, along the flank of the slope, and made a wide turn about a hundred metres out that took it well away from the tower and then brought it back — a proper turn, the kind you make for a gradient, not for a boundary.
And it did not end at the church.

It went past the church, on the north side, and there was a second line going off it at right angles that she found on the eleventh evening and that ran forty metres and stopped at a rectangle of stone about the size of a kitchen.
She drew all of it in a notebook, with the tower as the fixed point, pacing distances and writing them down.
She showed nobody for three weeks, because it was hers.
She did tell one person, on the second Saturday, which was a boy from the caravan site called Diogo who was there for a fortnight and who she thought would be interested.
He came out with her once, looked at a line drawn in mud, said it was cool, and asked whether there was anything to actually see.
She said no, not really, and he was perfectly nice about it, and they went back and played cards.
That was the last time she told anybody until September.
She told her grandmother in the middle of September, in the kitchen, on an evening when the rain had finally started and everybody knew the pools were going.
She did not lead up to it.
She put the notebook on the table and said, "This is the road into the village." Her grandmother wiped her hands and sat down and pulled it towards her, and looked at it for a long time.
Then she put one finger on the wide turn.
"That's wrong," she said.
Vera, who had paced that turn four times and was twelve and had a notebook, said that it was not wrong.
"It's wrong," her grandmother said, "because you've got it going round the outside, and it went round the inside.
There was a chestnut there.
It went round the other side of the chestnut." "There's nothing there now." "No.
There's a stump six metres down under two hundred million litres of water, and you didn't see it, and neither did the eel." She turned the notebook.
"But it went round the inside.
I've walked that road four thousand times." And then she stopped, with her hand flat on the page, and did not say anything for a while.
Vera did not say anything either.
What her grandmother said, eventually, was: "I couldn't have told you that yesterday." She said that she had not been able to get the village back for about ten years.

That she could see the kitchen and she could see the front of the school and she could see two or three faces, and that everything in between had gone soft and would not come when she called it — and that this had frightened her more than she had told anybody, including Vera's mother, and that she had stopped trying because trying and failing was worse.
"And then you put a road in front of me," she said, "and I'm on it." They did the rest of it over that winter.

Vera would put a question — what's here, what's at the end of this, why does it turn — and her grandmother would be somewhere in 1962 and would answer it, and about a third of the time she would answer a question Vera had not asked, and Vera learned quickly to write those down and not interrupt.
The map they finished in March has one hundred and nine things on it.
Houses with names on them, which are the names of families and not of streets.
The two shops.
The place where the bus turned.
A well that is not on any official plan.
The chestnut, drawn as a circle, with the road going round the inside of it.
The reservoir filled that winter and the tower went under in January and has not been seen since.

Vera is twenty-eight and the map is in the parish office at Aldeia Nova, framed, next to the photographs, and there is a copy in the district archive because a woman from the archive came out and asked for one.
Her grandmother died in 2021.
The thing Vera says, when people ask her about it — and they do ask, because of the framed map, and because it is a good story about a drought and a fish — is that the eel did not know anything.
It was an eel in a pool.
Eels lie up in pools.

The pools were on the line of the road because the road was the low ground, and the road was the low ground because roads are built on ground you can walk on, and the whole of the mystery collapses the moment you look at it properly.
What the eel did was make her kneel down in the right place.

Everything else in that story was an old woman at a kitchen table who had been quietly losing something for ten years, and who got most of it back over one winter because a twelve-year-old asked her the questions in the right order — starting from the north, coming down the slope, going round the inside of the chestnut.
There was a night in October when the geese went over Szentmárton, and it was the only night of the year that anybody in that village stayed up on purpose.
They came late — never before eleven, usually nearer one — and they came low.
Lower than geese have any business flying.
Bori's father said you could hear the wingbeats, which she had assumed for years was an exaggeration, and then had heard them at nine years old and had never argued about it again.
It is a sound like a room full of people shaking out sheets, and it goes on for a long time, and it goes over the roofs at a height that makes the dogs mad.
You did not go out and watch.
That was the first rule and nobody had ever explained it and everybody kept it.
Bori had asked about that one more times than about anything else, and the answers were all versions of the same shrug.
Her father said you just didn't.
Her mother said it was rude.
The priest said, in a slightly evasive way, that it was a matter of respecting privacy, and did not specify whose.
The only answer that ever satisfied her came from old Feri at the workshop, who said: "Because you'd look." "That's the same thing." "No it's not.
You'd look, and you'd see whose is whose, and you'd see which windowsill's got one on it and which hasn't." He went back to the lathe.
"It's not the geese we're being polite to." You put your letter out before dark and you went in and you shut the door.
The letters were not letters in any sense a postman would recognise.

There was no envelope, no name, no address, and above all no signature — a signed one, said Bori's grandmother, is worse than useless, and the one time somebody had signed one in her lifetime the whole business had gone badly for a family that was no longer in the village to be embarrassed about it.
You wrote the thing you could not say.
That was the entire specification.
Not a wish.
Not a complaint.
Not a prayer, and the priest had been quite clear about that from the pulpit in 1988 and had privately put one out himself in 1991, which everybody knew and nobody mentioned.
The thing you could not say.
To the person you could not say it to.
In as many or as few words as it took.
Then you folded it once and put it somewhere outside — a windowsill, a fence post, the hollow in the wall by the chapel, wedged in a hedge — and you went indoors and did not look out.
In the morning they were gone.
Bori had tested this once, at ten, in a spirit of pure enquiry, and would like it recorded that she did not put out a real one to do it.
She wrote *this is not a real letter* on a piece of paper, folded it once, and put it on the sill.
It was there in the morning, damp and perfectly ordinary, and she took it in and felt obscurely told off.
Not blown about the lane, not soaked in the ditch, not caught in the fence.
Gone, all of them, every year, from a village of two hundred and six people in a country where the wind in October takes anything not nailed down.
Bori's understanding of the arrangement, at twelve, came mostly from her grandmother, who had put one out every year since 1961 and who talked about it the way other people talk about the gas bill.
The most important thing — the thing that took Bori longest to accept, and that she got wrong at first the way everybody gets it wrong at first — was that the letters are not delivered.
Nobody receives one.
Ever.
There is no story in Szentmárton about a woman in Debrecen who found a piece of paper in her yard, and no story about anybody learning anything they did not know.
Bori went looking for such a story on purpose, at seven, asking seven adults, and got nine blank looks and one raised eyebrow.
They are taken away.
Bori's first version of the arrangement, at about eight, had been the obvious one: that the geese were postmen, and that somewhere there were people opening things.
She had liked that version.
It had a shape.

She had built quite a lot on it before her grandmother took it apart in about four sentences one afternoon, and she remembers being genuinely upset, and she remembers her grandmother being entirely unsympathetic about the upset.
That is what the geese do.

They come over low on one night in October and they take the year's unsaid things out of the village, and where they go with them is not anybody's business, and Bori's grandmother had views about people who asked.
"But then what's the point?" Her grandmother was mending something and did not look up.
"Say it out loud, then.
Say the thing to the person.
Go on." Bori said that was not fair.
"It isn't fair.
I know exactly what's in mine and I've known for sixty-four years and I'd sooner have my hand in the fire than say it in this kitchen." She bit the thread.
"But I can put it down.

Once a year I can put it down and it goes somewhere and it is not in this house any more, and in the morning I can look at your grandfather across that table." Bori did not have anything to say to that.
"It isn't a solution, kislány.
It's a place to put a thing.
There aren't many, and they're worth knowing about." Bori asked her, once, and only once, whether it was the same thing every year.
Her grandmother put the mending down, which she did not do, and looked at the window for a while.
"For about thirteen years it was," she said.
"Then it stopped being, and then for a long time it was small things, and now for the last few years it's been the same one again, but it's not the same one it was at the start.
It's the other end of it." That was the entire conversation and Bori has thought about it for twenty years.
There was one more rule, which was not a rule so much as a fact everybody had learned by observation.
Once it is out, it is out.
You do not go and get it back.
Not because anything happens to you if you do.
Nothing happens to you.

Bori's uncle had gone out and retrieved his in 2009 at about half past ten, having thought better of it, and had come in with the paper in his hand and had been perfectly fine and had burnt it in the stove.
But he had not put one out since, and he was not the same at that kitchen table, and Bori's grandmother had said one sentence about it in fifteen years, which was: *he's still carrying it.*
Bori wrote hers on the eighteenth of October in a temper, at half past nine at night, sitting on her bed with the door shut.
It was about Emese.

Emese had been her friend since they were four and had started at the gimnázium in Kecskemét in September, which meant the bus at ten past six and back at seven, and which meant that Emese now had a whole life seven hours a day that Bori was not in.
That was not the problem.
Bori had understood about the bus.

The problem was a thing Emese had said on the Sunday, at the shop, in front of two girls from Kecskemét, which was not cruel and was not even untrue and which had been said in a particular voice — a slightly amused, slightly explaining voice — and which had made Bori, for about four seconds, into somebody being described rather than somebody standing there.
Emese had almost certainly not noticed doing it.
That was the worst part.
Bori had watched her not notice.

That was the thing she could not get past: she had watched Emese's face for the whole four seconds, hoping to find something in it, and there had been nothing there at all — just Emese, being funny in a shop, in a good mood, with two new people she liked.

Bori had gone over it about two hundred times by Wednesday and was completely certain that if she said anything, Emese would be baffled, and would apologise, and would mean it, and would not understand, and then Bori would have spent the thing and got nothing.
So she wrote it.
She wrote about a page.
She was not proud of the middle section then and is not now.

She said the thing about the voice, and then she said several other things that had been sitting underneath it since about March, and one of them was true and specific and would have ended it between them for good.
She folded it once and went out in the dark and put it in the hollow in the wall by the chapel, and came back in and slept better than she had in a fortnight.
That is the part she wants understood.
She slept well.
She was not tormented; she did not lie awake regretting it.
She had done the thing you are supposed to do with an unsayable thing, and she had done it properly, and she had felt the exact relief her grandmother had described.
The date was the eighteenth.
The geese came on the twenty-first, every year, give or take a day.
She had three days.
The geese came that night.
They were three days early.

They had not been three days early in living memory — there was an argument about 1974 that nobody could settle — and Bori woke at some time after midnight to the dogs going and the sound of a room full of people shaking out sheets, going over low, for a long time.
She sat up in bed in the dark with her heart hammering and understood, before she was properly awake, exactly what she had done.
She got as far as the top of the stairs.
The rule about not going out is not enforced by anything.
There is no penalty and there is no watchman and her parents were asleep.
She stood at the top of the stairs in the dark for the length of the whole flight-over, with her hand on the rail, listening to the wingbeats going over the roof, and she did not go down.

She has never been able to decide whether that was obedience or cowardice or the first genuinely adult decision of her life, and she suspects it was all three and that they are frequently the same thing.
She went to the chapel wall at first light and the hollow was empty and there was frost on the stones.
She stood there for a while in the cold doing the only useful thing available, which was working out precisely what she had lost.
It was not that Emese would read it.
Nobody reads them.
She knew that, she had always known that, and she made herself say it out loud on the road to be sure she believed it: *nobody is going to read it.* What she had lost was the sentence.
She had put down, three days early, in a temper, the true and specific thing that would have ended it — and it had gone, and it was not available to her any more.
She could remember writing it.
She could not, standing at that wall in the frost, actually get hold of the sentence.
It had the shape of a word you cannot find, and it stayed like that for the rest of her life, and she has never once been able to reconstruct it.
Which left her with the other thing.
The small one.
The one about the voice at the shop.
She said it to Emese on the Saturday, at the bus stop, badly, in about four sentences, looking at the timetable and not at Emese.
Emese was baffled, and apologised, and meant it, and did not understand.
And then, about a week later, said — out of nowhere, in the middle of something else entirely — "I do do that.
The thing you said.
I did it to Réka on Tuesday and I heard myself." They are thirty-one now.
Emese lives in Budapest and Bori does not, and they speak most weeks, and they have had one serious falling-out in the whole of that time and it was about something else.
Bori has put a letter out every October since she was fifteen.

She has never once written in a temper again — she writes hers in the first week of the month now, in daylight, at the kitchen table, and takes several days over it — and she has never gone out to retrieve one, and she has never told anybody in her family what is in them.
She has thought a great deal about what her grandmother said, and she has an addition to it that she has not said to anybody either.
Her grandmother said it was a place to put a thing.
Bori thinks it is also a way of finding out which thing was the real one.
You can only put out one.

You sit down with everything you have been carrying, and you have to choose, and the choosing is the whole of it — because whatever you write down is going away for good, and whatever you do not write down is the thing you are going to have to say out loud to somebody at a bus stop.

Block C had a landing on every floor with a window in it, and the window on the fourth floor did not shut properly, and this was the reason Nadia heard it and the reason she spent four months believing she was the only one who did.
The gap was about the width of two fingers at the top corner of the frame.
In summer it was a good thing.
In November it meant that the fourth-floor landing was the coldest place in the building and that you went up the last flight quickly.

She heard it for the first time on the ninth of November at about twenty past ten, coming up with the recycling, which was not a job she was supposed to be doing at twenty past ten and which she had volunteered for in order to be out of the flat for fourteen minutes.
Her brother had people round.
That was the fourteen minutes.

Her brother was seventeen and had reached the stage of having people round who filled the whole flat with a specific kind of loudness, and Nadia had discovered that the recycling took fourteen minutes if you did it slowly and that nobody ever questioned a person carrying a bag.
Something said her name.
Not her name.
That is the whole of this story and it needs to be right the first time.

It said the other one — the middle one, the one on her documents and nowhere else, the one that had been her grandmother's and her grandmother's grandmother's, three syllables long, with a sound in the middle of it that does not exist in the language she does her homework in.
It said it clearly, at a conversational volume, from somewhere just outside the gap in the window.
Nadia put the bag down on the landing and did not move for a considerable time.
Then she went up to the flat and put the chain on the door and sat on her bed with her coat still on.
Her brother's friends were still in the front room.
Somebody was laughing at something on a phone.
It went on being an entirely ordinary Tuesday on the other side of her bedroom wall for another two hours, and Nadia sat on the bed in her coat for most of it.
She had been at that school for twenty weeks.
She had registered on the first day as Nadia K., because the form had a box for a middle name and she had left it empty, and the woman in the office had not asked.
Nobody in that building, that school, or that city knew the middle name.
Her mother knew it.
Her brother knew it and had been paid, in a formal arrangement involving actual money, not to use it.
And something on the fourth-floor landing had said it out loud into an empty stairwell at twenty past ten at night.
The first three explanations she tried were all sensible and all failed within about a day.
That somebody had seen the documents — but the documents were in a folder in her mother's wardrobe and had not been out of it since the school registration in September.

That her brother had broken the arrangement — but he had not been in the building, he had been at football, and when she checked his phone location history two days later in a way she is not proud of, he had been at football.
That she had misheard something else.
She gave this one four days and a great deal of effort, because it was the one she wanted.
She sat on that landing and tried to make ordinary sounds turn into those three syllables.
It cannot be done.
The middle sound does not exist in this country and there is nothing in a stairwell that makes it.
It is difficult to explain to an adult why a name is worth this much trouble, and Nadia has stopped trying.

The short version is that they had been in the country for two years and four months, and that the first eighteen of those had been in a different city, and that in the different city she had been herself and it had gone badly.
Not dramatically.
Nobody had done anything to her that would go in a report.

It had been six months of a particular kind of attention — of being asked to say it again, of watching a teacher decide not to attempt it in front of the register, of a boy in the year above who had made it into a noise and had done the noise, cheerfully, without malice, for most of a spring.
The worst of it was not the boy.
The boy was straightforward and Nadia had known what to do about the boy by about the fourth week, which was nothing, and it had worn out on its own by June the way those things do.
The worst of it was the teachers who were kind about it.

There was a woman who taught geography who used to stop at Nadia's name in the register every single time, and take a small breath, and attempt it, and get it not quite right, and then smile at her — a warm, apologetic, completely well-meant smile that took about a second and a half and that happened in front of twenty-nine people, four times a week, for a year.
Nadia has thought about this a great deal since and has arrived at something she finds difficult to say out loud, which is that she would rather have had the boy.
She had arrived in the new city in September with a plan.
The plan was Nadia K.
The plan was that Nadia is a name that exists in a dozen languages and belongs to nobody, that K.
is a letter, and that there is no purchase on either of them.
The plan had worked.
That is the part nobody ever wants to hear.
It had worked completely.
She had four people she ate lunch with and one she messaged in the evenings, and in twenty weeks not one person had asked her to say anything twice.
So when a voice on a landing said the other name, what she felt was not wonder.
She told her mother nothing.

She would not have known how to start, and there was a second reason underneath the first, which was that her mother had cried about the name business exactly once, in the old city, in a car, and Nadia had decided that afternoon that it was never going to happen again on her account.
For three weeks she took the stairs two at a time past the fourth floor.
Then, on the second of December, she stopped on the landing on purpose, and stood by the gap in the window in the cold with her hands in her sleeves, and waited.
It took about four minutes.

It was very close — the other side of the glass, on the sill outside, where there was a ledge about a hand's width — and it said the name once and then made the other noise that owls make, the one that is not a hoot and that sounds like a hinge.
Nadia leaned over and looked, and there it was.
She found out about the rest of the building by accident, in the lift, from Mr Petrov on the sixth floor, who was about eighty and who had a way of starting conversations in the middle.
He said: "You have been standing on the fourth landing." Nadia said she had been taking the recycling down.
"For twenty minutes.
On Tuesday." The lift went past two.
"It is all right.
I have also stood there." She said nothing at all.
The lift in Block C is slow and there are six floors and there is nowhere to look.
"Konstantin," said Mr Petrov.
"Not Kostya.
Not Kolya.
Konstantin, the whole thing, which nobody has said in this country since my mother died in 1994." The lift stopped.
"It gets it right, also.
The stress in the correct place.
Which the bank does not." She rode up to six with him and then down to four and then up to six again, because he was talking.
What she found out over that week, and over the following month, by asking about fourteen people in a building of forty-four flats, was this.
The owl said everybody's.

Not everybody heard it — you had to be on a landing at night, and most people are not on landings at night, and a great many of the ones who are had put it down to a bird making a noise that sounded a bit like something.
But the ones who had heard it properly had all heard the same category of thing: the name that is not the one on the buzzer.
Mrs Óspina on two, who had been Mercedes Alejandra for sixty-one years and had been Mrs Óspina for thirty of them.

A boy in the year above Nadia at school whose family had been in the country for four generations and whose middle name was his great-grandfather's and was, he said, "properly embarrassing," and who had heard it twice and told nobody until Nadia asked him directly in a corridor.
The building's caretaker, who said he did not believe in any of it and then, after a pause of about eight seconds, said his was Ferenc.
There were two people who had heard nothing and were annoyed about it.

And there was Mrs Deniz on five, who had heard it, and who had come out onto the landing with a broom, and who had been extremely clear with Nadia that she considered the whole thing an intrusion and that a name is private property and that she had written to the committee about the window.
Nadia thought about that one for a long time afterwards, because Mrs Deniz was not wrong.
It is an intrusion.
Something outside a window in the dark knows a thing about you that you have gone to considerable trouble to keep, and it says it out loud without being asked.
It only stops being an intrusion if you happen to be glad, and there is no version of the arrangement in which the owl checks first.
Nadia asked Mr Petrov, in the end, what he thought the owl was doing.

He said that was the wrong question and that she should ask a better one, which annoyed her a great deal at the time and which she has since decided was the single most useful thing anybody said to her that year.
The better question took her until about February.
The better question was: *why does it only say the middle one?* Because it does.
Nobody in Block C has ever reported hearing their first name out of that window.
Nadia has now asked, over nine years, something like thirty people, and the answer has never varied.
It says the one that is not in use.
Which means — and this is the part she worked out on a landing in February with her hands in her sleeves, and which she has never had a better theory for since — that it is not identifying anybody.
If it wanted to identify her it would say Nadia.
Nadia is what she answers to; Nadia is on the buzzer and the register and the library card.
Saying the other one is, as an act of identification, useless.
It is doing the opposite thing.
It is saying the part that is not being used, to the one person who knows it is not being used, in an empty stairwell, at night, where nobody else can hear.
Mr Petrov, when she put this to him in the lift in March, listened to all of it and then said only: "Yes." "Yes what?" "Yes, that is what it is doing." The lift went past four.
"You wanted me to say whether it is a good thing.
I am not going to.

Mrs Deniz thinks it is not, and Mrs Deniz has buried two husbands and I have buried none, so I have stopped assuming I know." She told her mother in April, in the kitchen, and did not manage it well, and her mother did not cry, and they sat there for a while afterwards not saying much.
Nadia is Nadia at work.

She wants that clear, because people who hear this story sometimes want it to end with her changing everything back, and she did not, and she does not intend to, and she does not think that would have been braver.
What she did do, when she was nineteen, was write it — all three syllables, correctly, with the sound in the middle — on the inside cover of every notebook she owns, where nobody else looks.

And she lived in Block C until she was twenty-three, and for the last four of those years she went up to the fourth-floor landing perhaps once a month, at night, in the cold, and stood by the gap in the window until something on the ledge outside said it out loud in the right voice with the stress in the right place.
The window has been fixed now.

She has been back twice and it shuts perfectly, and she has heard nothing either time, and she is entirely at peace about this and has told the building's committee that they did the right thing, which was a lie.
A ptarmigan in winter is white, and this is the least interesting thing about a ptarmigan.
Isla's great-grandmother had made this point to her at least thirteen times, always in the same slightly irritated tone, as though somebody had just that moment suggested otherwise.
Lots of things are white in the snow.
The hare goes white.
The stoat goes white.
Being white is easy and it does not work very well, because snow is not one colour and a white thing on it casts a shadow and has an edge.
Isla had been made to prove this to herself at about eight, on the slope behind the house, with a white plastic bag and a good deal of complaining.
Her great-grandmother had put the bag in the snow forty metres off and told her to find it, and Isla had found it in under two seconds and had said so, at some volume.
"Aye," the old woman had said.
"That's white.

Now find the bird." What the ptarmigan does is different, and Isla did not properly understand it until she was eleven and had spent forty minutes on the ridge above Cnoc Dubh looking directly at a bird she had been told was four metres away.
They do not hide themselves.
They hide.
They sit in a scoop in the lee of a stone, where the light is already flat, and they do not move at all, and the not-moving is not stillness — it is a positive act, sustained, for hours.
Everything about the animal is arranged to remove the two things an eye is actually looking for, which are the outline and the change.
The feathers go right down over the feet so there are no legs to make a line.
The black tail is tucked.
The eye, which is the one thing that cannot be white, is held behind the rock.
And when you do finally see one, you cannot then un-see it, and you sit there feeling foolish, and seventeen metres away there is another one you also cannot see.
The moment of seeing is the strangest part and it does not get less strange with practice.

There is nothing there, and there is nothing there, and there is nothing there — and then there is a bird, entire, obvious, four metres away, in a place your eye has crossed perhaps two hundred times in the last half hour.
Nothing has changed.
The bird did not move; that is precisely what it has been not doing.
What changed is on your side, and it happens all at once, and it cannot be undone: once you have seen that bird you will see it every time you look at it for the rest of the afternoon.
Which means, and Isla worked this out on the ridge at eleven with her hands going numb, that the entire trick is being run against something in your head rather than against your eyes.
"That," said her great-grandmother, "is the whole business.
It is not about looking like snow.
It is about not being findable." She was ninety-four that year.
She had been eleven herself in 1953.
Isla had heard the story of the storm since she was small and had heard it the way you hear a family story, which is to say in fragments, out of order, with the ending known before the beginning.

She got it properly in one go, on a wet afternoon in October, with a recorder on the table, because her school had set a local history project and Isla had realised on the bus that she was sitting on the best one in the county.
Her great-grandmother talked for fifty-one minutes and Isla did not interrupt once.
The storm came in on the second of February 1953 and it was, in that part of the country, the worst in a hundred years.
It is in the books.
There were people killed in it on the east coast and there was a ferry lost and the number is in every account of that winter.
At Cnoc Dubh there were fourteen houses in a hollow under the ridge, with a road in from the pass and nothing else.

Fourteen houses, sixty-one people, one telephone in the schoolroom that had gone with the line on the second night, and enough coal and meal in every house to sit out a fortnight without anybody thinking about it twice, because that was simply how you lived there in February.
That is the detail that people always miss, her great-grandmother said, and it is the one that matters most.
Nobody in that hollow was in trouble.
They were not running short and they were not frightened and they were not waiting to be found.
They were snowed in, in the ordinary way, in a place where being snowed in was a thing that happened most years and was chiefly a nuisance about the milk.
The road went on the first night.
That was normal; the road went most winters.

What was not normal was the second night, when the power line came down, and the third day, when the drifts across the mouth of the hollow were high enough that a man could walk over the top of a telegraph pole and one of them did, on purpose, to say he had.
By the fourth day the county had decided that Cnoc Dubh was a problem.
They sent a party from Ardmore, over the pass, thirteen men on foot with poles.
This is in the county record and Isla has since read the record, which is one paragraph long and extremely dry.
The party went over the pass on the morning of the fifth.
They came back to Ardmore that evening and reported that they had been unable to reach the settlement.
Isla found the actual wording in the county archive in Inverness, which took her two letters and a train.
*Party unable to reach Cnoc Dubh owing to conditions.
Returned 1740.* That is it.
Thirteen men, a full day on the hill in February, and one line.

She sat in the reading room and looked at it for a while and understood something about records that has stayed with her, which is that the paper is not the event; the paper is what somebody had the energy to write down at the end of a very long day.
They went again on the sixth, in better weather, with a local man who had been born in the hollow.
They came back and reported the same.
On the seventh an aircraft went over.
That is also in the record.
It flew the length of the glen at low level in clear conditions and reported no sign of the houses and no smoke.

And in the hollow, on the fifth, and the sixth, and the seventh, fourteen houses had their fires lit and their chimneys going and thirteen children were being made to do lessons at kitchen tables, and nobody in Cnoc Dubh had the faintest idea that anybody was looking for them.
Isla's history teacher liked the project very much and had one objection, which was reasonable, and which Isla had already thought of on the bus home.
Drifting.
Whiteout.
A hollow under a ridge fills, the geography changes shape, and a party on foot in a hundred-year storm walks past the mouth of a glen they think they know.
It happens.
It has happened many times, it is in mountain rescue literature, and there is nothing whatever mysterious about it.
The aircraft was harder but not impossible.
Low cloud on the seventh, said the teacher.
Wrong glen.
Smoke does not rise in that kind of cold; it lies down in the hollow and looks like more snow.
Isla wrote all of that in the project, fairly, in its own section, because her great-grandmother had told her to.
That was the thing that surprised her most about the whole business.
She had expected the old woman to defend it.
Instead, when Isla brought the objections back and put them on the table like an accusation, her great-grandmother listened to all of them and said: "Aye.
That'll be it, likely." Isla had come in ready for an argument and had a page of notes, and found herself entirely without a use for either.
"You don't believe that." "I didn't say I believed it.
I said it'll be it." She was doing something with her hands that she had done for eighty years.

"There's a difference between what happened and what you can say happened, and you're eleven, and it's about time you learnt which one goes in a school project." Then she said the other thing, which is the reason Isla has never stopped thinking about any of it.
She said that on the fifth of February 1953, at first light, she had gone out to the peat stack, and there had been a ptarmigan sitting in the scoop on the top of the ridge directly above the hollow.
That it had been there on the sixth.

That it had been there on the seventh, and that her father had seen it too, and that her father — who was not a fanciful man, who kept accounts, who had no patience with any of this — had stood in the yard looking up at the ridge with a bucket in his hand for a long time and had then come in and said nothing at all.
And that on the morning of the eighth it was gone, and by eleven o'clock the party from Ardmore came over the top and down into the hollow without any difficulty whatsoever.
Isla asked the obvious question, which was whether her great-grandmother thought the bird had done it.
The answer took a while.

"I think there was a bird on that ridge for three days and I think on the fourth day there wasn't, and I think thirteen men walked into this glen on the fourth day who couldn't find it on the second." She looked at Isla.
"That's what I know.
Everything past that is what I'd be making up, and I'm ninety-four, and I've watched a lot of people make things up about that week, and I've never once done it and I'm not starting now."
Isla is fifteen now and Cnoc Dubh has six houses in it and a tarmac road that is cleared by a machine from Ardmore, usually within a day.
Her great-grandmother died in the March after the project.
The storm came on the eleventh of December and it was not a 1953 storm and nobody has pretended otherwise.
It was a bad one.
The road went, the power went for nine hours, and the school in Ardmore was shut for three days, and the whole thing was on the regional news for about ninety seconds.
Isla went out on the second morning to see to the hens.
It was flat white and there was no wind at all, which is the thing that happens after, and the ridge above the hollow was a clean grey line against a sky the colour of a plate.
She stood in the yard with the feed bucket and looked up at the scoop.

She looked for a long time — long enough that her hands went, long enough that her mother came to the door and asked her what on earth she was doing — and she did not see anything at all, and she went in.
She has thought about this a great deal.
If it was there, she could not have seen it.
That is not a get-out; that is the entire, well-documented, un-mysterious biology of the animal.
Isla has sat four metres from a ptarmigan on a bare ridge in daylight and been unable to find it while being told exactly where to look.

So the honest position, and the one she has settled on, is that she does not know whether there was a bird on the ridge above her house on the twelfth of December, and that there is no available method by which she could have found out, and that this is not a failure of the investigation.
It is what the animal is.
What she does know is that the machine from Ardmore came on the fourteenth and that everybody was fine.
She goes out and looks anyway, every time, and she is aware that this is not evidence of anything.

Her mother thinks it is a habit picked up from an old woman and is gently amused by it, and Isla lets her think that, because the alternative is a conversation she does not want to have on a doorstep in the cold.
She has been up to the scoop once in summer, in July, when they are brown and much easier.
There is a hollow in the peat up there about the size of a dinner plate, in the lee of a stone, worn smooth, facing directly down the glen at the fourteen — now six — chimneys of Cnoc Dubh.
She did not measure it.
She sat beside it for a while and then went down.
The office was under the root of a beech on the boundary bank, and Orla got into it the way everybody gets into these things, which is by losing something and being unreasonable about it.
The thing she had lost was a watch.
It had been her grandfather's, it had come to her in April when he died, it had not worked since about 2011, and she had worn it every day since the funeral on a strap that was four holes too big.
She lost it in the wood on the ninth of October, and she knew exactly where, and it was not there.
She knew exactly where because she had felt it go.
