She had been climbing the bank at the far end by the stile, had put her hand down into the bracken to steady herself, and had felt the strap slide over her knuckles — a sensation so specific that she had stopped and looked at her wrist before she had even finished thinking about it.
Four holes too big.
She had been meaning to have a hole punched in it since May.
She went back twenty times.
She took a rake.
She took a metal detector belonging to a neighbour, which found two bottle tops and a horseshoe and put her in a very bad mood.

On the twelfth visit, in November, in the rain, she was on her hands and knees under the beech on the boundary bank with her arm down a hole between two roots, and something the other end took hold of her sleeve and pulled twice.
The hole was not on the bank by the stile.
It was two hundred metres away and she had no reason to be at it except that she had by then searched everywhere with a reason and had started on the places without one.
She did not scream.
She has thought about this since with a certain amount of pride.

What she did was take her arm out very slowly and sit back and look at the hole, and the hole looked back at her, and after a moment a badger came about a third of the way out of it and stopped, with its stripes on and its nose going, at a distance of perhaps forty centimetres.
It considered her for a while.
Then it went back down, and there was a sound like a drawer, and it came up again with something in its mouth and put it on the leaf mould between them.
It was a bottle top.
It was, she saw when she picked it up, quite an old one — the crimped kind, rusted right through in one place, with a lettering on the top that had gone.

Orla, who had had a very frustrating month, said, "That's not mine." The badger looked at the bottle top, and looked at her, and made a noise in its throat that she has never been able to describe and has never mistaken for anything else since, and went back down the hole.

She sat under that tree in the rain for another quarter of an hour, and when nothing else happened she went home and did not tell anybody, and came back on the Saturday with a torch and a good deal of nerve.
The office was not what she expected, and it took her four visits before she was let far enough in to see any of it properly.
The entrance under the root opens after about a metre and a half into a chamber that a person can sit up in if they do not mind their hair in the roof.
It is dry.
That was the first shock: it is completely dry, in a wood, in November, and Orla never worked out how.
The second shock was the light.
There is some.
Not much — enough to see shapes by after your eyes have had four or five minutes — and it does not come from anywhere.
There is no gap in the roof; she looked, on three separate visits, with a torch, thoroughly.
The light is simply the amount of light there is in that chamber, and it is the same at eleven in the morning and at half past four in December.
The things are in the walls.
Not piled.

Set into the earth in rows, each one pressed into its own small socket, the way you would set eggs into a box, and the rows go round the chamber and back into two passages that Orla was never allowed down.
She counted a hundred and seventeen things on her fourth visit before she gave up counting.

Counting was hard because the sockets go back into the passages and because she was not allowed to move anything, which was made clear to her early and unmistakably on the third visit when she reached for a key and got a noise she did not need translated.
A spectacle case.
Four knives.
A shoe.
A child's shoe and separately a man's boot, not a pair, not near each other.
A watch that was not her grandfather's.
A brooch.
A key with a wooden tag.
Six or twelve coins, none of them together.
A comb.
A thing that turned out, when she got a proper look at it, to be a set of false teeth.
And the catalogue.
The catalogue is on the floor of the chamber and it is not written and it is not a book.
It is marks.
There are marks on the packed earth of the floor, hundreds of them, in rows, cut in with a claw and re-cut, and each mark is directly below the socket of the thing it belongs to.
Orla could not read it and never learned to.

What she learned instead — over about six weeks, by pointing at things and being answered in the only way available, which was that the badger would take a thing out of the wall and turn it and put it back — was what the catalogue was *for*.
It was not an inventory.
It did not say what the thing was.
She established that beyond doubt when she pointed at the false teeth and got shown, in the marks, something nine strokes long.
It said what the thing had been doing when it was lost.
That sentence took her three weeks to arrive at and about a year to believe, and she would like to set out the evidence, because it sounds like something a child decided and it was not.
Two identical objects had different entries.
There were two ordinary iron keys in that wall, the same size, the same pattern, almost certainly from the same kind of lock.
One had an entry of four strokes.
The other had an entry of nine.
And one entry served two completely different objects.
The comb and one of the coins had the same mark under them — she checked this four times, on different days, from different angles, and once lay flat on the floor with a torch to be sure.
Whatever the catalogue was recording, it was not what the things were.

Her grandfather's watch was in the wall, third row, near the left-hand passage, and she saw it on the second visit and said so out loud in a voice that came out wrong, and the badger did not give it to her.
That was November.
She spent from November to March trying to get it.
She would like to be clear that the badger never refused her and never drove her off.
It did not hide the watch or block the row.

On perhaps half her visits it would take the watch out of the wall itself, without being asked, and put it on the floor between them and sit there — and if she reached for it, it would put a paw on it, and that was all, and there was never any question of a struggle.
She tried asking.
She tried asking politely.
She tried explaining, at length, out loud, in a hole in the ground, that it was hers, that it had been her grandfather's, that he had died in April, and that she wanted it back.
The badger listened to all of it every time — it always listened, it never once went away while she was talking — and did not give her the watch.
In January she brought a photograph of her grandfather, which she now finds embarrassing.
In February she got angry and said a number of things she regretted on the walk home.

In the first week of March she came in wet and cold and out of ideas and sat down on the floor of the chamber and said, "I don't know what you want." And the badger came over and put one claw on the floor and drew her grandfather's entry, slowly, twice, and then sat back.
Orla looked at it for a long time.
It was seven strokes.
She could not read it.

But she had by then spent four months watching that animal draw entries, and she had understood some time in February — without being able to prove it, and without ever telling anybody, because there is no way to say it that does not sound mad — that the entries were not descriptions of objects.
Seven strokes was not *a watch*.
Seven strokes was whatever the watch had been doing, on the ninth of October, on the wrist of an eleven-year-old girl in a wood.
And Orla, sitting on the floor with her back against the earth, realised that she did not know.
She knew what the watch was.
She did not know what it had been doing.
She did not know why it had stopped in 2011 and she did not know why he had gone on wearing it stopped for fourteen years, and she had never asked him, and she was not going to be able to now.
She asked her grandmother in the last week of March, in the kitchen at Ballyroe, sitting down, having planned the question for three days and then abandoning the plan entirely and just asking it.
Why did he wear a watch that didn't work.
Her grandmother put the tea down.

She said that it had stopped on the eleventh of June 2011, which was a Saturday, and that they had both been in the car outside the hospital in Galway at the time, and that they had been in that car park for a very long while that afternoon and had not gone in, and that the watch had stopped somewhere in that.

She said that he had taken it to be fixed twice and had brought it back both times unfixed, and that on the second occasion the man in Galway had told him it would cost twenty euro and forty minutes, and that he had said no thank you and had walked out.

She said that Orla should not make it into more than it was, because he had never once explained himself about it, and that she had asked him exactly twice in fourteen years and had been told, both times, that he was fond of it.
Then she said: "But he checked it.
That's the thing I'd say if you're wanting a thing to hold.
He'd look at it.

Two, three times in a day, all those years, he'd turn his wrist over and look at a watch that said twenty past four, and then he'd get on with what he was at." Orla went back to the wood on the second of April.
She sat down on the floor of the chamber and she said it out loud, all of it, the whole thing, taking about four minutes and getting it in the wrong order and having to go back twice.
The badger listened, the way it always listened.

Then it went to the third row near the left-hand passage and took the watch out of the wall and put it on the floor between them, and went back down one of the passages she was never allowed down, and Orla sat there on her own for a while and then went home.
She is thirty-four.
The watch says twenty past four.
She has never had it fixed and has been asked about it perhaps a hundred times, and what she says is that she is fond of it.

She has been back to the beech on the boundary bank six or seven times as an adult, and the hole is there, and she has never once put her arm down it, and she thinks about the hundred and five other things in that wall more often than she expected to.
Because that is the part that got her, in the end, and it took her until her twenties to see it properly.
The catalogue is complete.
Every single thing in that wall has an entry, and every entry says what the thing was doing, and the badger has kept all of it dry since 1911.
And almost nobody is ever going to come and say it.
Everything a net brings up that is not a fish gets thrown back, and Iro had been throwing it back since she was seven.
That was the job.
It was her job on her uncle's boat and it had been her mother's job on the same boat and it was, as far as Iro could tell, the entry-level position in the whole of the eastern Aegean.
You stand at the sorting table with the catch coming out of the net and you pull out what does not belong, and the fish go one way and the rest goes over the side.
The rest is mostly weed and stones and plastic.
Mostly plastic, if she is honest, and the proportion had changed in her lifetime in a way that nobody on that boat ever said out loud.
Her uncle had a word for the whole category and the word was not complimentary and it covered a fifteenth-century amphora sherd and a supermarket bag equally.
But not entirely.

Over six years Iro had put back a bicycle wheel, a printer, a great many single shoes, a mannequin's arm that had caused a considerable amount of shouting, and, on one morning in the March she was ten, a brass compass with a cracked glass that had made her uncle stop what he was doing and hold it for a while and then say, "Over." She had said it seemed a shame.
"It's a compass with no glass off a boat that sank before I was born," he said.
"What do you want me to do with it?
Put it in the house?" There was a version of the argument Iro could have made and did not, at ten, because she did not have the words for it yet.
It was that the compass was not rubbish and was not treasure and that the boat had no category for a third thing.
She had thought about that for years afterwards, because he was right and because she had also been right, and she had never worked out how both could be true at once.

The compass went over the side at about half past five in the morning three miles off Panormos, and Iro watched it go down through water so clear that she could follow it for what felt like an extremely long way.
And something came up and took it.
Not a fish.
Fish do not do that.

What came up out of the dark under the boat was pale and enormous and moved in a way that made her stomach turn over, and it came up perhaps four metres, and one arm went out and closed on the compass in mid-water, and the whole of it folded and was gone.
Iro did not say anything to her uncle.
She has never been able to explain why, and the closest she can get is that she was ten, and she had watched something happen that was clearly none of her business.
She thought about it for the rest of that day and most of that year.

The obvious explanation was the right one and she knew it even then: an octopus took a shiny object in mid-water, which is a thing they do, and which is on film, and which nobody who works on that sea would find worth mentioning at breakfast.
What stopped her was the timing.
It had come up before the compass reached it.

She had watched the brass going down and she had watched the pale thing coming up to meet it, and the two had arrived at the same point at the same moment, which meant it had started before it could have seen the compass at all.
It had started when the compass hit the water.
She found the shelves the following August, free-diving off the rocks at Agriolivado, which she was not supposed to do alone and did every day of every summer holiday of her childhood.
There is a ledge down there at about eight metres where the rock steps out and then goes on down into a slot too narrow for a person.
Iro had known that ledge since she was small.

What she had not known — because you cannot see it from above and because you have to be lying flat and looking sideways — was that under the overhang the rock has eight horizontal cracks in it, running back into the dark, one above the other, like a bookcase left out in the weather.
They were full.
She got about a second and a half of looking on the first dive, and eleven or twelve seconds on the fourth, and by the end of that August she had a fair idea.
Eight metres is not deep.
Eight metres is a nuisance: it is deep enough that you have perhaps twenty usable seconds on the bottom at thirteen years old, and shallow enough that you feel foolish for not having more.
She went down that ledge perhaps two hundred times that August.

She did it in the flat hour after lunch when the water goes glassy and the boats are in, and she did it with a mask that leaked, and she came up each time with about two shelves' worth of information in her head and lost half of it on the way to the surface.
A shelf of cups.
Not one kind — a tin mug, a china cup with no handle, a plastic beaker, a thing that might have been a chalice and was probably a trophy.
A shelf of things you hold up to your eye.
The compass was on it.
So were a pair of spectacles, a small brass telescope in bad condition, and something Iro is fairly sure was a broken camera.
A shelf of shoes, all of them singles.
A shelf of things with edges: knives, a plane blade, half a pair of scissors, a razor.

And so on, eight of them, down to the bottom shelf, which was the hardest to see and which held things Iro could never quite categorise until she was about fifteen and worked it out in the middle of a maths lesson: they were all things that had held something else.
A tin.
A wallet.
A box.
A shoe would have gone on the shoe shelf, but a purse went here.
She has never seen the octopus at the shelves.
She wants that stated plainly, because it is the weakest part of the whole account and because people always assume she has.
She has seen one on that ledge twice in thirty years, both times moving, neither time doing anything.
The den — if there is a den — is somewhere down the slot, and the slot goes into the rock at an angle and Iro has looked into it with a torch and seen nothing but rock.
The arrangement is not by material and it is not by size and it is not by age.
There is a plastic beaker two centimetres from a bronze cup.
It is by what the thing was for.
She told him when she was fifteen, and she chose the moment badly, which was on the boat, at the sorting table, with a net coming up.

He listened to the whole thing without stopping work, which is his way, and at the end of it he said: "So there's an octopus with a shelf of cups." "Eight shelves." "An octopus," said her uncle, "with eight shelves." He put a fish in the box.
"Iro, they collect.
That is a thing they do.
They pick up shells and stones and bottle tops and they pile them round the den.
There's a word for it.
It's in the books." She said she knew that.
She said she had read the books, which was true; she had read every book about them the library on the island had, which was two.
She said that piling things round a den is not the same as putting all the cups on one shelf and all the shoes on another.
Her uncle worked for a while without answering, which with him is not avoidance; it is the answer being assembled.
"So it likes cups." He said it without any cruelty at all, which made it worse, and he handed her a bucket.
"It doesn't like cups.
There's a plastic beaker next to a bronze one.

It's not liking anything, it's *sorting* —" "For what?" And Iro stopped, because she had no answer, and because the thing her uncle had done was the only useful thing anybody did for her in six years of thinking about it.
*For what.* An octopus that piles shells round a den is doing something with an obvious purpose: it is building a wall.
Every book says so.
The pile is a defence and the animal moves in behind it.
Nothing on those eight shelves was a wall.
She measured it, eventually, at nineteen, with a slate and a pencil, over four dives.
The shelves are set back under an overhang in cracks too shallow to hide in, arranged along a face that faces out.
If you wanted to hide behind that stuff you would have to bring it out and heap it up, which would take about an hour, and would work, and is not what has been done.
The things are set out.
There is a difference between a heap and a display and every human being alive can tell them apart at a glance, and Iro has never met anybody who could say what the difference consists of.

They are set out where a thing swimming past at the level of the ledge would see them, and they are set out in an order, and the order is not one that any octopus has any use for whatsoever — because *what a thing is for* is a fact about people.
A cup is only a cup if you know about drinking.
A compass is a lump of brass unless you know about being lost.
Iro is thirty-nine.
She works for the port authority and she dives most weekends and the ledge at Agriolivado is still there.
The shelves are still there.
Some of the things have changed.

The mannequin's arm turned up on the fourth shelf about eleven years ago, which she took personally and which she has never mentioned to her uncle, who is seventy-six and who has not been over the side of a boat since 2009 and who still says *over* about anything that is not a fish.
She has had a long time to think about it and she has three positions, and she holds all three at once, which she has stopped apologising for.
The first is her uncle's and it is almost certainly correct.
Octopuses collect.
They are extremely clever and they manipulate objects constantly and they arrange the things round a den.
Any pattern she has found in eight cracks in a rock is a pattern she has brought with her, and a person who dives the same ledge for thirty years will find whatever they went down for.
This position is dull and well supported and she has never been able to knock it over.
The second is that the order is real.
She has photographs.
She has, in a folder, six hundred pictures of those eight shelves taken over twenty years, and the categories hold.
Things have moved shelf — the broken camera was on the edges shelf for a season and then was not — and every move she has recorded has been in the direction of a better fit, never a worse one.
The third is the one she does not say out loud very often.
She said it once, at a conference in Heraklion, to a marine biologist she had been talking to for about an hour and who had been extremely interested up to that point.
The conversation ended shortly afterwards in a friendly way and the woman was perfectly nice about it.
Iro does not blame her and would probably have done the same.
It is that the shelves are not for the octopus.
Everything about them is arranged for something with eyes at the height of that ledge, that swims past, that understands what a cup is.
There is exactly one animal in that sea that fits, and it is the animal that has been throwing things over the side of boats off Panormos since before anybody kept records.
Somebody down there has been sorting our rubbish for a very long time, by what we made it for, and putting it out along a face where we would find it.
Iro has never taken anything off those shelves.

She took the compass back once, in 2011, having found a second one in a junk shop in Kalymnos — the same pattern, the glass intact — and she put it on the ledge at the end of the second shelf, and came up, and went home.
It was on the shelf, in the row, in the right place, the following weekend.
It has been there fourteen years and it has never moved, and she checks every time, and she has never worked out whether that means it was accepted or whether it means nothing at all.
There was a word for what was happening to Joaquim and by the end of that spring he had heard every adult he knew avoid it.
His mother said *your eyes*.
The consultant in Porto said *the condition* and then, when pressed, said the actual name in a fast quiet way, once, and went back to *the condition*.
His aunt said *this business*.

His grandfather, who was in general the most reliable person in the house, said *what you've got*, which was somehow the worst of the lot because his grandfather did not otherwise talk like that about anything.
The word is retinitis pigmentosa.
It is not a difficult word.

Joaquim had looked it up in the second week and had been reading about it steadily ever since, and he was thirteen and he knew a great deal more about it than most of the people carefully not saying it in front of him.
What it means, in his case, is that the outside is going first.
That is the part nobody outside the house ever gets right.
People assume it is like a light going down.
It is not.
It is the edges: the field narrows, slowly, unevenly, over years, so that what he has is a good clear middle and a growing amount of nothing round it.
He can read a page.
He cannot see the person standing beside the page.
By that spring he had walked into three door frames, a bollard, and, in front of most of his year, a fire extinguisher.
The fire extinguisher is the one people always want to hear about and it was not the bad one.

The bad one was a Tuesday in April when he put his hand out for a glass on the kitchen table and the glass was not where his hand went, and he knocked it, and his mother came across the room fast — genuinely fast, at a speed she had no reason to be capable of — and caught it before it went off the edge.
Neither of them said anything.
She put it back in the middle of the table, four centimetres from where it had been, and went back to what she was doing.
Joaquim sat there and understood that she had been watching his hands for some time.
And what he had noticed — what he had come to mind far more than the door frames — was that people had started arranging themselves.
His mother put things away.
His aunt moved chairs.
At school there was a system, which nobody had discussed with him, whereby a boy called Rafa was always somehow on his left in a corridor.
All of it was kind.
All of it was done by people who loved him.

And all of it happened in a silence so complete that Joaquim had begun to feel that the actual event — the thing occurring inside his own head — was a subject the entire world had agreed to handle by rearranging the furniture.
He started going up to the attic in the evenings because it was the only room in the house nobody had prepared.
His grandfather's house had a lot of rooms and every one of them had been quietly gone over.
The rug in the hall had gone.
The low table in the front room had gone.

The chest on the landing had moved back against the wall in about February and nobody had ever remarked on it and Joaquim had walked past its new position four hundred times without once mentioning that he had noticed.
The attic had a ladder and boxes and a water tank and no plan.
The attic at his grandfather's was reached by a ladder and had one bulb that had not worked since before Joaquim was born.
He went up in the dark on purpose.
That was the point of it.
In the dark his condition was irrelevant, because in the dark nobody has any edges, and for an hour a night he was exactly as capable as anybody else in the world, which is to say not very.
He sat with his back against a trunk and did nothing at all.
It was the only hour of his day in which nothing was being managed.
He would like that understood without it sounding like a complaint about his family, because it is not one.
Every single thing they did was the right thing and he would have done the same.

But there is a particular tiredness in being the object of continuous careful attention, and it does not go away by being grateful for the attention, and at thirteen he had no way at all of saying so.
In the dark of that attic he was not the boy whose eyes were going.
He was a person sitting in a dark room, which is a thing anybody can be, and it was restful in a way he has never quite got back.
He heard her on the fourth or fifth evening.
Not the flying — he had heard the flying from the first night and had assumed birds.
What he heard on the fourth or fifth evening, when he had been sitting still long enough, was the other thing.
It is a series of clicks and it is mostly too high for a person.
What comes down into human range is the low edge of it: a fast dry ticking, right at the top of what an ear will take, that goes across the room and comes back.
He could not hear all of it and he knows that now.

What reaches a thirteen-year-old ear is the bottom of the range and there was a great deal going on above it, and one of the strange satisfactions of his twenties has been putting equipment on that attic and finding out how much he had been missing.
At the time he had the low edge and it was enough.
She was working.
That is the word he arrived at and has never improved on.
It was not flapping about.
It was a search pattern — out along the ridge beam, down the gable, across, back — with the ticking speeding up whenever she came near anything and slowing when she was in open air.
Joaquim sat in the pitch dark of that attic and listened to something map a room.
It took perhaps forty seconds, which he timed on later evenings and which never varied by much.
Out, down, across, back.
Then a pause.
Then again, and the second pass was faster than the first, because by then she was not mapping — she was checking what had changed.
Nothing had changed.
Nothing changes in an attic.
She did it anyway, every night, for the whole of that spring and summer.
He did not move for a long time, and when he finally did, the ticking came at him fast and hard and then stopped and went away, and he understood that he had just been drawn.
He read everything the library had, which was one book and a chapter in another, and then read online for six weeks, and this is what he found out.
She sends a sound and the sound comes back and the time it takes tells her how far.
That much everybody knows.
What almost nobody knows is how much comes back with it.
The pitch of the return tells her whether the thing is coming or going.
The shape of the return tells her the texture — a curtain and a plank at the same distance sound completely different, and the difference is not subtle to her.
Overlapping returns give her a moth's wingbeat frequency, which is how she can tell one insect from another in flight, in the dark, at four metres, in about the time it takes a person to blink.
She does not build a fuzzy sense of the room.
She builds a room.
The bit that took him longest to accept was the resolution.

He assumed, because everybody assumes it, that sound must be a coarse instrument — that she would be getting an approximate lumpy version of the world compared to the crisp one a person gets from eyes.
That is not what the numbers say.
At close range a bat can resolve a difference of well under a millimetre in the distance to a surface.
She can find a wire in the dark that a person cannot see in daylight.
There is no sense in which she is getting a rough draft.
Joaquim sat with that for about a week and then got hold of the thing that mattered, and he got hold of it in the attic at nine at night with his back against a trunk.
That bat has never seen the room.
Not once.
That attic has not had a working bulb since the 1990s and she is nocturnal and she has spent her entire life in and around a black space under a roof.
There is no version of that room in her head made of light.
There has never been one and there is not going to be one.
And she knows it completely.
Better than he does.

She knows where every beam is and every nail and the loose board by the water tank and the exact position of the trunk he sits against, and she has never once bumped into any of it, and she is not managing or coping or compensating.
She is not doing a worse version of seeing.
She is doing a whole thing, all the way, that arrives at a room.

He wrote that sentence in the back of an exercise book and looked at it for a while and then wrote underneath it, in smaller letters, the thing he had actually been trying to get at: *Nobody feels sorry for a bat.* Nobody stands in a doorway watching a bat's hands.
Nobody moves a chest on a landing for a bat.
Every book he had read described what she does with something close to awe, and not one of them had ever once described it as a way of getting by.

He tried to explain this to his mother in the kitchen and made a mess of it, because it came out as *there is a bat in the attic* and then as *no, listen*, and then as nothing, because she had gone pale at the bat and it took eleven minutes to get her off the subject of bats in the roof.
He tried it on the consultant in Porto in July and got a smile.
He got it out properly, in the end, to his grandfather, in the car, on the way back from Porto, because in a car you are side by side and nobody has to look at anybody.
He said that everybody kept talking about what he was going to lose.
He said that nobody had said a single sentence to him, in four months, about what he was going to have.
His grandfather drove for about a kilometre.
Then he said: "That's fair.

That's a fair thing to say and I've been as bad as the rest." And then, after another while: "What is it that you'll have?" Which was, Joaquim thought at the time and still thinks, an enormous question to be asked by an adult, and the first one anybody had put to him that was not about appointments.
He said he did not know yet.

He said that there was an animal in the attic that had built a complete room out of nothing but sound and had never wanted a bulb, and that he was not saying he was going to be a bat, and that he was aware of how it sounded.

His grandfather said: "Say it anyway." So Joaquim said that he had spent four months being handled by people who thought the important thing was the part going dark, and that he had started to think the important thing was going to be whatever he built instead, and that nobody could tell him anything about that because nobody in that house had ever had to build one.
They were about six kilometres outside Amarante.
His grandfather said, "Right," and put the indicator on, and pulled into a lay-by, and sat there for a bit with his hands on the wheel.
Then he said: "Retinitis pigmentosa." "What?" "That's the name of it.
I've not said it out loud since March and I've been ashamed of that for about a month." He put the car back in gear.
"It's a rotten word and I'm not fond of it.
But it's yours and you've had to carry it round on your own and that was not right of any of us." They did not talk for the rest of the way and it was a good silence.
Joaquim is twenty-six.

He has about eleven degrees of field left in the right eye and less in the left, and he works in acoustics, which everybody in his family finds either enormously moving or extremely funny depending on which of them you ask.
The attic at his grandfather's has a working bulb now.
It was done in 2019 by an electrician who was not told about anything.
Joaquim goes up there when he visits, in the evening, and does not turn it on.
Sleep came up the hill from the bottom, and it took about ninety minutes to get to the top, and everybody in Casal do Meio knew their own place in the order.
The bottom houses got it first.

That was the tannery row, along the stream, six houses in a line with damp walls and the best sleep in the district — children down by half eight, adults gone by ten, nobody in that row awake past eleven for as long as anybody could remember.
Then the middle: the square, the shop, the six or seven houses behind the church.
Then the terrace on the bend.
Then the four houses at the top, where Duarte lived, which got it last, and which had got it last since before his grandmother was born.
The top houses were a joke in that village and had been for generations.
Anybody at the top who complained about being tired was told they had brought it on themselves by living up there, which made no sense and was said with great satisfaction.

There was a rhyme about it that Duarte's grandmother knew four lines of and that nobody knew the rest of, and there was a thing the tannery row said about the top houses at weddings, and there was a particular way of saying *ah, you're from the top* that had been in use in that village since at least the 1930s.
None of it was unkind.
All of it was extremely tiresome if you happened to be twelve and living in one of the four.
Duarte had never much minded until he was twelve, when he started at the school in the town and had to be at the bus at ten past seven.
Ninety minutes is nothing when you are nine and there is no bus.

Ninety minutes is a considerable amount of your life when you are getting up at a quarter past six five days a week, and Duarte spent the whole of that autumn doing an arithmetic that had never occurred to anybody in his family: that over a school year the top of the hill loses something in the region of two hundred and seventy hours to the bottom of it.
He put this to his mother, who said that was very interesting and asked whether he had done his Portuguese.
The donkey came up at about half past eight.
You did not have to watch for her.
Everybody in Casal do Meio has seen her at some point, usually by accident, usually from a window, and the thing they all say is the same: she is entirely ordinary.
She is a small grey donkey with a dark cross on her shoulders and one ear that goes sideways, and she comes up the road at a walk, and she is carrying two panniers, and the panniers are full.
Full of what is not a question anybody in that village asks, and Duarte had learned by about six that asking got you a look.

He had got the look from four different adults by the time he was eight and had eventually stopped, and the interesting thing — the thing he only understood as a grown man — is that the look was not disapproval.
It was embarrassment.
Nobody knew, and nobody had ever known, and a village does not enjoy being asked a question about a thing it has lived beside for two hundred years without ever once looking into.
She goes up the road and turns in at the tannery row first and stands in the middle of it for a bit.
Then the square.
Then the terrace.
Then, last, up the track to the four houses at the top, where she arrives at about ten o'clock, and after that the whole village is asleep and the road is empty.
She came up on the Monday and there was something wrong with her off fore.
Duarte saw it from the window because he was awake, because he was always awake, and because at the top of the hill you have a long time to fill between eight and ten.
She came round the bend and she was not walking wrong exactly — she was walking short.
A shortened step on the right, and a pause at the top of it, of the kind you would notice in an animal you had watched for years and in no other circumstance.
She did the tannery row and the square and the terrace at about the usual time.
She got to the top at twenty to one in the morning.

Duarte went to school on the Tuesday having had about four hours and spent the whole of the bus journey with his forehead against the window, and got seven out of twenty in a maths test he had actually revised for.

Duarte knows the time because he had been lying in the dark for four hours by then in a state he had never been in before, which was not being unable to sleep so much as sleep simply not having arrived in the room.
There is a difference and anybody who has had a bad week knows it.
Tuesday she got there at ten past one.
Wednesday she did not get there at all.
That was the worst of it and it was not the tiredness.
He had been tired before.

What Wednesday night had in it was the other thing — the specific experience of lying in a bed, in the correct position, with the light off, at the correct hour, and finding that the room simply did not contain the material.
It is not the same as insomnia and Duarte has been careful about that distinction his whole life, because he has since had ordinary insomnia and it is nothing like it.
Insomnia is a mind that will not stop.
This was a mind perfectly willing to stop and nothing there to stop into.

He heard her turn back at the terrace — the hooves stopping, the long pause, and then the hooves going away down again — and he lay in his bed at the top of Casal do Meio and stared at a ceiling he could not see until the light came up behind the ridge at about six.
On Thursday morning there were four households at the top of that hill in a state that the rest of the village found extremely funny for about a day and then stopped finding funny.
The stopping was quite sudden and it happened at the shop.

Senhora Aurora came down on the Thursday for bread, which she did every day, and she stood at the counter and could not remember what she had come for, and stood there working at it in front of five people for the better part of a minute.
She was eighty-one and there was nothing whatsoever wrong with her memory.
Everybody in that shop knew it.
And by that afternoon the joke about the top of the hill had gone out of circulation and did not come back for years.

Senhora Aurora at the top house, who was eighty-one and had lived up there her whole life, called a meeting in her kitchen, which meant four adults, Duarte, and Duarte's little sister who was asleep on a chair by nine, which nobody remarked on because she was six and six-year-olds get theirs early wherever they live.
They went through the options.
It should be said that this was, by the standards of Casal do Meio, an extraordinary event.
There had never been a meeting about the donkey.

In two hundred years of that hill, as far as any of them could establish, nobody had ever sat down in a kitchen and discussed her out loud with other adults present, and all four of them were visibly uncomfortable about doing it.
The first was to move down.
This is not as ridiculous as it sounds — there were two empty houses in the middle that week — and it was rejected in under a minute by everybody, and Duarte noticed that nobody gave a reason.
The second was to go down and meet her.
Senhora Aurora's son-in-law had tried this on the Tuesday: had walked down at half nine and stood at the terrace, in the road, and waited for her to come past.
He said that she had come past.
He said that she had gone round him.
He said, with some difficulty, that he had walked back up feeling exactly as awake as when he set out, and that he was not going to try it again and would rather not discuss it.
Duarte asked him one question about it, weeks later, when the whole business was over, and got one answer.
He asked what it had been like when she went round him.
The son-in-law thought about it and said: "Like being furniture." The third was to do something about the foot.
That was Duarte's, and it got the reaction that ideas from twelve-year-olds get in a room of adults, which is a pause and then somebody else saying it again slightly differently eleven minutes later.
The trouble with the third option was that nobody in Casal do Meio had ever touched her.
There was no tradition of it.
She was not anybody's donkey and had never been in anybody's field and did not, as far as anyone knew, exist during the day.

Senhora Aurora said that her mother had told her that you leave her alone and she comes, and that in eighty-one years she had never heard of anybody trying anything else, and that there was probably a reason for that.
Duarte asked what the reason was.
Senhora Aurora said she had no idea and that this was exactly the sort of question that had made his grandfather difficult.
She said it warmly, and Duarte took it as a compliment, and it was probably meant as one.

The meeting broke up at about eleven with nothing decided and four adults going home to houses in which they were about to lie awake, and Duarte's mother put a hand on the back of his neck on the way out of the door and did not say anything, which in that family was a whole conversation.
He did it on the Friday, on his own, without telling anybody, which he now accepts was not a good decision and which he would do again.

He went down at half eight with his grandfather's farrier's rasp — the old one, in the shed, from when there had been mules on that hill — and a torch he did not turn on, and he sat on the wall at the bottom of the terrace and waited.
She came at twenty past nine, going short on the off fore.
He did not stand in the road.

That was the whole of his plan and it was the only part he had thought about properly: he had watched Senhora Aurora's son-in-law stand in the road and get gone round, and he had decided that the mistake had been the standing.
So he stayed on the wall and let her come past, and then he said, to her back, in a completely normal voice: "It's your right front and I've got a rasp." She stopped.

Duarte has told this part perhaps four times in his life and he has never told it well, and what he says is that she stopped, and stood for a moment, and then turned round in the road and walked back to the wall and put her nose against his knee.
It took a long time.
He was twelve and he had used a rasp exactly twice, on a horse belonging to a neighbour, under supervision, three years earlier.

What was in the foot was a stone — not a dramatic one, a flat grey stone the size of a thumbnail, wedged between the wall and the frog, which is exactly where they wedge, and which had been there since about the previous Sunday.

He got it out and rasped the wall down a little where it had grown over, because his grandfather had told him once that you always tidy the edge, and he was not certain that was right and did it anyway.
Then she put the foot down and stood on it, and walked four paces up the road and back, and stood in front of him again.
Duarte says the next bit is the part he cannot explain and would not want to.
She was carrying two panniers.
He had never been closer to them than fifty metres.
From a metre away in the dark he could see that they were ordinary panniers of woven cane, the kind still made in Barcelos, and that they were full, and that what was in them was not anything.
She went up the hill at twenty past ten and the top houses were asleep by eleven.
Duarte is forty.
He lives in the middle now, behind the church, which he did not plan and which his mother has never let him forget.
He goes back up to the top house on Sundays because Senhora Aurora is ninety-nine and has outlived everybody who ever laughed at the order of that hill.

And once every year or two he wakes at about half eight for no reason and lies there and hears, from the road below, the sound of an animal going up at a walk, on four sound feet, entirely ordinary, on its way to somebody else.
The wind at Sanngiq came from the north-north-east and it came from a particular place, and this was not a figure of speech.
Everybody has a wind.
Every settlement in the world sits in some relationship to a prevailing direction and the people there know it in their bones and build their doors accordingly.
That is ordinary and it is not what Kenna is talking about.
What she is talking about is that at Sanngiq you could walk to it.
Nine kilometres north-north-east, up the long shallow rise past the two lakes, there is a place where the ground flattens out into a saddle between two low hills.
On one side of that saddle there is no wind at all.
On the other side, three metres further on, there is the wind — the whole of it, at full strength, exactly as it arrives at the settlement nine kilometres away.
Not building.
Not gathering.
At full strength, immediately, the way water is at full depth the moment you go off a shelf.
There is no gradient.
There is a line.
Kenna has spent a good deal of her adult life explaining to people why this is not how weather works, which is a strange position to be in, since she agrees with them.
Wind is a pressure gradient.
It does not begin.
It is a slope of air from a high place to a low one, and it is smeared out over hundreds of kilometres, and asking where it starts is like asking where a hill starts.
Every meteorologist she has ever worked with has told her this, patiently, and she has told it to herself, and it remains true.
There is still a line in the saddle north-north-east of Sanngiq and you can stand on it.

Kenna walked to it for the first time when she was nine, with her father, on a day in April, and she remembers standing with one boot on either side of it and being unable to make sense of what her face was reporting.

Her father let her stand there for a while and then said the thing that everybody at Sanngiq says to a child at that point, which is: "Don't go over and stand in front of him." He did not explain it and she did not ask, because at nine you take that kind of instruction the way you take *don't go on the ice by the outflow* — as a rule about a real danger that adults have already thought about on your behalf.
It was years before it occurred to her that her father had never said what the danger was, and years after that before she worked out that he did not know either.
He is a bull musk ox and he is on the far side of the line, about forty metres in, facing south-south-west.
That is all he does.

Kenna has seen him perhaps two hundred times in her life and she has seen him move on four occasions, all of them small: a shift of weight, a turn of the head, once a step of about a metre and a half to the left which caused a certain amount of discussion in the settlement for a fortnight.
The step to the left was in the autumn she was fifteen and there were about six theories about it within a week.

Kenna's own, which she kept to herself, was that his foot had gone through the crust into a hollow and he had corrected — which is the dullest available explanation and which she still thinks is right.
What she found interesting was not the step.
It was that ninety people in a settlement with a fuel crisis and a school problem spent a fortnight discussing a metre and a half.
He is enormous and extremely old.

The horns have the full boss across the forehead, which takes six years, and the guard hairs come down past his knees, and he is grey at the muzzle in a way that Kenna's father says he was already grey when *he* was nine, which is either a story or a fact and which nobody has been able to settle because nobody has photographs from the 1980s of a musk ox nobody thought worth photographing.
He is alone.
Musk oxen are not alone.

That is one of the strongest things about them: they live in herds and their entire defensive behaviour is a herd behaviour, and a solitary bull in that country is either sick, driven out, or dead within a season.
There is a herd.
It works the ground east of the two lakes and it has perhaps thirty animals in it in a good year, and Kenna has watched it since she was small.
It does not go to the saddle.
She has never seen one of them within two kilometres of him and she has looked, deliberately, with binoculars, over years.
He has been there for at least forty years.
Nobody feeds him.

Nobody in Sanngiq has ever been able to say what he eats, and Kenna has looked at that ground in every season and it is the same thin stuff as the rest of the rise — lichen, some dwarf willow in the hollows, nothing that would keep an animal of that mass through a winter, let alone forty of them.

She has an answer to this that satisfies about half of her, which is that musk oxen are extraordinarily efficient and that the country supports them and that a bull does not need much and that her sense of what is enough is a townish sense.
The other half of her has done the calculation.

The wind comes out of the ground behind him, or through him, or from wherever it comes from, and goes south-south-west down the long shallow rise past the two lakes and into Sanngiq, where it takes the roofs off things about once every four winters and where the school has a rule about the door.

Kenna was thirteen the winter the wind took the roof off the fuel store, and the roof off the Aqqaluks' porch, and — on the fourteenth of February, at about four in the morning, in a way that the whole settlement heard — most of the roof off the school.
Nobody was hurt.
She wants that first, because it is a story about a roof and not about anything worse.
The school roof went in three pieces.

The first went at about four in the morning and made a noise that Kenna's mother described as a shipping container being dropped, and the settlement was out in it within about six minutes — everybody, in the dark, in a wind you could not stand up in, checking houses in a rota that nobody had to be told because everybody in Sanngiq had known the rota since they were small.

By half five the two youngest families were in the hall and somebody had the stove going and the Aqqaluks had made an enormous amount of tea, and Kenna sat on a bench with her boots on the wrong feet and watched the adults be extremely calm at each other.
But the school was out for nine weeks.
The fuel store business was expensive in a way that a settlement of ninety people feels for years.

And the Aqqaluks' porch was where their grandmother sat, and after February she did not sit anywhere much, and she died in the November, and there is no causal chain there that anybody could prove and Kenna has never entirely stopped drawing one.

The porch had a window in it that faced south down the inlet and a chair that had been in that position since 1979, and Anaana Aqqaluk had sat in it every afternoon of Kenna's life, and children going past waved at the window and she waved back, and after the fourteenth of February there was a sheet of ply where the window went.
They meant to fix it in the spring.
Everybody meant to fix it in the spring.
The spring at Sanngiq is about eleven days long and there was a school with no roof.
She decided in March that she was going to go and ask him to stand somewhere else.
She was thirteen and she was in the ninth week of no school and she had thought about it for a long time, and she had a case.
Nine weeks is a long time in a settlement with no cinema.
She had read everything in the hall, twice.
She had taken the snowmobile carburettor apart under supervision and put it back together without.
She had, by the end of March, arrived at the state of mind in which a thirteen-year-old decides to solve a structural problem that ninety adults have lived with for two centuries.
The case was this.
There is a valley running east from that saddle, and there is nothing in it, and nothing east of it for a hundred and forty kilometres.

If he stood forty metres east of where he stands, the wind would go down that valley, and it would hit nobody at all, ever, and Sanngiq would have the ordinary weather that every other settlement on that coast has.
She wrote it out.
She had a map.
She had, she thought at the time and thinks now with a certain amount of affection, an extremely good argument.
She told nobody, because she knew exactly what four different adults would say.
The walk is nine kilometres and it is not hard walking, and she did it in April on a still bright day, which at Sanngiq means still everywhere except the last three metres.

She crossed the line and it was like walking into a wall of moving air, and she leaned into it and went the forty metres, and she stopped about eight metres short of him, which is closer than anybody at Sanngiq had been in her lifetime.
He looked at her.

That was the first thing that went wrong with the plan, and it went wrong immediately, because in her head he had been a fact about the landscape and in front of her he was an animal, breathing, with ice in the hair round his mouth, and he turned his head about fifteen degrees and looked at her with one eye and Kenna's whole prepared speech went out of her like water out of a jug.
She said something.
She does not remember what.
She thinks it began with the fuel store.

She got through some of it — the porch, the school, the ninth week, the valley to the east with nothing in it for a hundred and forty kilometres — shouting, because you have to shout there, with her hood up and her eyes streaming from the cold.
And then she stopped, because she had worked out, standing eight metres from him, the thing that was wrong with the whole of her argument.
He was not making the wind.
He was standing in front of it.
She could see it.
From the settlement, from nine kilometres away, from any point south of the line, the wind comes out of that saddle.

From eight metres in front of him, facing north, into it, she could see that it came from behind and around and past him — and that he was standing precisely in the middle of it, side-on to nothing, facing the way it went, taking it on the whole length of his body.
The guard hairs come down past the knees.
Under them is the qiviut, which is eight times warmer than sheep's wool and which musk oxen shed every spring and which, on him, had not been shed for a very long time.
He was not a tap.
He was a windbreak.
And the wind that took the roof off the school on the fourteenth of February was what got past a single animal who had been standing in front of it since before her father was nine.
Kenna went home and did not tell anybody for two years.

She is thirty-one now and she works for the weather service and she has been back a great many times, with instruments, which she is aware is a kind of answer to a question she is no longer sure she is asking.
The line is real.
She has measured it.

It is not a line, at the resolution of her equipment; it is a transition of about two point four metres, which is the sort of correction that means nothing to anybody at Sanngiq and that she reports honestly every time.

What she has never published, and what is in a notebook, is the other set of numbers: what the wind does at eight metres in front of him, and at forty, and at four hundred, and what those three figures imply about a body standing at the front of it.

She has done that arithmetic perhaps a dozen times over eleven years and it comes out the same, and what it says is that Sanngiq has ninety people in it because of an arrangement nobody in Sanngiq has ever been party to.
She goes up in April.
She does not take the instruments every time.
The Bois de Herbeuval ran seven minutes behind the rest of Belgium and had done since 1944, and Sidonie grew up assuming this was normal, in the way that children assume whatever is around them.
It is not a figure of speech and it is not about clocks.
There is no clock in that wood.
What there is is a toad, under the third stone up from the ford, and everything in that wood takes its time from him.
Sidonie has looked at him perhaps thirty times in her life and has never once found him interesting to look at.
He is a common toad, *Bufo bufo*, of the size and colour and general demeanour of every other common toad in the Ardennes.

If you turned that stone over on a wet evening you would think nothing of him whatsoever, and every visiting biologist who has ever been shown him has thought nothing of him, and two of them have said so out loud in a way that Sidonie's grandfather never entirely forgave.

She had it explained to her at about six by her grandfather, who was the forester there for thirty-one years, and who explained it the way he explained the difference between beech and hornbeam — patiently, once, on the assumption that she would remember.
Dusk in a wood is not a time.
It is an event.
The birds go down in an order — blackbird, then robin, then wren — and the order is fixed and the intervals are fixed and every wood in Europe does it.
The deer come out.
The bats come off the roof of the old sawmill.
The moths that come to the lime trees come, and they come within about ninety seconds of each other, every night, all summer.
All of that is triggered by light, in the books.
And the books are right, and Sidonie would like that on the record before anything else, because she has a diploma and she is not going to spend it on this.
Light level drops below a threshold; the blackbird's eye reports it; the blackbird goes.
It has been measured a thousand times in a thousand woods and there is no mystery in it at all.
In the Bois de Herbeuval it is triggered by him.
You can watch it happen if you know where to stand.

There is a moment — a small dry sound, not a croak, more like a stone dropped in leaf litter — and about four seconds after it the blackbird goes, and then the whole thing unwinds down the valley in order, and the wood puts itself to bed.
The four seconds is the part that undoes people.
Sound travels.
If the blackbird is two hundred metres up the valley it should hear the sound about six-tenths of a second after it is made, and if it is four hundred metres away it should be later still.
It is not.

Sidonie's grandfather put two people with two watches at two distances on eleven separate evenings in the summer of 1978 and the delay was four seconds at both, and he did it again in 1981 with three people because he did not believe himself the first time.
Sidonie's grandfather had timed it against a wristwatch on and off for thirty years and had it written in the back of a notebook, and the notebook is where the seven minutes comes from.
The wood's dusk is seven minutes later than it should be for that latitude, that longitude, and that date.
It is not seven minutes later than sunset — that would be normal; every wood is later than sunset by some amount that depends on the canopy.
It is seven minutes later than *itself*.

Her grandfather had a hundred and forty pages of it, going back to when he took the job in 1961, and the whole of it is consistent to within about forty seconds, and the whole of it sits seven minutes behind the tables.
Forty seconds of scatter over sixty years is, in Sidonie's professional opinion, the most impressive thing in that notebook.
Nothing biological is that consistent.
Her own measurements since 2019 sit inside the same band and she has far better equipment than he ever had.
He had not discovered this.
That was the part that took Sidonie longest to get out of him.

He had gone to the man who had the job before him, a man called Pirlot, in about 1963, with two years of measurements and a great deal of excitement, and Pirlot had listened to the whole thing in his kitchen and then said: "Oui.
Sept minutes." And that was all he said, and he changed the subject, and he was not rude about it, and he never discussed it again in the eleven years before he died.
Sidonie's grandfather described that kitchen to her once and the description has stayed with her.
Pirlot at the table.
The two years of figures spread out on it.
An old forester looking at the work of a young one, recognising every column of it, and saying two words.
Her grandfather asked twice more over those years and got the same nothing.
So he did what anyone would do, which was to ask around, carefully, in a village where his family had not been for four generations and where he was therefore permanently new.

And what he found was that everybody over the age of about forty knew, that nobody would say how they knew, and that the subject was not exactly forbidden — it was worse than forbidden, it was *declined*.
People would go quiet, and be pleasant, and start talking about something else with real warmth, and there was nothing in it you could take offence at and no way at all to get past it.
He gave up in about 1971.
Not on the measurements.
He kept those up to the week he retired and for eleven years after it.
He gave up on the asking, which is a different thing, and Sidonie thinks the difference between those two is most of what she knows about him.
Sidonie did not give up, because she was twelve and because he told her about it in the summer she was twelve, which he has since admitted was not entirely an accident.
She got it out of Madame Grandjean in the September, and she got it by doing the one thing thirty years of adults had not done, which was to ask a question about something else.
Madame Grandjean was ninety-three and had been eleven in 1944 and had lived in the last house before the ford her entire life.
Sidonie went down there on a Wednesday with a school project about the war that was real, that she had actually been set, and that she had chosen deliberately.
She did not ask about the toad.
She asked about the wood.
This was not cunning.

She had thought about it for a fortnight and arrived at it honestly: every adult in that village had spent sixty years declining one specific question, and it had not occurred to any of them, or to her grandfather, that the question was the wrong shape.
And Madame Grandjean, who had declined the other question from four generations of foresters, answered the one she was actually asked, and talked for an hour and ten minutes.
There had been people in that wood in the September of 1944.
Not soldiers — a family, and then two families, from Marche, in the four days when the front went through and nobody in that part of the Ardennes knew from one hour to the next whose road it was.
They were in the old sawmill, which was a ruin then as it is now, and there were nine of them and four were children.
The village fed them.
That is how Madame Grandjean, at eleven, was involved: she carried a basket down the track past the ford, in the evening, because a child with a basket is a child with a basket.
You went at dusk.

That was the arrangement and it was not negotiable — not in the light, because you would be seen, and not in the dark, because you could not find the sawmill in the dark and a torch was out of the question.

Madame Grandjean described the basket in detail — the cloth over it, the two jars, the weight of it on a child's arm at the point where the track goes up — and Sidonie understood that she had described that basket to herself a great many times over eighty years.
Dusk is about twenty minutes long and you had to be back over the ford before it closed.
"And on the third evening," said Madame Grandjean, "there was a patrol on the Bastogne road." Sidonie did not write anything down.
"I was on the track.

I heard them and I got into the ditch by the hornbeam and I lay there and I could not go on and I could not go back, and it was going dark, and my mother did not know where I was." She said that she had lain in that ditch for a long time.

She said that when she finally got up and went the rest of the way, it was still just light enough to find the sawmill, and that it should not have been, and that she had known it should not have been even at eleven, because she had walked that track at dusk every evening of her life.
"How long?" "About seven minutes," said Madame Grandjean.
Sidonie went home and did not tell her grandfather for two days, and when she did tell him he sat at the table for a while and then went out to the shed and did not come back in for an hour.
Here is what neither of them has ever been able to establish.
Whether the toad did anything.
Whether an eleven-year-old in a ditch in September 1944 was right about seven minutes, or whether she was a frightened child with no watch who has had eighty years to make the number tidy.
Whether a wood can run late.

Whether the whole of it is a hundred and forty pages of one careful man's measurements against tables that were, in fact, slightly wrong for that valley all along, which is the explanation Sidonie's mother offers and which nobody in the family has ever been able to knock over.
What they did establish is why nobody would say.
It is not superstition and it is not shame.
Sidonie worked it out on the walk home from Madame Grandjean's and she has never had a better version of it.
If you say out loud that the wood is seven minutes slow, then the next thing anybody says is: *shouldn't it be put right?* And there is no way to answer that question.

There is no mechanism for putting it right, and there is nobody to ask, and there is a toad under the third stone up from the ford who has done one thing, once, extremely well, at a moment when it counted more than anything else that happened in that valley that year — and who has apparently not given the seven minutes back, and who is not going to, and who has never once been consulted about any of it.
So they leave it.
Sidonie has tested this on herself more than once and it holds.

Every time she gets as far as imagining saying it out loud to somebody at the village hall, the next sentence in her head is *and what are we going to do about it* — and there is nothing to do about it, and the only thing that can happen is that a valley which has got on perfectly well for eighty years starts having a difficult conversation with itself about a toad.

Every forester of the Bois de Herbeuval since Pirlot has known and has said nothing, and the notebook has been handed on twice now and has a hundred and sixty pages, and the whole of it still sits seven minutes behind the tables.
Sidonie is the forester there now.
She took it in 2019.
She measures it in May and September, which is more than her grandfather did, and she writes it in the same notebook in a hand nothing like his.

She has never mentioned it to anybody in the village, and last summer a boy from the last house before the ford asked her a very direct question at the edge of the wood, and she went quiet, and was pleasant, and started talking about something else with real warmth.
She heard herself do it and she has thought about it since.
She is fairly sure she will tell him.
Not this year.
It happened at the mouth of the river on one morning in June and it took about four minutes per person and there was nothing to look at.
Xuan had been to eleven of them before he was old enough to do it himself, standing at the back with the other children, being extremely bored.
That is the thing nobody warns you about: the most serious event in the year at Ribadesella is also, if you are seven, the dullest hour you will spend outdoors.
You queue.
That is most of it.

Forty or fifty people queue along the shingle on the north side where the water goes green, in no particular order, and when it is your turn you walk down to where the river is about knee deep and you stand in it.
The queue is the thing outsiders never understand and the thing everybody from Ribadesella would defend to the death.
It is not organised.
There is no list.

People simply arrive between about eight and eleven in the morning and stand about on the shingle, and at some point each of them goes down to the water, and it works out, and it has worked out every year for as long as anybody can establish.
Xuan has watched a man from Oviedo try to introduce a numbered system in 2011 and has watched the entire town be extremely polite to him about it for a whole morning and then not do it.
Then you wait until one comes past.
They are going up.

In the first fortnight of June they come in off the sea in numbers and they hold in the pools at the mouth, waiting for the water, and they move up through the shallows in ones and twos with their backs half out.
You can see them from the bank.
You can see them extremely well from knee deep, which is why the thing is done there.
There are fewer than there were.

Everybody says so and everybody is right, and the counts at the trap above the bridge say so too, and this is a subject that can take over an entire evening in the bar and that Xuan has learned to leave alone.
When he was seven the wait was under a minute.
When he was thirteen it was four or five.

A woman ahead of him in the queue that year stood in the water for the better part of twenty minutes and came out shaking with cold, and the whole shingle went quiet for her, and nobody has ever put a time limit on it and nobody ever will.
When one comes past you say a name.
Out loud, at a normal volume, once.
You do not shout it and you do not whisper it and you do not repeat it, and Xuan's grandmother had told him that people who repeat it are the sort of people who repeat everything.
Then you come out of the water and the next person goes in.
That is the whole ceremony.

There is no priest and there is no register and there is nothing written down anywhere, and the mayor of Ribadesella has for about forty years given a short speech at the start that everybody agrees is unnecessary.
There is no religion in it either, which visitors also get wrong.

The church has never had anything to do with it and has never tried to, and the one priest in living memory who attempted to attach a blessing to the front of it was, by all accounts, handled with the same courtesy as the man from Oviedo with his numbers.
There is one rule and it is the only thing about the whole business that anybody argues over.
The name cannot be your own.
There is a second rule that is not really a rule, which is that you do not tell anybody afterwards whose name you said.
Nobody enforces that one either.

It gets broken constantly by children and almost never by anybody over about twenty, and Xuan has never worked out at what point in a person's life it stops being a game and starts being the sort of thing you keep.
That is absolute and it is enforced by nothing at all, which Xuan found remarkable when he first understood it.
Nobody can hear what you say.

You are twenty metres out in a noisy river with your back to the bank and there are fifty people talking behind you, and if you said your own name every year of your life not one person would ever know.
He asked his father about this at about ten, in the way children ask a question they think is clever.

His father said: "And?" "So how do you know nobody does?" "I don't." "So the rule doesn't do anything." His father was mending a net, which is when the useful conversations happened in that house, and he did not look up.
"It does everything," he said.
"It's the only part of it that does anything at all.
You stand in a cold river in June and you have got about four minutes to pick one person out of everybody you have ever known, and it can't be you." He pulled a knot.
"That's the whole event, Xuan.

Everything else is queueing." Xuan thought about that for a year and came back at eleven with what he considered to be a serious objection, which was that most people obviously just said their mother.
"Most people do," his father agreed.

"The first six or seven times." "So it's still nothing." "Ask your uncle Nel who he said in 1994." Xuan did, eventually, about four years later, and got an answer that took him completely by surprise and that is not his to write down.
Xuan asked what happened to the name.
"It goes upriver." He said it the way you would say that a road goes to Oviedo.
"And then?" "And then nothing.
It gets to the top and that's the end of it.
There's no more to it than that and anybody who tells you different is selling something." Xuan said, with some heat, that in that case the whole thing was pointless.
He was ten and he had been building to this for the whole conversation and he delivered it with a certain amount of triumph.
And his father put the net down for the first time in the conversation and said: "Yes.
That's right.
And the whole village turns out for it every June and has done since before anybody can tell you, so you might want to have another think about what *pointless* means."
Xuan did his first one at thirteen and said the name of a friend, which he now describes as the correct answer to a question he had not understood.
He did his second at fourteen and said his grandmother, who was ill.

He had thought about that one for six weeks and had gone into the water knowing exactly what he was going to say, and he has since decided that this was the mistake — that a name you have carried around for six weeks is a name you have already used up.
What he remembers is not the saying.

What he remembers is that the water was very cold and that a fish went past him about a metre away, going up, hardly moving, with its back out and the light on it, and that it was much bigger than he had understood salmon to be.
She died in the October, and in the following June — and this is the part he has never fully explained to himself — he did not go to the river at all.
He stayed at the house and helped with a gate that did not need fixing, and his father did not say a word about it either that day or since.
At fifteen he went to the source instead.
The Sella rises in the Fuente del Infierno, in the mountains, and it is about forty kilometres by the road and rather less if you are willing to be uncomfortable.
Xuan was willing.

He told his mother he was going walking with two friends, which was two-thirds a lie, and he went up on the bus to Cangas and walked from there and slept out one night in a way that he does not recommend.
What he expected — and he is prepared to be laughed at for this — was something.
Not a marker.
He was fifteen and not stupid.
But he thought there might be a place.
A pool that people had visited.
A cairn.

Something with the shape of an ending on it, because a thing that has been going for four hundred years and that delivers something to a specific location ought to have worn a mark into that location.
The Fuente del Infierno comes out of a cliff.
It is a good spring and it is a great deal of water and it makes an enormous noise, and there is wet rock and beech and a smell of cold stone, and there is nothing there.
No cairn.
No path except the ordinary one.
No names cut into anything.
Nothing anybody has left, ever, apart from a Fanta can that Xuan carried out with him for forty kilometres out of a feeling he could not have named.
He sat on a rock for most of an afternoon.
He had walked forty kilometres for it.
He had slept in a bus shelter above Cangas with his coat over his legs.
He was fifteen and extremely tired and there was a great deal of cold water coming out of a cliff and making a noise, and he sat there and waited to feel something, and what he felt was hungry.
And no salmon can get up there.
That is the thing that finished it.

He had known it before he set out and had somehow managed not to think about it: there are four weirs and a fall between Ribadesella and Cangas alone, and above Cangas the river becomes something no fish has ever gone up.
The salmon spawn in the middle reaches, in the gravel, in November, and they die there, and they have never once been anywhere near the Fuente del Infierno in the whole history of either species.
He came home on the Thursday and asked his father, at the net, and this time he asked it properly.
He said: whose name did you say.
His father worked for a while.

Then he said: "The first year I did it I was twelve and I said your grandfather, and he was alive and well and standing on that bank about thirty metres behind me, and I remember thinking it was a waste of a turn." He put the shuttle down.
"I've said your mother's name most years.

I said yours the year you were born and the year you had the pneumonia and I have not said it since, and you can work out what that means about how I think you're getting on." Xuan said that he had been to the source.
He said there was nothing there.
He said that no salmon in history had ever got within twenty kilometres of it and that his father must have known that.
"Of course I knew that." "Then what is it *for*?" And his father said the thing that Xuan has been carrying around for twenty-two years and has never improved on.
He said: "You stood in a river, in front of the whole village, and you had four minutes, and you had to choose one person and it could not be you.
And you chose.

And then you said it out loud, in the open, with your mouth, which you have never done for any of those people on any other day of your life and you never will." Xuan started to say something about the fish.
"I know about the fish," his father said.

"I've known about the weirs since I was younger than you and I went up there myself when I was about nineteen, and I sat on the same rock, and I came home the same way you did with the same face on." He said that he had not told Xuan because being told is not the same as going, and because his own father had not told him.
He picked the net back up.
"The fish takes it up the river.
Maybe.
I don't know and neither does anybody.
But you *said* it, Xuan, and there's about eleven hundred people in this town and every one of them has said one, and that is what the river is for." Xuan is thirty-seven.
He goes every June.
He has said his father's name for the last nine years running, which his father is aware of, because Xuan told him once, in a car, and neither of them has mentioned it since.
Mornings at Fuentelosa were an hour and forty minutes long and mornings everywhere else were not, and Rocío did not find this out until she was eleven and went to stay with her cousins in Palencia.
She came back arguing about it and got nowhere for about a year.
The argument, as she put it at eleven, was that mornings in Palencia were over almost as soon as they had started.

Her cousins got up, and had something, and were doing things, and by half past eight the whole apparatus of the day was running at full speed with the previous part of it having lasted, as far as Rocío could see, about twenty minutes.
Her aunt said this was because Palencia was a city and cities are busy.
Rocío said that Fuentelosa was not busy and the morning was longer, and that if being busy made mornings short then it should be the other way round.
