Ice bends before it breaks and what it can carry depends on thickness squared, so the numbers climb fast.
Eighteen centimetres holds a car.
Twenty-five holds the van with children in it.
What Henryk actually measures for is thirty, because the card was written by somebody sensible.
A wolf is nothing.
A wolf is a rounding error on that card and it can walk on ice that would not take a bicycle.
Which is precisely why the track is worth following, and Zofia did not understand this until she was about eleven.
The wolves are not testing the ice.
They are avoiding places where the ice is *wrong*, and a place where the ice is wrong at four centimetres is a place where the ice is wrong at forty.
Learning to read a wolf track on lake ice is not romantic and it took Zofia three winters.
The difficulty is that ice is not blank.
It has skate marks and ski marks and dog tracks and the drag lines of last week's timber, and it has wind-scour and snow-crust and the long white cracks that look exactly like a path and are not.
A wolf track is a line of prints, in single file, extremely straight, with the stride between them almost identical every time.
That last part is what identifies it.
A dog wanders; a dog's stride varies by a third depending on what it has just smelled.
A travelling wolf puts its feet down at the same interval for three kilometres.
And they walk in each other's prints, which is the thing that made Zofia believe the whole business at about ten.
Four or five animals crossing that lake leave what looks like the track of one, and you cannot tell how many there were until they split at the far reeds.
They cross most nights from January.
They are going about their own business and they have no interest whatsoever in Rusiec, and in eleven years Zofia has seen one from the shore, once, at about six hundred metres, in bad light.
She was nine.

It was going north along the far reeds at a trot and it took about forty seconds to cross the gap she could see, and she did not call anybody, and she has never described it to her father because she has a superstition about it that she is aware is ridiculous.
The village does not feed them, does not photograph them, and does not discuss them with the two men from the national park who come round in April.
What the village does is get up before light and go down and look at the ice.
There is a small formality to it that Zofia did not recognise as a formality until she left.
Whoever is first down puts a stick in the snow at the reeds where the track comes off, so that the next person can find it in the dark without walking about on the shore and confusing it.
The stick has been the same kind of stick for as long as anybody has been doing it: a metre of hazel, peeled at the top.
Nobody organises this.
There is no rota.
It has simply always been done by whoever gets there first, and in nine winters Zofia has never once come down and found no stick.
The winter Zofia was thirteen the track went wrong.

It came off the reeds at the usual place and then, instead of running south-west across the open middle the way it had every winter of her life, it turned north and went almost a kilometre up the lake before turning back down, and it reached the timber yard from the north side, having covered something over five and a half kilometres to do a crossing of three and a half.
It did this on the fourth of January and on every night after.
Zofia's father followed it for a week, on foot, and lost forty minutes a day to it, and said nothing.
He is not a man who says nothing.
Zofia would like that understood.
He has opinions about the road, the school, the parish, the price of timber, and the two men from the national park, and he expresses all of them at length and mostly at dinner.
About the track he said nothing, for the whole of January, and Zofia now thinks that was the closest thing to a statement he made all winter.
On the eleventh of January a man called Pawełek, who had a contract to get timber out and who was behind, took the direct line with a loaded trailer.
Nothing happened.

He went across in eleven minutes on ice that rang like a drum, and came back the same way loaded, and came back again the next day, and by the third week of January about half the village was going direct.
Not all at once and not by anybody deciding.
Somebody was late.
Somebody had a load.
Somebody had watched Pawełek do it nine times and had felt increasingly foolish walking a kilometre north in the dark.
Zofia has thought about that a great deal since and has decided that the foolishness is the whole mechanism.
Nobody in Rusiec stopped believing anything.
If you had stood in that shop in the third week of January and asked whether the wolf track was safer than the direct line, every person in there would have said yes, including Pawełek.
They knew.
They had known since they were seven.
What they could not do was keep walking an extra kilometre and a half in the dark every morning while a man with a trailer went past them on the flat in eleven minutes.

Zofia's father kept walking the long way and she went with him, and there was an evening in the last week of January when her mother said, at the table, in a perfectly reasonable voice, that it was forty minutes twice a day and that Pawełek had been over about thirty times now.
Her father said that Pawełek had been lucky about thirty times.
Her mother said that at some point that stopped being a useful description.
Nobody was angry.

Zofia remembers that clearly and thinks it matters: it was not a row, it was two sensible people looking at the same thirty crossings and drawing opposite conclusions, and Zofia sat between them and could not have told you which of them was right.
Her mother's position, which Zofia can still make better than her mother made it, was this.
The wolf track is a heuristic.
It has worked for a hundred years because for a hundred years nothing about that lake changed.

If it has now started producing a five-and-a-half-kilometre answer to a three-and-a-half-kilometre question, the sensible thing is to check whether the heuristic has broken — and thirty-one crossings on a drum-hard direct line is a check, and it came back negative thirty-one times.
That is a good argument.
It is the argument a careful person makes, and Zofia has since met a great many careful people who make it about other things.
The ice went out that year in the third week of March, the way it always does, from the north end first.

On the twenty-ninth of March Zofia walked round the shore to the point on the lake that the wolf track had been avoiding, which she had marked in January with a bearing off the church tower and the timber yard chimney because her father had taught her to take a bearing before he taught her to swim.
There was open water.
It was perhaps sixty metres across and roughly round, and it was the last place on that lake where you would expect open water, because it is nowhere near either shore and nowhere near the outflow.

She went back with her father the following day and he stood and looked at it for a long while and then went and found the reason, which took the two of them about four hours and involved walking a kilometre and a half up the inflow stream on the north-east side.
He did not say anything at the hole either.
He looked at it, and took a bearing off the church tower himself, and compared it with hers, and grunted, which in that family is a substantial award.
A beaver dam had gone, some time in the previous autumn, about two kilometres up.
It had held a pond back for years and the pond had gone into the lake slowly, spread out, cold.

With the dam gone the stream came down in one channel, faster and warmer than the lake, and it went in under the ice and it did not spread out; it ran along the bottom and came up, the way moving water does, in a plume, at a spot about eight hundred metres from the north-east shore.
Nobody in Rusiec had known.
There is no reason why anybody in Rusiec would have known.
The dam is two kilometres up a stream that nobody has any business on in November.
The wolves had known on the fourth of January, in the dark, walking on a metre of ice with sixty metres of water under it.
Zofia is twenty-six and she does hydrology, which her father finds funny and her mother does not.
The thing she says, when people ask her about it — and it comes up, because it is the only interesting thing about her — is that the story has no accident in it.
Pawełek did thirty-one crossings over ice that was, in the second week of January, almost certainly fine.
Half the village went direct for two months and every single one of them got to the other side.
There is no version of that winter in which anybody was punished for anything.
That is what makes it worth telling.

The wolves went a kilometre north from the fourth of January because they could hear or smell or feel something that was going to become sixty metres of open water in eleven weeks, and being right about that in January bought them precisely nothing, and cost them a kilometre and a half a night all winter.
She has never been able to decide whether that is the most impressive thing she knows about an animal or the most impressive thing she knows about anything.
A black woodpecker makes a nest hole about eight metres up and shaped like a keyhole, and there are forty or fifty of them in the Bjurholm forest and Nils could show you every one.
The doors are different.
They are at eye height — his eye height, and his father's, and his grandmother's, which is a range of about thirty centimetres and which is the first thing about them that does not make sense.
Nils measured all nine at fourteen, with a tape, because he had got tired of people saying *about eye height* as though that meant anything.
The lowest is a hundred and forty-one centimetres and the highest is a hundred and seventy-two.
His grandmother's eye, at the time, was a hundred and forty-eight.
His own is a hundred and seventy-nine and he has to stoop for every single one of them, which he did not expect and which annoyed him for about a year.
They are round and they are the width of a fist and they go straight in, and there are nine of them in about four hundred hectares.
They are always in a living tree.
Never a snag, never a stump, never anything rotten.
Four of the nine are in spruce, which no woodpecker in Sweden would bother with, and one is in a birch that Nils's father says has been there since the war.
That is the part a forester notices first.
Woodpeckers go for dead and dying wood because dead wood is soft and full of what they eat, and a healthy spruce is the last thing on the list — hard, resinous, and empty.
There is also no woodpecker in that forest that makes a round hole a fist wide at a metre and a half.
The great spotted makes a smaller one higher up.
The black makes a bigger one, oval, at eight metres.
Nils has looked this up in three books and has never found a species that would account for a single one of the nine.
And you can look in.
That is the whole of it and it is not much to say out loud.
You put your eye to a hole in a tree and you look, and you see the inside of the tree.
Not a hollow.
There is no hollow; if you put a stick in, the stick goes in about four centimetres and stops on solid wood, and Nils has done this and can confirm it and has felt extremely stupid doing it.

What you see, with your eye against the bark, is the wood from inside — the whole cylinder of it, going away from you in both directions, and every ring lit from somewhere and stacked outward from the middle in the order they were made.
It is lit.
He does not know from where and neither did his grandmother and there is no light source anywhere in a tree.
What there is is enough of it to see by, evenly, with no shadows and no direction, in the way that a page in a book is lit when you are not thinking about the lamp.
You are looking at the years.
Nils's grandmother taught him to read them, over about two summers, in the way she taught everything, which was by standing behind him saying nothing until he asked a question worth answering.
The first question he asked that she thought was worth answering was, at eight, why the rings on one side were wider than on the other.

She said that the tree grows more on the side that has more light and that this is called reaction wood and that if he wanted to know which way was south in that forest without a compass he could look at a stump.
The rings are not labelled.
Nothing tells you what year you are looking at.
But they are not all alike, and once you can see the differences you can work outwards from the bark, which is now, and count.
A wide pale ring is a good summer.
A narrow dark one is a bad one.

There are two rings in the birch that are so thin they are almost a line, and those are 1867 and 1868, and every tree of that age in northern Sweden has them and every forester in that country knows what they are.
There is a black band in the pine by the marsh at about the sixtieth ring in and it goes right round, and that is fire.

And there is one, in the big spruce at the top of the ridge, about a hundred and twenty rings in, where the wood on one side goes suddenly thick and buckled for four or five years and then settles down — which means that in about 1904 something took the top off that tree, or leaned another tree against it, and it spent five years correcting and then got on with its life.
Nils could find that one in the dark by his fifteenth birthday.
His grandmother had a name for it — *det stygga året*, the bad year — and Nils has never found anybody else in Västerbotten who uses that phrase and suspects she made it up.
None of this is magic.
He wants that established.
Everything he has described is in the wood of every tree in that forest and you can see all of it by cutting one down and looking at the stump, which foresters do every day of the week.
The only strange part is that you can see it from outside, through a hole the width of a fist, in a tree that is standing up and alive and has another two hundred years in it.
The rule in the Bjurholm forest is that you do not look alone.

Nils's grandmother gave it to him at eight, at the second door, on the day she first let him put his eye to one, and she gave it in a way that was not a warning and was not really an instruction either.
She said: "Getting in is easy.

Getting out is a separate arrangement, and I am the arrangement." He did not understand and she did not explain, and she stood behind him with a hand on his shoulder while he looked, and after a while she said his name and he stood back.
He asked how long he had been looking.
He asked because his legs had gone and because the light had changed and because there was a mosquito bite on his neck that had not been there.
She said eleven minutes.
He had thought it was somewhere under one, and he said so, and his grandmother said, "Yes," and they walked home.

She did this eleven or twelve times over the next two summers and every time she told him the true number afterwards and every time it was between six and twenty minutes, and every time Nils would have sworn on anything that it had been about forty seconds.
He tried counting once, at eleven, on the theory that if he counted seconds he would have a check on it.

He got to about thirty and then found that he had stopped counting at some point he could not identify, and when his grandmother said his name he was on thirty-one and had been at the tree for fourteen minutes.
That is the whole of the phenomenon and Nils has never found a way to make it sound serious.
He knows exactly how it sounds.
It sounds like being absorbed in something — like reading, like a screen, like the thing that happens to every human being who has ever been interested in anything.
He thought that himself, at twelve, and was quite pleased with the thought, and said it to his grandmother.
She said: "Try it in the dark." He went out that November at four in the afternoon with a head torch, to the third door, and he looked in, and his father came and got him at ten past seven.
His father was not pleased and Nils has never blamed him.

It was minus eleven and Nils had been standing still against a tree for three hours in a jacket meant for walking, and his father had gone out on the snowmobile at half six having tried the phone eleven times, and there had been a real and entirely ordinary danger in it that had nothing to do with anything strange.
That is the argument Nils's father has always made about the doors and it is a good one: the interesting thing is not the tree, the interesting thing is a boy standing still in the dark in November.
He went alone at thirteen and he did it on purpose and there is no version of the story in which he did not know exactly what he was doing.

It was the second week of June, which in that part of Sweden means the light does not go, and he told his sister he was walking to the ridge and he took a phone and a bottle of water and he went to the big spruce with the buckled rings.
He wanted to see 1904 from the inside and find out what had happened.
That was the whole ambition and he thinks now that it was a reasonable one.

There is a hundred and twenty-first ring in that tree that goes wrong on one side, and Nils had a theory involving a windthrow in the neighbouring stand, and he had worked out that if he could see the buckling properly he could tell which direction it had come from.
His sister found him at twenty past four in the afternoon.
She was sixteen and had not wanted to come out and had spent the walk composing what she was going to say to him.

She had come out at about three because he had not answered his phone and had not come back for lunch, and it took her the best part of an hour to find the tree, and when she got there he was standing with his forehead against the bark and his hand flat on the trunk beside him and he did not respond to his name the first two times.
He had been there since half past nine in the morning.
He was not hurt.
He was not cold, in June.
He had drunk none of the water.
He had, by his own account, been looking for something in the region of ten minutes, and had been about to stop.
His sister did not tell their parents and Nils has never known whether that was the right call.

What she did was hit him, once, hard, on the arm, which he has always thought was fair, and then sit down on the moss and cry for a while, which he had not expected at all and which is the part he thinks about.
He sat down next to her and did not say anything useful.

He was thirteen and had nothing available except *I'm fine*, which he said about four times and which was true and which was not the point, and it took him until roughly his twenties to work out what the point had been.
She had walked into a clearing and found her brother standing against a tree not answering to his name.
Whatever was or was not happening inside that spruce, what she had was fifteen seconds of not knowing, and nothing that happened afterwards took those back.
He is thirty-one.
He works in the forest, which surprises nobody.
He does thinnings and windthrow clearance and he has taken down perhaps eleven thousand trees, which he does not find difficult and which people always expect him to.

He looks perhaps four times a year and he has never gone alone again, and the arrangement is now his sister, who lives in Umeå and who drives up for it, and who has never once suggested that they stop.
He never did work out 1904.

He can see the buckling perfectly well and it is the direction he expected, and there is a hundred and twenty-first ring in a living spruce on a ridge in Västerbotten that has an answer in it and does not have a question, and Nils has come to think that this is true of most of what is in there.
In the villages along that stretch of the Ill the storks go in the last week of August, and in the third week of August you can send an apology.
Camille had known the rules since she was small and had never had occasion to use them.
You write it on paper.
Not a card and not a screen; paper, and small, because it has to fit.

You do not sign it and you do not put a date and you do not include anything that identifies you, and this is not optional — an apology with a name on it comes back, or does not go, or goes and is not delivered, and nobody in Hindisheim can tell you which of those three things happens because nobody has ever seen one arrive with a name.
You fold it in four and you put it in the wire basket on the church wall, which is about the size of a shoebox and which is empty for fifty-one weeks of the year.

The basket is at about chest height on the north side, out of sight of the square, which everybody assumes was deliberate and which the parish records show was where the old poor-box bracket happened to be.
Nobody watches it.
That is a rule too, and it is the one that is taken most seriously.
You do not stand in the square in the third week of August.
You do not walk past twice.
If you are going to the church at that time of year you go round by the school, and visitors who do not know this get told, once, kindly, by the first person who sees them.
And in the last week of August they are gone, and some time in the following fortnight, people get them.
Not everybody.
Nobody keeps count and there is a certain amount of arguing about the numbers, but a reasonable estimate for a village of nine hundred is somewhere between forty and eighty a year.
The arguing is not about the mechanism.
Nobody in Hindisheim argues about whether it happens; everybody has had one or knows four people who have.

The arguing is about whether it is fewer than it used to be, which is a conversation that village has been having since at least the 1950s and which is conducted with the same weary vigour as the one about the storks themselves, of which there are, in fact, measurably more.
They arrive on doorsteps and windowsills and once, memorably, on the roof of a car.

The car was in 2016 and belonged to a man from Sélestat who had parked in the square overnight, and there is no agreement in the village about whether the apology was for him or whether his roof was simply in the way, and he took it home with him, which several people thought was poor form.

They are folded in four and they are unsigned and they are unmistakable, because there is a particular way the paper is creased along the fold — a hard flat crease with a slight bevel to it that nobody in Hindisheim has ever been able to reproduce with their hands.
Camille got hers on the ninth of September when she was twelve.
It was on the windowsill of her bedroom, on the outside, which is on the first floor.
It was three lines long and she is not going to reproduce it, and the reason is not that it is embarrassing.
The reason is that in the years since she has come to understand that an unsigned apology is the property of two people and only one of them chose to be in the arrangement.

Her mother asked what it said, once, in the October, and Camille said she would rather not, and her mother said all right and never asked again — which Camille understood at twelve as ordinary politeness and understands now as the single most useful thing that woman ever did for her.
What she is prepared to say is this.

It was an apology for something that had happened when she was nine, at the school, over about three months, and that she had told nobody about at the time and had told nobody about since, and that she had assumed for three years that she had entirely got over.
It was specific.
That is the part that took the ground out from under her.
It named the thing.
It named the room.

It got a detail right that Camille herself had half forgotten and that came back complete the moment she read it, and it was not a large detail and it was not one that anybody would remember unless they had been there.
She checked the paper against the crease.
It was the crease — the hard flat fold with the bevel that everybody in that village can identify by feel and nobody can make.
She checked the windowsill.

It is on the first floor above a stone wall with no drainpipe and there is no way to reach it from the ground, and she went out into the garden that evening and stood underneath it and looked up at it for a while.
She sat on her bed and read it perhaps forty times.
The first thing she felt was not relief and it was not comfort, and she has been careful about this ever since because people expect a story about an apology to arrive at relief.
The first thing she felt was that somebody had known.

For three years the entire weight of that autumn had been that it was hers alone — that whatever had happened in that room had happened only inside her head, that everybody else had walked out of it and gone on with their lives, and that being the only one still carrying it was proof that she had made too much of it.
The paper on the windowsill said, in three lines, without a name on it: no.
Then she went downstairs and had dinner and did not mention it, and it stayed in the pocket of a coat for the rest of that autumn, and she got it out roughly every second day.
She made a list, which she now finds difficult to look at.
There were eleven names on it.
She wrote them in the back of a maths book and she went at it the way she went at everything, which was thoroughly and without much idea of what she would do at the end.
The eleven were everybody who had been in that room in 2019 and who still lived in Hindisheim.
She did not seriously consider the two teachers and put them on the list anyway, out of a completeness she now recognises as a way of not starting.

She ruled some out by handwriting, which took a month and involved a quantity of low cunning she is not proud of — asking people to write things down, getting hold of a class list from 2019, comparing capitals.
She got the eleven down to four.
The class list came from a folder in the corridor outside the office and she took a photograph of it and put it back, and she has never decided whether that counts as anything.
She ruled one of the four out because he had moved to Colmar in 2020 and the crease is not something you can do at a distance, or so everybody says.
Three.
And then she stopped, in the second week of November, on the road home from the bus, quite suddenly, and did not go back to it.
What stopped her was not a scruple and she wants that clear, because she has had eleven years to be honest about it and she has decided to be.

What stopped her was that she worked out, standing at the corner by the Speck farm, that she was about four questions away from knowing — and that the moment she knew, the apology would stop being an apology and would become a fact about a person she had to see at the bus stop every morning.
Right now it was the truest thing anybody had ever said to her.

In four questions it was going to be a thing somebody had done and had felt bad about, which is smaller, and which she would then have to have opinions about, and manage, and be gracious or ungracious about for the rest of her life in a village of nine hundred people.
She went home and put the maths book in the stove.
It went up in about four seconds and she stood and watched it and then went and did her homework, and she has never told anybody about the list, including the person she married.
She sent her first in the August she was fifteen.
It is difficult to describe how much harder it is than it sounds.
You have a week.
You have a piece of paper the size of a hand.

You cannot sign it, which means you cannot explain, which means you cannot say *this is why I did it* or *I was going through something*, because every one of those sentences narrows you down and the whole arrangement depends on not being narrowed down.
So what you can write is the thing itself and nothing else.
That constraint is the whole design and Camille did not see it until she was about nineteen.
An apology with a reason in it is not an apology; it is a case.

Everybody who has ever apologised knows the pull of the next sentence — the *but*, the *I was*, the *you have to understand* — and every one of those sentences is a small request that the other person do something for you.
The basket on the north wall will not take them.
Not for any moral reason: purely because a reason narrows you down, and a narrowed-down apology comes back or does not go.
Camille sat at the kitchen table for four evenings and produced, in the end, two lines, and she has sent one nearly every year since and has never got past four.
The first one was about a girl called Léa and a thing that had gone round the year before, and Camille's part in it had been small and entirely deliberate.
She has never found out whether any of them arrived.
That is the other half of the arrangement and it is the half nobody warns you about.
There is no receipt.

The person does not tell you, because they do not know it is you, which is the entire point — and you will be in the shop with them in October and they will be perfectly ordinary and you will have no idea whether they are perfectly ordinary because it landed or because it did not.
Her mother told her, when she was about seventeen, that this was the part people find hardest and that a great many people in Hindisheim send one once and never again.
Camille is twenty-three and works in Strasbourg and comes home for the third week of August, which her colleagues assume is about the holidays.
One of them worked it out in 2024 — not the mechanism, only that the week was fixed and non-negotiable — and asked, and Camille said it was a family thing, which is true.

She has three of them, received, in a tin: the one from when she was twelve, one from eighteen, and one that arrived last September that she has read perhaps four hundred times and that she cannot place at all — no room, no year, no detail she recognises, an apology from somebody about something that as far as she can establish never happened.
She has thought about that one a great deal.
The explanation she has settled on is the dull one, which is that somebody got the wrong windowsill, and it is almost certainly right.
The other one, which she takes out about twice a year and looks at and puts back, is that it is not the wrong windowsill and that she is the one who has forgotten.

The nightingale in the elder scrub behind the Romanian Orthodox church at Vălișoara does not sing words and Ilinca would like that established before anything else, because every single person she has ever told has assumed words.
It sings like a nightingale.

It sings the whole ridiculous performance — the phrases repeated four and five times, the long trill, the two or three seconds of absolute silence that they do in the middle for no reason anybody has ever established — and it does it from about eleven at night in May and June, and it is loud enough to be a nuisance to two houses.
What happens is not that it says anything.
What happens is that you remember something.
Not at random.

There is a specific character to it that everybody in Vălișoara knows and nobody has ever written down: you are lying in bed with the window open and the bird is going, and after a while a thing surfaces — a detail, a name, a room, a Tuesday — and it is always something you knew, and it is always something you had stopped having.
Ilinca's grandmother described it as *the bird finds your pockets*.
It is not always anything.
That has to be said, because a story about a bird that returns lost things sounds a great deal more reliable than the bird is.
Most nights it is a nuisance and nothing else.

Ilinca lay under it for eleven Mays and got something perhaps nine times, and four of those were entirely trivial — the smell of a shop that closed in 2014, the name of a boy who came for one summer, where a key used to be kept.
That is the actual hit rate and everybody in Vălișoara knows it, which is why the whole business is discussed there with roughly the enthusiasm of a bus timetable.
The village's understanding of what it is doing is entirely practical and slightly bored.
Nobody there thinks it is a ghost or a saint or an omen.
What they think, and what they will tell you if you ask in the right tone, is that the bird sings the parts of a story that have fallen out of the telling.
Which is a claim about stories, not about birds, and it took Ilinca until she was twelve to see that.
Because stories in a village of four hundred people are told out loud, constantly, for decades, and every telling wears them.
There is no written version of anything in that village before about 1995.
Nothing is in a book.
The war is a set of things that get said at tables; the collectivisation is a set of things that get said at tables; and every one of them has been through perhaps ten thousand mouths.
Things drop out.

The parts that are hard to say drop out first, and the parts that make somebody look bad, and the parts that require a piece of context nobody has any more — and after thirty years what is left is a smooth thing about the right length for a kitchen table, and everybody believes it, and it is not a lie, and it is not what happened.
The story of the fire at Vălișoara is the story that village has instead of a history.
The school burned on the eleventh of March 1987, at about half past two in the afternoon, with sixty-one children in it.
Nobody was hurt.
That is the first line of the telling, always, and it is true.
Ilinca has checked.
There is a report from the fire service in Brad, two pages, and it says the same: sixty-one pupils, two staff, no injuries, structure a total loss, cause electrical.
The way it is told is this.
The teacher, Doamna Pop, was in the second room.
She smelled it before she saw it.

She got the two rooms out through the back in under four minutes, in order, in coats, and she counted them twice in the yard, and it was only when the roof went at about three o'clock that anybody in the village understood what had nearly happened.
The bell was rung.
Men came from the fields.
There was nothing to be done and they did not try; they stood in the yard with the children and watched it go.
Doamna Pop died in 2011 and there are ninety people at her grave every eleventh of March, and the school that was built in 1989 has her name on it.
Ilinca has been to the eleventh of March every year of her life and would like to say clearly that she is not writing any of this in order to take anything away from that woman.
Doamna Pop was thirty-four in 1987.

She had two rooms with a wall between them and one door out of the back, and she got the second room moving before she had seen a flame, on a smell, at half past two on an ordinary Wednesday afternoon, and she counted them twice in a yard in March with children crying, and she got the number right both times.
Ilinca had heard that story perhaps two hundred times before she was twelve.
Her mother had been in the first room, aged nine.
Her uncle had been in the second.

It is told at weddings and at funerals and on the anniversary and any time a stranger asks about the building, and it is told, as far as Ilinca could ever tell, in more or less the same words by everybody.
That last part is the thing that ought to have bothered somebody sooner.
Sixty-one children and about forty adults were in that yard in 1987 and the account has one shape.
Ilinca did not think about this at all until the May she was twelve, when she lay awake with the window open and the bird going in the elder, and remembered a woman's hands.
What surfaced was not a story.
It was about a second and a half long.

She was small — four, five — and she was in a kitchen that was not hers, and a woman was cutting bread with her sleeves pushed up, and there was a long shiny mark up the inside of the right forearm from the wrist to the elbow, and Ilinca had asked about it and had been told something, and she could not get the something.
She lay there for about an hour trying to get the rest and the rest did not come.
This is what the bird does and what it does not do.
It had given her a kitchen and an arm.
It did not give her a name, or a year, or the answer she had been given at four, and it did not give her the faintest indication that any of it was important.
What she had was: a kitchen, a woman, an arm, and the certainty that she had been given an answer once and had not kept it.
She asked her mother at breakfast.

She described the kitchen and the arm and her mother said, without any pause at all: "Tanti Sabina." Then her mother put the pan down and stood at the sink with her back to the room for slightly too long.
Ilinca has thought about that pause a great deal.
Her mother was nine in that yard.
Her mother has told the story of the fire in Ilinca's hearing perhaps a hundred times and has never once said the name Sabina Crețu in it.
She was not hiding anything.
That is the part that took Ilinca longest.

When Ilinca asked her directly, at fourteen, whether she had left it out on purpose, her mother thought about it for a long time and then said, honestly, that she did not think she had ever noticed it was not in there.

Sabina Crețu was seventy-nine and lived at the top of the village and Ilinca knew exactly who she was in the way you know everybody in a place of four hundred, which is to say completely and not at all.
She had never spoken to her.

She was aware, in the vague way children are aware of these things, that there was a coolness — that Tanti Sabina was not at things, that her name came up in a particular register, that something had happened a long time ago about land.
The land business was real and it was from 1994 and it involved a boundary and a lawyer in Deva and it split that village for a decade and it has nothing whatsoever to do with this.
Ilinca said: "What's the mark on her arm?" And her mother said: "She was in the fire."

It took Ilinca the rest of that spring to get the whole of it and she got it in pieces from five people and never once from Tanti Sabina, who she did not have the courage to approach until she was nineteen.
Sabina Crețu was twenty-nine in 1987 and she lived next to the school and she was in the yard by the time the second room came out.
Two of the five people Ilinca got it from were in that yard as children and remembered her being there.
One was in the yard as an adult and remembered her going in.
One remembered only the arm afterwards.
The fifth was the priest, who was not there in 1987 and who told Ilinca where the parish papers had been kept, which was the piece that made the rest of it make sense.
Doamna Pop got the children out.
Nothing in the telling is false; she smelled it, she moved fast, she counted twice, and every account of her that Ilinca has ever heard is deserved.

But at some point between the second count and the roof going, Sabina Crețu went back in through the front and came out with the register, the attendance book from 1954 onward, and the two framed photographs from the corridor, and a wooden box of parish papers that had been kept at the school because the school had the only safe.
She was in there about ninety seconds.
The mark on her arm is from the doorframe on the way out.

And every single one of those things — the register, the photographs, the parish papers going back to 1911 — is the reason Vălișoara has any documents at all before 1989, and they are in the new school in a case, and the case has a card on it that says they were *recovered from the fire*.
Ilinca is twenty-four and she has never made a fuss about this and does not intend to.
What she has worked out, over twelve years, is that nobody edited Sabina Crețu out of that story.
There was no decision and no meeting and nobody was malicious.

What happened is that the land business started in 1994, and for about ten years after that her name was awkward in that village, and a story told two hundred times at kitchen tables by people who find one name awkward is a story that will smooth around it without anybody once choosing to.
By 2004 the awkwardness was over and the story had already set.
The bird sings in the elder every May and June and it is a nuisance to two houses, and what it gave Ilinca at twelve was a second and a half of a woman cutting bread with her sleeves up.

She went to see Tanti Sabina at nineteen with a question she had rehearsed for a month, and got about forty minutes, and the thing she remembers is that the old woman was not bitter about it and did not want it corrected and said, at the door, that Doamna Pop had got sixty-one children out and that she herself had gone back in for some paper.
There is a card in a case in the new school and Ilinca has written to the comuna twice about the wording of it, politely, and has had no reply, and will write again.
The wording she has proposed is nineteen words long and names one person and does not take a single thing away from anybody, and she has it saved on her phone.
Things go missing at Skálanes and everybody knows which things.
Not tools.
Not keys, not phones, not the small metal objects that vanish in every house on earth.
What goes missing at Skálanes, and has gone missing for as long as anybody can produce a complaint about it, is anything made of wool.
Gloves, principally.
Ari's mother reckons the household has lost somewhere between four and nine gloves a year since he was born, which over twelve years is a number she does not like saying out loud.
There is a box in the porch at Skálanes with about thirty single gloves in it.
Every farm on that road has one.

It is understood in that part of Iceland that you do not throw away a widowed glove, because the other one might come back, and about one in six of them does — turning up in a ditch in the spring, or under a fence, or once, memorably, folded on a gatepost.
Also: a hat off a fence post.
Three pairs of socks off the line, always the socks and never the shirts.
The lining out of a boot.
Half a sheepskin that was under the back door for people to wipe their feet on and that was there on a Tuesday and gone on a Wednesday, and which weighed about four kilos.
The village had a theory and the theory was the wind, which is not a stupid theory in a place where the wind takes roofs.
It accounted for most of it.
Anything on a line, anything on a wall, anything left on the seat of the quad — the wind at Skálanes will take all of that and has taken a trampoline.
Nobody had ever had to look any further, because the wind is a complete explanation that requires no thought and is right about eight times out of ten.
Ari stopped believing it at eleven for a reason that had nothing to do with anything clever.
He watched a glove go.

It was on the wall by the byre, in April, in a dead calm — the first properly still day of that year, so still that the smoke from the Hansdóttir chimney was going straight up — and he was thirty metres away doing something with a bucket, and he looked up because of the movement, and there was a glove going along the top of the wall about a foot above the stone.
Under it, going at a fast trot with her head up and the glove in her teeth, was a fox.
She was in the blue phase — grey-brown in summer, small, low, with the short round ears they have — and she was not skulking.
She went along the base of that wall in full daylight thirty metres from a boy with a bucket at a pace that said she had somewhere to be and had done this route a great many times.
Ari stood there with the bucket until she was out of sight, which took about forty seconds, and then went in and said nothing to anybody for the rest of the day.

He found the cache in the June and it took him two months and a great deal of walking, and the method was not sophisticated: he watched, and he wrote down the direction, and he did that eleven times over eight weeks.
Watching is most of it and watching is dull.

He sat on the wall by the byre with a book he was not reading for something in the region of forty hours across that spring, and he saw a fox six times, and only three of those were carrying anything.
The other five directions came from his mother and from the Hansdóttir boy, who both agreed to tell him and who both, he is fairly sure, thought he was wasting a summer.
Everything went north-east.

The cache is under a slab on the seaward side of the ridge, about two kilometres from the last house, in a place with no particular features that Ari has ever been able to describe to anybody without drawing a map.
He got the slab up with a fence post and he sat back on his heels and looked at it for a long time.
There were, by his count that afternoon, ninety-four items.
He counted them twice, out on the grass, in two rows, and then put every single one back before he left, which took the better part of an hour and which he has always been glad about.
Gloves: forty-one, not one of them a pair.
Socks: nineteen.
Four hats.
The boot lining.
A great deal of raw sheep's wool of the kind that comes off a fence in June and that nobody would ever miss.

Two lengths of knitting still on the needles, which he took home and which turned out to have gone from a windowsill in 2021 and which caused, when he produced them, the largest reaction of the entire summer.
And the sheepskin, folded, at the back, four kilos of it, dragged two kilometres uphill by an animal that weighs three and a half.
It was dry.
That is the thing that undid him.
It is under a slab on a seaward ridge in Iceland and there is drainage under it that Ari has never been able to work out, and the whole of it was dry and none of it was chewed.
Nothing had been eaten.
Nothing had been shredded for bedding.
It was not a nest — there was no den within sixty metres and he checked properly, with a torch, over two visits.
It was a store, and it had been sorted.
He has been back perhaps sixty times since and the number goes up and down.
The highest he has counted is a hundred and forty-one, in the September he was seventeen.
The lowest was thirty-eight, one April, after a winter that everybody on that coast remembers.
That April is the only real evidence he has that any of it is for anything.
Fifty-odd items of wool went out of that cache between October and March and none of it was in the ditches and none of it came home.

The wool was at the back and the manufactured things were at the front and the four hats were together, and Ari has never once been able to decide whether that last observation is real or whether he is a person who found ninety-four objects under a rock and wanted them to mean something.
The dull explanation is right and Ari has known it since he was about fourteen.
Arctic foxes cache.
It is one of the most thoroughly documented things they do.

A fox on a seabird cliff will take and bury hundreds of eggs in a season — there is a study from Wrangel Island with a number over nine hundred — and they bury them one at a time, in scattered places, and they remember where.
They cache anything that might be worth having later.
In a hard winter a cached egg from July is the difference.
The behaviour is not fussy about what the thing is; it is triggered by *surplus*, and a fox that finds something it cannot use now and might use later will take it and put it somewhere.
Wool smells of sheep and of people and of lanolin, which is to say it smells strongly of something that was recently alive.
And a fox does not have a category for *glove*.
It has a category for *smells of animal, portable, not currently useful*, and a hand-knitted mitten off a windowsill fits that description exactly and so does an egg.
That is the whole of it.
There is no puzzle.
Every wildlife biologist Ari has ever mentioned it to has said essentially the same four sentences, cheerfully, and one of them said it was a nice example and asked for photographs.
What none of them accounted for, and what Ari has stopped raising because it makes him sound like a person with a theory, is the sorting.
And the fact that in twelve years and something over three hundred items, not one thing that was not warm has ever been in that cache.
No plastic.
No paper.
No rope, and there is rope all over that farm.
No leather that had not been lined.
He has tested it, which he thinks is the only genuinely scientific thing he has ever done.
At fifteen he put four objects out on the wall by the byre on the same evening, all about the same size and weight: a woollen sock, a nylon sock, a strip of tarpaulin, and a length of baler twine.
The woollen sock went that night.
The other three were on the wall a week later and he brought them in.
He did it again the following spring with the same result and a fifth object, a fleece hat, which also went.
That is a sample of two trials and he is aware that this would not get past anybody.
He took one thing out of it and put four things in, and that is the arrangement he has kept for eleven years.
The thing he took was a mitten.

It was blue and it was hand-knitted with a pattern round the cuff in a way that nobody in Iceland does by accident, and it had belonged to his grandmother, and it had gone off a windowsill in the November of 2019 about four months before she died.
Its pair was in a drawer in his mother's room.

It had been in that drawer for six years because you do not throw away one of a pair when the person who made both is gone, and Ari had watched his mother open that drawer perhaps a hundred times and not say anything.
He knew the pattern round the cuff before he had the whole mitten out from under the slab.
There is a way of turning the eight-pointed rose at the wrist that his grandmother did and that is slightly wrong, and every person in that family can identify it across a room.
He carried it down the ridge inside his coat and he did not tell anybody for two days, and then he put it on the kitchen table.
His mother picked it up and turned it over and said, "Where." He told her.
All of it — the eight weeks of watching, the directions, the slab, the ninety-four things, the sheepskin folded at the back.
She listened the whole way through and then she went and got the other one and put the two of them together on the table, and neither of them said anything for a while.
It is not a good story about a woman being given something back.
His mother did not cry and did not thank him particularly.
She turned the recovered one inside out, looked at the wrist, said that the tension had gone at the end and that his grandmother's hands had been bad by then, and put both of them in the drawer.
They are still in the drawer.
Nobody wears them.
Ari has thought about that and has concluded that a pair in a drawer is a different object from a single in a drawer, and that this was the whole of what he had brought home.
Then she said: "What did you leave?" He had not left anything.
It had not occurred to him.

He went up the next weekend with an old fleece cut into four pieces and put them under the slab, and he has done something similar three or four times a year ever since — offcuts, mostly, and the wool that comes off the fence in June that he now collects on purpose.
He does not know whether it makes any difference to anything.
He is aware that a fox does not have gratitude and does not keep accounts and would take the fleece whether he had ever found the cache or not.
Ari is twenty-three and works on the boats and comes home in the winter.
The gloves still go.
His mother still loses between four and nine a year and complains about it in exactly the same words, and Ari has never once suggested that she stop.
He has told her where they are.
She knows.

She has never been up there and has never asked to go, and once, when he offered to take her, she said that it was two kilometres and that she had a farm to run and that if a fox wanted her gloves it was welcome to them.
Ari thinks she means it and also thinks she would rather they were somewhere than nowhere.
Behind the houses at Ferrel there is a wood of holm oak and in it there are the mounds, and the mounds are the largest thing about that village that visitors never notice.

There are four of them and the biggest is chest high and about three metres across and it is made of needle litter and it has been there, according to a man who did a survey in 1998, for at least a century.
It is a wood ant nest and there are perhaps a quarter of a million animals in it and it is entirely ordinary and there are ten thousand like it in Portugal.
Mariana has stood next to it a great many times.

In August it is loud — you can hear it from about four metres, a dry continuous crackle that is nothing but a quarter of a million small feet on dry needles — and it is warm, properly warm, several degrees above the air, which is a thing wood ant nests do and which has been measured and is not mysterious.
There is nothing about that mound that would make anybody look at it twice.
That is the point everybody in Ferrel makes when it comes up.
It is a completely ordinary nest of a completely ordinary species that any child in southern Europe can find in an afternoon.
The way you ask is this.
You open the window on the wood side of the house, the whole window, at dusk, and you leave it open all night, and you do not shut it and you do not go into that room.
That is all.
There is no phrase and no offering and nothing is left on the sill.
In the morning the house has stopped arguing.
That is the phrase.
Not *the argument is over* and not *you have made up*.
The house has stopped arguing, which is a claim about the house, and Mariana did not notice the grammar of it until she was about nineteen.
Mariana had known the mechanism since she was small and had never seen it done, because it is not done often.
Her grandmother reckoned three or four times a year across a village of a hundred and sixty people.

It is not a secret and it is not a ritual and there is no shame in it, and if you go past a house on the wood side at ten at night in April and the big window is open you look away, the way you would look away from a car with somebody sitting in it not driving.
Mariana saw an open window twice before she was twelve.
The first was the Estrela house in 2016 and she was seven and did not know what she was looking at.
The second was in 2019, in the summer, and she was ten and knew exactly what she was looking at and did not tell the person she was walking with, who was her friend Rita, whose house it was.
Rita has never mentioned it.
Mariana has never mentioned it.
They are still friends.
She asked her grandmother, at nine, what it cost.
Her grandmother said: "It costs the argument." Mariana said that was the point.
And her grandmother said, "Yes," in the particular way she said yes when a conversation had reached the edge of what she was going to say, and Mariana did not get any further with it for four years.
She tried again at eleven with a better question, which was whether her grandmother had ever done it.

Her grandmother said that she had, once, in 1981, and that she was not going to say what about, and that Mariana was to leave it, and that if she ever needed to know more than that she would find out for herself and would not enjoy it.

Her grandmother died in the February she was twelve and left the house at Ferrel to Mariana's mother and her mother's brother jointly, which is the most ordinary thing in Portugal and the beginning of a great deal of trouble.
The argument was about whether to sell it.
Her uncle was in Lisbon and had two children and a mortgage and wanted it sold, and he was not wrong.
Her mother wanted to keep it and could not have told you exactly for what, and she was not wrong either.
It was a stone house with a leaking roof in a village that has a shop three days a week, and it was worth something to a person from outside and nothing at all to anybody in Ferrel.
Mariana's parents argued about it from March to November.
Not constantly and not loudly.
It is important to describe this accurately because it was not a shouting house.

What it was, from March to November, was a house in which a specific subject was under everything — at dinner, in the car, when the phone went and it was Lisbon, in the silence after her mother came off the phone.
Mariana was twelve and she got very good that year at reading a room from the doorway.
The tells were: whether her mother's phone was face down on the table.
Whether her father said *your brother* or *Zé*.
Whether anybody mentioned the roof.
The roof was the worst one.

The roof was leaking from about the June and everybody knew the roof was leaking, and it could not be discussed, because a roof is either worth fixing or it is not and that is the whole argument wearing a hat.
By September her mother had stopped sleeping properly and her father had started being extremely reasonable, which in that marriage was worse than anything.
By November the house had been empty for nine months with the roof going and nobody had been able to have a conversation that reached the end of itself.
Mariana opened the window on the fourteenth of November.

She did it at about seven in the evening, when her parents were out, in the room at the back that faces the oaks, and she opened it the whole way and put the catch on and went and sat in the kitchen with the door shut and did not go back in.
She had thought about it for nine days.

She would like it on the record that she was not being impulsive and that she knew perfectly well that it was not her house and not her argument and not her decision, and that she did it anyway, at twelve, in November, and that if she could go back she is not certain what she would do.
Nothing happened in any sense that anybody could have filmed.
There were no ants in the house in the morning.

Mariana went in at seven and the room was exactly as she had left it, cold, with the window open, and there was nothing on the sill and nothing on the floor and nothing on the wall, and she shut the window and went and had breakfast.
Her mother came down at half past.
She looked at the window, which Mariana had shut, and at Mariana, and said good morning, and put the kettle on.
She had not slept properly since about August and she looked it and she was, that morning, ordinary.
And the thing that Mariana noticed, over the following four or five days, was not that the argument had stopped.
It was that nobody was avoiding anything.
That was what had been in the house since March: a shape everybody was walking around.
She had not known it was there until it was not, in the way you do not know a fridge is running.

The phone went from Lisbon on the Tuesday and her mother took it in the kitchen instead of going out to the yard, and talked about her uncle's daughter's school for eleven minutes, and put the phone down and made the tea and did not sit at the table afterwards with her hands flat on it.
Her father stopped being reasonable and went back to being ordinary, which was a considerable relief.
He argued with her about her phone on the Thursday, properly, at some volume, and Mariana went to bed almost cheerful.
Mariana did not tell anybody what she had done, and she did not feel guilty, and for about two years she thought she had got away with something clean.
She told her grandmother, in a manner of speaking, at the grave, in the February after, which she is aware is not the same as telling anybody.
The house at Ferrel is still empty.
The roof went properly in 2019 and there is a tarpaulin on it that Mariana's father put up and that has been there for six years.
The gutter is off the back.
There is a fig growing out of the wall by the chimney that was a seedling when she was fourteen and is now taller than she is.
Mariana goes and looks at it about twice a year.
She has a key.

She goes in and stands in the kitchen where her grandmother made her sit down and drink milk and told her, at nine, what the window cost, and then she comes out and locks it and drives back to Caldas.
The room at the back faces the oaks and the window in it does not open any more, because the frame has gone, and that is the only thing in that house that Mariana is glad about.
Nobody has sold it and nobody has fixed it, and the reason is not that they cannot agree.
The reason is that the question does not come up.
Mariana has watched this for eleven years and she can describe the mechanism exactly, because she has tested it.
She has raised it herself, deliberately, at dinner, four times.

It goes like this: she says the house, and her mother says yes, they must sort that out, and her uncle says the same thing on the phone at Christmas, and everybody agrees entirely, with real warmth, that something ought to be done.
And then it goes.
Not refused.
Not deflected.

It simply does not have any weight — the subject comes up and slides off and the conversation is on to something else, and if you ask anybody afterwards what was decided they will tell you, honestly, that it was a good talk and that they will get to it.
She has tried writing it down and putting it in front of them.
She did that at twenty-one: two pages, the state of the roof, three options with numbers, a recommendation.
Her mother read it and said it was very good and that Mariana had always been the sensible one.
Her uncle read it and rang up and was warm about it for twenty minutes.
Nobody disagreed with a single line of it and nothing happened, and when she brought it up again at Christmas her mother could not remember which of the three options she had preferred.
Her mother and her uncle have not had a cross word in eleven years, which in a Portuguese inheritance is close to a miracle, and everybody in both families says so.
Mariana is twenty-three and she has said this out loud to one person, who was kind about it.
The person was a woman she shared a flat with in Coimbra, who listened to all of it and then asked one question, which was whether Mariana had ever told her mother.
She has not.

She has thought about it perhaps four hundred times and she has worked out that there is no version of that conversation that does not end with her mother going and standing in front of the question for a while and then getting on with the dinner.
What she says is that the ants did exactly what they are asked to do and what her grandmother told her they do, and that nobody in Ferrel has ever misdescribed it.
The argument was taken.
It has not come back and it is not coming back.

What nobody had ever said to her — and she does not think anybody was hiding it, she thinks it is simply not the sort of thing that gets said to a child, and she is not sure she would have heard it at twelve — is that an argument is a thing standing on something.
They took the argument.

The house is what the argument was standing on, and the house is still there, with a fig in the wall, and there is nobody left in that family who can hold the question in their hands for long enough to answer it.
The tidal range at Kerlouan is eight metres on a big spring and that number is the reason for everything about the place.
Eight metres means the harbour is a harbour for about five hours out of every twelve and a field of mud for the rest.
It means the wall is enormous.

It means every boat there has legs, and the whole of the working life of that village is arranged around a table of numbers that has been published in an almanac since 1839 and that is now on everybody's phone.
Maëlle grew up inside that arrangement the way other children grow up inside a school timetable.
Meals moved.

Her father's working day started at a different hour every day of her childhood and moved fifty minutes later each time, and she could tell you the state of the tide from the smell coming off the harbour before she could tell the time.
Everybody in Kerlouan does that arithmetic constantly and nobody there thinks of it as arithmetic.
The tables are extremely good.
Maëlle would like that said first, because the story sounds otherwise like it is against them.
They are astronomy.

The tide is the moon and the sun pulling on a rotating planet, and that is a solved problem, and the tables for Kerlouan are accurate to about four minutes and eleven centimetres a century in advance.
What the tables do not have is the weather.
A hard low pressure system lifts the whole sea.
Wind piles it up against a coast or holds it off.

On a bad day in Brittany the actual water can be sixty or seventy centimetres above what the table says, and once in a generation a great deal more than that, and the table cannot know because the table was calculated in 1974.
Which is what the shoal is for.
There is a bar across the mouth of that harbour and on the flood there is a shoal of mullet over it, and there has been for as long as the village has records of anything.
Two or three hundred fish, grey, unremarkable, doing the entirely normal thing that mullet do in an estuary.
They are grey mullet and they are the least regarded fish on that coast.
Nobody eats them if there is anything else.

They come in on the flood to work the mud and they go out on the ebb and they have done that in every estuary in Europe since before there were estuaries in Europe, and there is nothing whatever unusual about the shoal at Kerlouan except that people used to look at it.
And where they sit tells you the water.
Maëlle's grandfather could read them and so could about six other people in Kerlouan and by the time she was twelve there were two.
The reading is not mystical and he could describe it, and did, at length, to anybody who would sit still.

You look at the shoal about ninety minutes before high water, from the end of the wall, and you look at three things: how far up the bar they are sitting, whether they are strung out along the channel or bunched over the shallow, and how deep they are holding.
Bunched and shallow and well up the bar is more water coming than the table says.
He would say it exactly like that, in that order, every time, and then he would make her say it back.
Strung out down the channel and holding deep is less.

And there is a third state that his own father had a word for that does not translate — a nervousness, a shoal that will not settle in either position — and that means the water is going to arrive early and hard, and that you get everything above the line and you do it now.
Maëlle has seen the third state twice in eleven years.
Her grandfather claimed to have seen it nine times in sixty.
Le Guen, asked about it once at a funeral, held up four fingers and did not elaborate.
Maëlle asked him how it worked and he said he had no idea and that it was not his business to have an idea.
He was not being difficult.

He genuinely did not think that knowing how a thing works and being able to use it were connected, and he had spent sixty-one years on that harbour among men who all thought the same, and Maëlle has since met a great many people with degrees who could learn something from that position and a great many others who could not.

She asked her physics teacher at fourteen and got a much better answer, which is that mullet in an estuary are exquisitely sensitive to salinity and to pressure and to the speed of the water over the bar, and that all three of those things start changing well before the water level does, and that a fish sitting in a current is a very good instrument for measuring that current.
The fish are not predicting anything.
They are simply reacting, immediately and accurately, to conditions that a table calculated in 1974 has no access to.
Which is a better story than a mystery, and Maëlle has never got anybody in Kerlouan interested in it.
She tried, at fifteen, at a family lunch, with a diagram.
Her uncle said that was very interesting.
Her father said that his father had been reading those fish before there was salinity, which is not an argument and which ended the conversation.
The app came in about 2016 and it is a good app.

It does the astronomy properly and it also pulls a surge model from the national service, which means it does have the weather in it — a forecast of it, on a grid, updated four times a day — and it is right about the water at Kerlouan very nearly all of the time.
The reading died in about four years.
Maëlle can date it, roughly, from who stopped coming to the wall.
Four men stopped in 2017.
Two more in 2019.
Her grandfather went out every day until the September he was seventy-nine, and after that only when there was weather in it, which is what she does now.
Nobody decided to stop.
There was no argument and nobody in that harbour ever said that the fish were nonsense.

What happened is that a thing which took forty years to learn and ninety minutes of standing on a wall was replaced by a thing that took no time and required nothing, and it was right, and the men who could read the shoal got old.
That is the whole mechanism and Maëlle has stopped being angry about it, because when she is honest she cannot construct the argument for the other outcome.
What was anybody supposed to have done?
Told a twenty-two-year-old with a mortgage to spend forty years learning a skill in order to be occasionally slightly better than a free app?
The reading was not lost through carelessness.
It was outcompeted, fairly, by something that works.
By the time Maëlle was twelve there were two: her grandfather, who was eighty-one, and a man called Le Guen who did not come down to the harbour any more.

She learned it because her grandfather was dying and because she was the only person in the family who would sit on that wall for ninety minutes, and she is entirely clear that she learned it for the wrong reason and got it by accident.
He did not set out to teach her.
He set out to go and look at the fish, which he had done nearly every day of his life, and he could not get down the wall on his own by then and Maëlle was twelve and had nothing else on.
So she went with him.
And he talked, because he had always talked, and about four months in she said something about the shoal being higher than yesterday and he stopped walking.
It took eleven months.
She was not good at it.

She is still not good at it — her grandfather could call the water to about fifteen centimetres and Maëlle, at twenty-four, can call it to about forty, which is the difference between forty years and eleven months.

He died in the October and she went out on the wall on the day of the funeral because she could not think what else to do with the afternoon, and the shoal was strung out down the channel and holding deep, and the water that evening was under the table by about thirty centimetres, and she got it right and there was nobody to tell.
The seventeenth of December was a Tuesday and the app said a high of six point one metres at eleven forty.
The surge model had it.
There was a low coming through and the model had put about twenty centimetres on, and everybody in the harbour had looked at that on a phone on the Monday evening and had planned an ordinary day.
Maëlle went out on the wall at about ten because she went out on the wall.
The shoal was bunched, and shallow, and further up the bar than she had ever seen it.

She stood there for about eleven minutes doing the thing her grandfather had taught her, which is to look away and look back and see whether you get the same answer, and she got the same answer four times, and the answer was a great deal of water.
She had no number.
She has never had a number; the reading does not give you a number, it gives you *more* or *less* or the third thing.
She rang her uncle, who was at the yard, and told him, and he said the app said six point one and she said she knew what the app said.
There was a pause on that phone that Maëlle has thought about a good deal since, because in it her uncle had to decide whether to move eleven boats on the say-so of a twelve-year-old and a fish.
He moved four of them.
The four that were cheapest to move.
High water at Kerlouan on the seventeenth of December was six metres ninety-four at eleven fifty-one.

The low had deepened faster than the model had it and had come through further south, and the surge at Kerlouan was about eighty centimetres instead of twenty, and the national service issued a corrected bulletin at eleven fifteen which nobody in that harbour saw because nobody looks at a phone at eleven fifteen when the app told them at seven that it was an ordinary day.
Nothing terrible happened.
Two boats took water over the transom and one man got extremely wet and there was a quantity of gear lost that everybody was cross about for a fortnight.
The four cheapest boats to move were fine.
Maëlle is twenty-four and she works for the harbour and she has the app on her phone and looks at it every single day.
Her job is mostly moorings and paperwork and telling visiting yachts about the sill.
She also goes out on the wall about ninety minutes before high water when there is weather in it, which is perhaps forty times a year, and she looks at the bar for eleven minutes.
She has never published anything and does not intend to.
She has taught it to one person, who is nine, and who is her cousin's daughter, and who is bored by it.
What she says, when the men in the yard ask her about the Tuesday — and they do, in a way that is not entirely friendly and not entirely unfriendly — is that the app was not wrong.
The app had the best forecast anybody had.
The fish had the water.
The pond is not much and Elin would like that clear, because people hear about it and imagine somewhere.

It is about forty metres across and it is in a dip in a field below the farm, and it has reeds along the north side and a willow that came down in 2015 and has gone on growing lying down, and it has a wooden thing at one end that was a jetty in about 1970 and is now four posts.
Her family have farmed above it since 1911.
Elin has swum in it.
Her father learned to swim in it.
There are newts in it and in April there is frogspawn and in a hot July it smells.
It is on the farm's land and nobody outside the family has been down there in years.
There is no path to it and no sign and no reason for anybody to go, and the gate at the top of the field has been tied with the same orange baler twine since about 2012.

The dragonfly is a golden-ringed and it is the largest species in Britain, which is not saying an enormous amount — about eight centimetres — and it is black with yellow bands and green eyes that meet in the middle.
There is one on that pond every summer.
Not the same one.

Elin is entirely clear about this and gets slightly short with people who want it to be the same one: a golden-ringed dragonfly lives as an adult for a few weeks and spends the previous two to five years as a larva in the mud, and there is no version of the biology in which an insect on that pond in 1994 is an insect on that pond in 2024.
What is the same is the reed.
Elin has thought about whether that is even remarkable and has decided it probably is not.
A dragonfly perch is a position, not a plant: a stem that stands clear at a particular height with a particular view of the water and the sun behind it in the afternoon.
If the geometry of a pond stays the same, the best perch stays the same, and a reed clump on a bank stays where it is for decades.
That is almost certainly the whole of it.
It lands on the same reed.
Third from the left of the clump at the north end, about sixty centimetres up, facing the water.

Elin has counted from the left every time and has been careful to count from the same end, which sounds obvious and which she got wrong twice before she made herself write down which end the willow was at.

Elin has photographs from four different summers and her father has one from about 1996 that his mother took, and it is the same reed clump and it is very nearly the same position within it, and Elin has no explanation for this at all and does not think it is the interesting part.
The first time happened in the July she was eleven and it lasted about four seconds.
She was lying on the bank on her front, about three metres from the reeds, watching it.
It had been there for perhaps a minute doing the thing they do, which is nothing whatsoever with the body while the head goes round.
Then it took off, and came back, and landed in the same place.
It is worth saying what that looks like at three metres, because most people have only seen dragonflies going past.
It does not flutter and it does not settle.

It goes from stationary to about eight metres away in something under a second, in a straight line, and then it is stationary again in mid-air over the water — properly stationary, not hovering with effort — and then it is back on the reed, and the whole excursion has taken perhaps three seconds and there has been no part of it in which the animal looked like it was making an effort.
And the pond changed.
Not dramatically and not all at once and not, at first, in any way she could name.
Something about the light.
Something about the noise, which went slightly down.
Then she saw the willow.
The willow was standing up.
It came down in the January of 2015 in a gale and Elin had been in the kitchen when it went and had heard it, and she had walked past its trunk lying in the water every summer of her conscious life.
And there it was, upright, on the far bank, in leaf, a different shape entirely.
She looked at the rest of it and the jetty had planks on it.
And there was a boy on the far bank.
He was sitting on the end of the jetty with his feet not in the water and he was doing nothing.
He had his elbows on his knees.
He was perhaps eleven or twelve and he was wearing a red T-shirt and he was looking at the reeds at the north end, which is to say approximately at her, and he did not react in any way at all.
Then the dragonfly moved, and the willow was lying down, and the jetty was four posts, and the bank was empty.
Nothing came with it.
No sound, no cold, no smell, none of the things people ask about.
The transition in both directions was instantaneous and she did not feel it happen either time; there was a pond, and then there was a different pond, and then there was the pond.
Elin lay on the grass for a considerable time.
She was eleven.

What she did about it, over the following week, was to construct four explanations, of which the strongest was that she had fallen asleep in the sun, and she was reasonably satisfied with that until it happened again at thirteen while she was standing up.
She worked out the year over about two years, and she did it the boring way, which was photographs.

There are perhaps two thousand photographs of that farm in three boxes and a biscuit tin, and Elin went through all of them twice between the ages of eleven and thirteen, on the floor of the back bedroom, and told her mother she was doing a project.
The willow standing up gives you before January 2015.

The jetty with planks on it is harder; her father reckoned the planks came off in the late nineties and her grandmother said 1997 and there is a photograph from a christening in 1999 in which they are already gone.
So: before 1999.
And then she had the T-shirt, which is not much of a clue, and the boy, who was somebody's child on their own land in a valley of four farms.

She had ruled her uncle out on height and there were no other boys of that age in the valley in the nineties, which left one candidate and which she had known perfectly well from about the fourth second and had spent two years not looking at directly.
She got it in the end from a box in the back bedroom.
It is a photograph from the summer of 1994 of her father, aged eleven, on the end of that jetty, with his elbows on his knees, in a red T-shirt.
It is not the same moment.
