She has been very careful about this and has looked at that photograph perhaps a thousand times: in the picture he is looking at the camera and slightly annoyed, and the boy she saw was looking at the reeds and was not annoyed at all.
It is the same afternoon, or the same fortnight, or the same summer.
It is not the same second.
Which matters, because the obvious explanation is that she saw the photograph as a small child, forgot it, and reassembled it on a hot afternoon at eleven.
Elin thinks that is probably what happened.
She has said so out loud to the two people she has told.
It accounts for the boy and the T-shirt and the jetty and even the willow, because the willow is standing up in about four hundred other photographs in those boxes.

What it does not account for is the second one, at thirteen, standing up, in which there was a bicycle on the grass — and there is no photograph of a bicycle by that jetty in any of the three boxes or the tin, and she has looked, and her father says he had a bicycle then and used to leave it exactly there.
Elin was thirteen when she worked it out and she did not tell anybody for nine years.
It has happened to her four times.
Eleven, thirteen, sixteen, and twenty-two.
Always at that pond, always with the dragonfly on that reed, always between three and six seconds, always the same summer on the other side.
She has been down to that pond, on a conservative estimate, four hundred times.
She has lain on that bank in July with a dragonfly on that reed perhaps sixty times.
Four.

That is the rate, and she puts it in whenever she tells this, because a story about a thing that happens is a completely different story from a story about a thing that has happened four times in eighteen years to one person with nobody else there.
She has never seen the boy again.
Three of the four times there was nobody on the far bank at all; once there was a bicycle lying on the grass by the jetty.
She has no mechanism and she is not going to offer one.

What she has is four occasions, two of which happened after she was old enough to be sceptical about the first two, and a photograph that she found afterwards and not before, which she thinks is the only part of the account that would interest anybody who does this properly.
She told her father in the November she was twenty-two, at the kitchen table, badly, over about twenty minutes.
He listened all the way through without interrupting, which is not like him.
Then he said: "Red T-shirt." "Yes." "I had that until I was about thirteen.
My mother hated it." He turned his cup round.
"What was I doing?" "Nothing.

Sitting on the jetty with your elbows on your knees looking at the reeds." And her father sat there for a while and then said the thing that Elin was not remotely prepared for, which was: "That'll be the summer my father was ill." He said that he had spent most of that July down at that pond because there was nothing to do at the house and because there were people in it all the time, and that he had sat on that jetty for hours, and that he could not now remember one single thing he had thought about in the whole of that month.
He said he had been fine.
He said he was not saying it had been bad.

He said that when he thought about that summer at all what he got was the pond and the heat and the smell of it and nothing else, and that he had never told anybody that and had not known he was going to tell her.
Her grandfather recovered, as it happens, and lived until 2011, and Elin knew him and he taught her to reverse a trailer.
That is the part that nearly everybody gets wrong when she tells it.
They want the summer to have been the last one.
It was not.

It was an ordinary frightening summer in the middle of a life that turned out fine, and the thing her father could not remember a single thought from was eleven weeks of being a boy at a pond while adults he loved were doing something difficult upstairs.
Elin is twenty-nine.

She goes down to the pond in July, most years, and lies on the bank on her front about three metres from the reeds, and waits for a dragonfly that is not the same dragonfly to land on the third reed from the left.
She has never once thought of anything she would say.
At Sveti Duh there is a ledge on the north wall of the church, about two metres up, where the buttress meets the stone, and it is about the size of a windowsill and it is where you put things out.
You put out four or five objects.
Never one; one is not a trade, it is an offering, and an offering gets left exactly where you put it.
You put them out at dusk and you go away.

Going away is not optional and it is not superstition; anybody who has ever waited round that corner has got nothing, and the village's explanation for this is that she can hear you, which is almost certainly correct.
Nobody watches.
There is no tradition of watching and there is no story in Sveti Duh about anybody having seen the exchange, and Jakob has never met a person who claimed to.
In the morning one of them is gone and there is something else in its place, and the something else is always better.
Not more valuable.

Nobody in that village has ever got a coin off that ledge and Jakob's grandmother would tell you, at some length, about a man in the 1960s who put out a watch and a ring and two buttons in an attempt to establish an exchange rate, and who got back a piece of blue glass, and who was extremely annoyed about it for eleven years and who kept the glass until he died.
Better means better.
That is the whole of the definition and there is not a better one available, and everybody in Sveti Duh finds this obvious and no visitor ever has.
What comes off that ledge, in Jakob's lifetime: a bootlace.
A key.
A plastic dinosaur.
Four marbles that he knows of.
A brass washer.
A cigarette lighter that did not work.
A piece of dark green sea glass from a coast three hundred kilometres away that caused a certain amount of discussion in 2014.
There is no pattern in the objects.
The pattern, if there is one, is entirely in who got which, and it is not a pattern you can see from outside a family.
The marten is a pine marten and she lives in the roof of the barn behind the church and she has been seen perhaps thirty times in Jakob's life, mostly as a shape going along a wall at speed.
She is not tame and she is not friendly and she has bitten one person, in 1998, who reached up onto the ledge while she was on it, which everybody agreed at the time was entirely his own fault.
Martens take shiny things.
That is well documented and every naturalist Jakob has ever mentioned it to has said so within about a minute.
They are curious, they cache, they will carry off a spoon, and there are people all over central Europe who have lost car keys to one.
The village has never disputed a word of that.
The village's position, as Jakob's grandmother put it, is that knowing what an animal does is not the same as knowing what it is doing.
The rule is that you may not choose what she takes.

You may choose what you put out — that is the whole of your part in it — but which of the four or five goes is not yours, and there is no known method of influencing it, and every single person in that village has tried.
Jakob's mother tried at fourteen by putting out four things she did not want and one she did, arranged so that the one she wanted was at the back.
It went.

His uncle tried by putting out five things he was equally indifferent to, on the theory that this was a fair test, and got nothing at all — everything was still on the ledge in the morning, which is what happens when there is nothing in the set worth taking, and which is the most common outcome and which nobody in Sveti Duh finds interesting.
About two-thirds of attempts come to nothing.

Jakob's mother's estimate is that in a village of two hundred and forty there are perhaps eleven or twelve completed trades a year, and that most people in Sveti Duh do it three or four times in a lifetime and then stop.
Jakob's grandmother's position, which she stated once and would not elaborate on, was that the trade only works if there is something in it you would rather keep.
Jakob pushed her on it exactly once, at eleven, at her table, and got four more sentences than he expected.
She said that she had done it three times.
She said that the first was at nineteen and that she had not understood what she was doing.
She said that the second was in 1979 and that she had understood perfectly well and had done it anyway and had been right to.
He asked about the third and she said that it had not been taken, and that this had told her something, and that she had never gone back.
And that everybody knows which one that is, and that pretending otherwise is a waste of a dusk.
Jakob did not accept this at twelve and would like it recorded that he had reasons.
It sounded, to him, like the kind of thing adults say to make a coincidence into a lesson.
He had a plan and he thought the plan was good.
His father left in the March he was nine and there was nothing dramatic about it and Jakob has never described it as anything else.

He went to Austria for work, which about a third of that valley has done, and the arrangement was that he would come back at Christmas and he did, in 2019 and 2020, and then there was a period in which it was complicated, and then there was a woman in Graz, and by the time Jakob was twelve his father was a voice on a phone every second Sunday who was entirely pleasant and who talked about football.
Jakob's mother has never once said anything against him in Jakob's hearing, in eleven years, which he has recently begun to understand was not easy and was a decision she made early and stuck to.
Before he went he gave Jakob a knife.

It was a folding knife with a wooden handle and a brass bolster and it had been his own father's, and he gave it to Jakob in the kitchen on a Tuesday and said the things you say, and Jakob carried it every day for three years.
It was not a comfort.
That is the part he could not have said at twelve and can say now without any difficulty at all.
It was a weight in a pocket that he checked for about forty times a day.
It was a thing he could not use for anything, because using it would have wrecked it.

It was an object that made every second Sunday harder rather than easier, and by the summer he was twelve he had reached a state in which he was angry with a piece of wood and brass and could not have explained why to anybody including himself.

He had taken it out at school in the June and a boy had asked whether he could see it and Jakob had said no, and had said it in a voice that made the whole table go quiet, and had thought about that for the rest of the term.
He went to the ledge in the August.
He went at dusk on the fourteenth, which is a Thursday in his memory and which the calendar says was a Sunday, and he has decided not to worry about that.
He put out five things.
A good torch.
A tin whistle.
A knot of copper wire he had made and was pleased with.
A fossil from the quarry.
And the knife, at the front, in the middle, in the open, because he had worked out that the way to beat the rule was to stop hiding the thing.
His reasoning, at twelve, was that she took what you were protecting, so if he protected nothing she would have to take something else.
He has thought about that reasoning for eleven years and he still cannot find the flaw in it and it did not work.
The knife was gone and there was a marble in its place.

It was about two centimetres across and it was glass and it had a twist of blue and white through the middle and it was chipped in one place, and it was, by any measure anybody could apply, a completely worthless object.

Jakob was twelve and he stood at the north wall of that church at seven in the morning and cried, which he had not done about his father leaving and had not done about the Christmases and did not do again about anything for six years.
Then he put the marble in his pocket and went home and did not tell anybody for three years.
His mother worked it out inside a fortnight.
She did not say anything about it for three years either, and when he finally told her she said, "I know," and put the kettle on, and that was the whole conversation.
He was furious about it for most of a year.
He went back to the ledge eleven times that autumn with progressively worse ideas and never put anything out.
He worked out four separate theories about how she had done it and one of them involved his mother.
Somewhere in the following spring it stopped mattering, in the ordinary way that things stop mattering, without an event.
Jakob is twenty-three.
He is a joiner and he lives forty minutes down the valley and he sees his father about once a year in a way that is fine.
He has the marble.
It is in a dish on a shelf with some screws.

His mother put it in that dish about six years ago, along with everything else that lives on that shelf, and it has been there since, and Jakob has never moved it into anywhere better and thinks that would be the wrong thing to do to it.

What he says about the whole business — and he does not say it often, and he said it once to his mother and once to a girl he was seeing and once, badly, to his father in a car — is that at twenty he realised he could no longer picture the knife.
He could tell you it was folding, and wooden, and had a brass bolster.
He cannot see it.
He tried for about a fortnight, deliberately, and got nothing but the words.
And he could draw that marble from memory in about four seconds, including which side the chip is on.
He does not think the marten knew any of that.

He is quite clear that a pine marten is an animal that takes shiny objects and that there is a documented behaviour and that his village has built four hundred years of a very good social institution on top of an entirely ordinary mustelid.

What he says is only that he asked, at twelve, in the way you are allowed to ask, and that he tried to rig it, and that what he got back was worth less than what went and he would not trade it now for anything on that ledge.
He went back to the ledge once as an adult, at twenty-one, and put out five things, and thought about it for a fortnight beforehand the way you are supposed to.
Nothing was taken.

He stood there in the morning looking at his own five objects in the wet and worked out, on the way down, that this was the answer his grandmother had got at the third attempt and had never explained, and that he now knew what it told her, and that she had been right not to say.
He has not been back.
He is not unhappy about it.
It is, he thinks, a fairly good thing to be told about yourself at twenty-one by an animal that owes you nothing.

The herd on the Cairngorms is free-ranging over about four hundred hectares of the high plateau and it comes down to the enclosure at Glenmore when it wants to, which is mostly in the winter, and there is nothing at all mysterious about that.
There is grazing up there in summer and there is not much in December.

Reindeer are extremely good at digging for lichen through snow and extremely bad at coping with the wet warm winters that part of Scotland has been getting, and when the tops go hard they come down and the herders put food out and everybody is happy.
That is what the visitors are told and it is true.
Morag has said it perhaps two thousand times.

It is on a laminated card and it is in the talk and it is what she tells the families who come up the hill in waterproofs in July to see reindeer in a Scottish summer and are usually surprised by how much they smell.
What Morag was told, by her mother, who has worked with that herd since 2004, is the other thing.
The herd comes down when it likes.
Some of them come down in October and some hang about until January and there is no order to it that anybody has ever been able to chart.
Except the bull.

There is one bull — his name in the herd book is a number and the herders call him something else that Morag is not going to write down, because that name is theirs and she does not think it belongs in a story — and he comes down alone, ahead of everything, in a straight line off the Cairn Lochan side.
And it snows within about thirty hours.
Morag grew up with this the way other children grow up with a family saying.

Her mother would come in and take her boots off and say *he's down*, and Morag's father would look at the window, and there would be snow on the tops by the following afternoon, and nobody ever remarked on it because remarking on it would have been like remarking that the kettle had boiled.
Not sometimes.
Every year that anybody in that family has kept track of, and Morag's mother has kept track since 2004 in a notebook that also has feed orders and a recipe for flapjack in it.
Twenty-one years.
Twenty-one first snows on the plateau, twenty-one bulls walking down off Cairn Lochan somewhere between one and thirty hours before, and eighteen of them accurate to within a day.
It is not always the same animal.

That is the part visitors get stuck on and that Morag's mother is brisk about: a bull is good for perhaps eleven or twelve years and there have been four of them in twenty-one, and each one has done it, and nobody taught them, and there is no lineage — the current one is not the son of the last.
What there is, as far as anybody in that family can see, is a plateau, and a set of conditions on it, and whichever animal happens to be the one that notices first.
The three that are not are 2022, 2023 and 2024.
In 2022 he came down on the fourth of November and the first lying snow on the plateau was on the nineteenth.
In 2023 he came down on the ninth of November and the snow came on the twenty-eighth.
In 2024 he came down on the second and the snow came on the sixth of December, which is thirty-four days, which is not a margin of error.
It is a different month.
Morag's mother wrote all three of those in the notebook without any note attached.
Fourth of November, fifteen days.
Ninth of November, nineteen days.
Second of November, thirty-four days.
She has never underlined anything in that book and she did not start.

Morag was eleven in 2024 and she was in the enclosure with her mother on the afternoon he came down and she said, before she thought about it, "He's wrong again." Her mother did not answer for a while and then said: "He's not wrong." Morag said that thirty-four days was wrong.

And her mother — who is not a sentimental person and who has spent twenty-one years putting food out for animals in horizontal rain and has views about people who anthropomorphise them — said: "He came down when the tops stopped being worth staying on.
That is the only thing he has ever done.

He has never once been telling us about the weather." Morag remembers exactly where they were standing and that it was raining and that her mother said it without any heat at all, in the voice she uses for saying that a gate is broken.
Morag said that if that was true then the eighteen years were a coincidence.
Her mother said no.

She said that the tops stopping being worth staying on and the first snow used to be the same event, and that they are not the same event any more, and that this is the whole of it and there is nothing else in it.
Morag did the arithmetic that winter because she wanted her mother to be wrong.

She had twenty-one years of her mother's notebook — the date he came down, in her mother's handwriting, in among the feed orders — and she got the snow dates from the weather station at Cairngorm summit, which has been recording since 1977 and which is public and which anybody can download.
She was expecting to find that the gap was noise.
Eighteen good years and three bad ones is exactly what a coincidence looks like, and she was twelve by then and had done a term of statistics and was extremely pleased with herself about it.
The plan, which she had thought about for a week and which she still thinks was a reasonable plan, was to show her mother a scatter plot with no trend in it and say *there*.
The gap is not noise.
It is a trend.
It is not a dramatic one and it does not go up in a straight line, and there are two years in the middle where it goes backwards.

But you can put a line through those twenty-one points and the line has a slope, and the slope says that the interval between him coming down and the snow arriving has been getting longer by a bit under a day a year since about 2011.
She checked it against the summit temperature series and got the thing she was not looking for, which is that the two lines are the same shape.
She would like to be clear about the limits of this.
It is twenty-one points.
It is one bull at a time on one plateau, and the come-down dates were written by one woman who was mainly writing about feed, and Morag was twelve and taught herself the regression off the internet.

She has since had it looked at by a teacher who does statistics properly and who was kind about it and who said the sample was small, the effect was real, and the conclusion was correct for reasons that had almost nothing to do with the reindeer — because the summit temperature series alone says the same thing on its own without any animals in it at all.
He is not late.
That is what Morag understood, sitting on the floor with a laptop in the January she was twelve, and it took her about a fortnight to stop feeling sick about it.
The fortnight is worth explaining because she was not upset about the climate, which she had known about since she was seven and which is on the news.
What got her was smaller and more specific.

For eighteen years there had been an arrangement — an animal came down a hill and the weather did a thing — and it had been in her family and in that notebook and nobody had built it or maintained it and it had simply been true.
And it had stopped being true during her own childhood, quietly, in three years, without anybody doing anything wrong.
He is doing exactly what he has always done, on exactly the same cue, at more or less the same point in the autumn.

The lichen goes, and the ground gets soft and sour, and a bull who has been on that plateau for eleven years decides it is not worth it any more and walks down off Cairn Lochan in a straight line the way he has every year of his life.
The snow is what has moved.
Morag is fifteen and she works weekends at the enclosure in the summer and she is very good with the visitors, everybody says so.
She tells them the true and cheerful things.
That reindeer hooves spread in summer and harden in winter.
That they are the only deer where the females keep antlers through the winter, which is why every Christmas card in Britain is wrong.
That this herd came from Sweden in 1952 and that the man who brought them was called Mikel Utsi and that the first three arrived by boat.
She tells them that reindeer can see ultraviolet, which is genuinely the best fact on the hill and which stops a group of eight-year-olds dead every single time.
Snow reflects UV and lichen absorbs it, and so does fur, and so does urine, which means that a landscape that looks blank white to a person is, to a reindeer, covered in writing.
She does not tell them about the bull.

It is not a secret and there is no rule about it and if a visitor asked her directly she would answer honestly, and one man did, in 2026, who turned out to know a great deal about herds in Norway, and she talked to him for forty minutes.

He said that the same argument was going on in three places in Finnmark and that nobody there had twenty-one years of dates either, because the people who know are herders and herders write down what they need and nothing else.
He gave her an email address and she has not used it, and it is in the front of her mother's notebook on a piece of card.
The reason she does not tell them is that it does not work as a nice fact.
Every other thing she says on that hill can be said in a cheerful voice to a family with a four-year-old.
*He comes down and it snows within thirty hours* is a wonderful one — it is the best one she has — and it was true for eighteen years and she cannot say it any more without saying the rest.

And the rest is: he still comes down, and he is still right about the plateau, and the plateau is not what it was, and the notebook her mother keeps with the flapjack recipe in it is now a record of something nobody set out to record.
Her mother has kept it up.
Twenty-third of November 2025, thirty-one days.
She writes it in the same handwriting in among the feed orders and does not comment.
Morag has asked her twice whether she is going to send it to anybody.

Her mother says she is a herder and not a scientist and that the notebook is for the feed, and that if somebody wants it after she is finished with it they are welcome to it, and that in the meantime there are animals to see to.
Morag has a copy.
She made it at fourteen, over about six evenings, photographing every page on her phone, and she has it in two places and one of them is not in that house.
She did not ask permission and she did not hide it either.
Her mother came in halfway through the third evening, looked at what she was doing, said nothing whatsoever, and put the kettle on.
That is the only conversation the two of them have ever had about whether the notebook matters, and Morag thinks it was a fairly complete one.
Colle and Fonte are eleven hundred metres apart across a wooded ridge in the Abruzzo and there is no road between them.
There was a road.

It went over the top and it was a mule track that had been a mule track since the Romans, and it is still there under about fifty years of hornbeam and it is perfectly walkable if you know it, and Dario has walked it, and he is not supposed to have.
The road that exists now goes down from Colle to the valley and along and back up to Fonte and it is twenty-nine kilometres and takes fifty minutes.
Nobody makes that drive.

That is the thing to understand about the geography: it is not that the two villages are far apart, it is that they are eleven hundred metres apart and might as well be in different countries, and the fifty minutes exists as a fact and has almost never been used.
Dario has been to Fonte twice in his life.
Once at seven, for a funeral of somebody related through a marriage in the 1950s, in a car, with his mother, without his grandfather.
And once at nineteen.
The thing that happened in 1974 was about water.
Dario would like to set out the whole of it, because everybody assumes it must have been something enormous.

There is a spring on the Colle side of the ridge and it had fed both villages through a masonry channel since 1911, and in 1972 the comune of Colle put in a new tank and the channel was cut, and it was almost certainly not deliberate — the men who did it were from Pescara and they were laying a pipe — and Fonte was without water for eleven days in the August.
There was a meeting.
It went badly.
There was a second meeting that went worse, and there was a court case that ran until 1979 and that Fonte won, and by then it was not about water.
Dario has read the judgment.

It is in the comune archive at Colle and it is fourteen pages and it is extremely boring, and the operative part is about who owns a masonry channel built in 1911 under an agreement that nobody could produce.
Fonte got the water back in the September of 1972, eleven days after it stopped.
The whole of the actual problem lasted a week and a half.
Dario's grandfather has not spoken to anybody from Fonte since he was twenty-two.
He has spoken to people from Fonte.
Dario has watched him do it — at a hospital in Sulmona, at a market, once at a wedding — perfectly civilly, about the weather, for two minutes at a time.
What he has not done in fifty-one years is have a conversation.
He is not a bitter man.
That is the part Dario has never got anybody outside the valley to understand.

He tried it once on a girlfriend from Rome, who said, reasonably, that it sounded as though everybody should get over it, and Dario found that he could not construct a single sentence in his grandfather's defence and also could not agree with her.

He is a cheerful, decent, extremely funny old man who has three friends in the valley and goes to everything and helps everybody, and if you say the word Fonte at his table the temperature goes down four degrees and stays there for the rest of the meal.
There are wolves in that part of the Abruzzo — properly, verifiably, in numbers, since the protections came in — and everybody in both villages knows it and nobody makes a fuss.
The one on the ridge is different only in that she is regular.
She walks the old mule track.

Not near it, not roughly along it: on it, the full length, from the last house at Colle to the last house at Fonte, most nights between October and March, and she has been doing it for something over eleven years.
There is nothing remarkable in a wolf using a track.
It is the least remarkable thing about her.

A wolf on the move will take the easiest line through cover exactly the way anything does, and a mule track cut into a hillside in the Roman period is, by construction, the easiest line over that ridge, and it does not stop being the easiest line because two comuni stopped speaking in 1974.
She is not walking between the villages.
She is walking over the ridge, and the villages happen to be at the two ends of the only sensible way over it, which is why they are where they are.
Both villages know.
Both villages have known for a decade.

There are camera-trap photographs of her in the bar at Colle and there are camera-trap photographs of her in the bar at Fonte and they are, as far as Dario can establish, the same photographs, because they came off the same trap.
The trap belongs to the national park.

It is on a beech about halfway up on the Colle side, in a place that is technically in the comune of Colle by about sixty metres, and the park sends the images to both village halls because the park does not have a position on 1974 and has never been asked to develop one.
That is the joke, and both villages make it, separately, in exactly the same words, and neither of them knows the other one makes it.
Dario found the mule track at eleven because he was following her tracks in snow and did not think about where he was going until he came out at the top and saw the roofs of Fonte below him.
He stood there for a long time.
He was closer to Fonte than to his own house.
He had never in his life seen it from above.
It is a completely ordinary Abruzzese village.
Twenty-odd roofs, a bell tower, a road going down, a football pitch with one net.
He had spent eleven years understanding Fonte as a word people did not say at his grandfather's table and it turned out to be twenty-odd roofs.
Her name is Sara and she was twelve and she was standing on the track about four hundred metres down the Fonte side with a phone in her hand, and she had been following the same tracks up.
They looked at each other for a while.
He has thought about that pause a great deal and he does not think either of them was frightened.

What they were doing was arithmetic: two children on a track that neither village used, each working out which village the other was from and what that was supposed to mean, and both of them arriving at *I have no idea what I am supposed to do here* at about the same moment.

What Dario says about that moment, at twenty-four, is that he knew exactly who she was before she said anything, because there are two families in Fonte with that hair and one of them is the family from the court case.
Neither of them said hello.

What Sara said, eventually, holding up the phone, was: "Have you got her on anything?" And Dario said no, and that his was a rubbish phone, and that she had gone past his uncle's shed at about half five.
Sara said that she had her going up past the chapel at twenty past six.

And the two of them stood on a mule track that neither village had used since 1974 and worked out, from two sightings fifty minutes apart, roughly how fast a wolf walks, which is about four kilometres an hour, which is a fact Dario has never forgotten and has never needed.
They did that for two winters.
Not often.
Perhaps nine or ten times a year, in the snow, when the tracking was good, always on the track, always by accident to begin with and then, from about the second January, not by accident at all.
They did not become friends exactly.
Dario wants to be precise about this because the story gets away from him otherwise.

They were two children in different schools in different valleys who had one subject in common, and the subject was an animal, and they talked about the animal for a couple of hours a winter for two years and about almost nothing else.
They had no way to contact each other.

That is a detail people find hard to believe now and it is central: neither of them ever gave the other a number, for two years, because the number would have had to be explained at some point to somebody.
So it worked like this.
If it snowed, and the tracks were on the Colle side, Dario went up.
If it snowed, and she could get out, Sara went up.
Roughly a third of the time the other one was there.
He knows that her grandmother was in the 1974 meetings.
She knows that his grandfather was.
Neither of them ever raised it and Dario cannot now remember which of them decided that.
Nothing was fixed.

Dario is twenty-four and his grandfather is eighty-two and has not spoken to anybody from Fonte, and the road is still twenty-nine kilometres, and the mule track is still under the hornbeam, and there is no version of this story in which two villages made it up because some children met a wolf.
He wants that stated plainly, because he has told this at university twice and both times somebody has tried to give it an ending.
The endings offered were: that the two villages should hold a joint festival, and that Dario and Sara should have got married.
He is not making either of those up.
What happened is smaller and he thinks it is the only kind of thing that actually happens.
He told his grandfather about Sara when he was nineteen.

He did it badly and at the wrong moment, at a table, with people there, and his grandfather went the four degrees down and said nothing for the rest of the meal, and then came and found him in the yard about an hour later and asked one question.
He asked what her grandmother's name was.
Not what Sara was like.
Not what they had talked about.
Not whether Dario had told anybody.
One question, in a yard, an hour later, having plainly thought about nothing else during the meal.
Dario told him.
His grandfather stood there for a bit and then said: "She was two years above me at the school in the valley.
Before all this.
She could sing." And went in.
That is the whole of it and it did not lead to anything.
There was no reconciliation and no visit and his grandfather has not said her name since.

But Dario is twenty-four and Sara is twenty-four and they are in touch about four times a year, and when his grandfather and her grandmother are gone there is going to be one family in Colle and one family in Fonte in which the word does not drop the temperature, and neither of those families will be able to point to a moment when that changed.
The wolf is dead or gone.
The track stopped in the winter of 2019 and there is a photograph from the trap in the February of that year which is the last one, and eleven years is a good run for a wolf.
Both bars still have the photographs up.
Dario checked the one in Fonte in 2023, on the second visit of his life, and it is in a frame by the door and it is the same image as the one in Colle and it has a different caption.
There is another one on the ridge now.
She does not use the mule track.
There is a post at the end of the inner wall at Porthallow that used to hold a light and has held nothing since 1988, and a cormorant sits on it.
The light was taken off when the new one went on the outer arm and the post was left because taking a post out of a Cornish harbour wall is a great deal more work than leaving it in.
It is oak, about two metres proud, black, with four iron bolts in it that have wept rust down the stone for forty years.
Cormorants sit on posts.
It is what they are for, more or less.

They have wettable feathers, which is the trade they have made in exchange for being able to chase a fish underwater at a depth that would kill most birds, and it means that after a session in the water they have to get out and stand somewhere with their wings open like a wet umbrella until they are dry.
Every harbour in Britain has one on a post and nobody looks at it twice.
Merryn has since spent a career explaining to people that this is not a design fault.

A bird that could stay dry would float too well, and a bird that floats too well cannot get down to forty metres and stay there for a minute, and the cormorant has traded comfort for a hunting depth that no other British seabird of its size gets anywhere near.
The wet umbrella on the post is not a bird recovering from a mistake.
It is the running cost of being extremely good at something.

What Merryn's family will tell you about the one at Porthallow — and what her grandmother will tell you at length, and what her uncle will tell you shortly and while looking at something else — is that she is on that post at the start of the ebb, when the boats go, and she is on it when they come back.
And in between, if they are all in, she goes.
If they are not all in, she does not.
Nobody in Porthallow claims she is counting.
Merryn wants that on the record because it is the version that gets repeated by visitors and it is not what anybody there actually says.
What her grandmother said, always in the same words, was: *she's not off yet.* Merryn tested this properly at twelve because she had reached the age at which you test what your family tells you.

She did it for the whole of a summer with a notebook and a pair of binoculars from her bedroom window, which looks down the harbour, and the method was simple: count the boats out, count the boats in, and record whether the post was occupied at three-hourly intervals.
She was rigorous about the parts she could be rigorous about, which is a thing she is still proud of.
She wrote the boat count before she looked at the post, every time, so that she could not adjust one to fit the other.
She had a rule that a bird had to be on the post at the moment she looked and not within a minute of it.
She had no rule at all about how hard she looked, which is where the whole thing falls apart, and it took her until about nineteen to see it.
Fifty-eight days.
Eleven days on which every boat was back within the usual window and the post was empty by an hour after.
Forty-four days on which she could not get a clean count because of visitors, weather or her own laziness.
The forty-four is the honest number and it is the one she puts in first now.

Doing anything properly for fifty-eight consecutive days at twelve turned out to be about four times harder than she had estimated, and the reason she remembers that summer at all is mostly that she failed at it.
And three days on which a boat was late, and on all three of those the post had a cormorant on it, and on two of the three that cormorant was still there in the dark.
The third one came in at half past four in the afternoon with a broken hydraulic and the post was empty by six.
Merryn is thirty-one and she works in fisheries science and she will tell you exactly what is wrong with all of that.
Three is not a number.
Fifty-eight days of a twelve-year-old with binoculars is not a study.
There is no control, no blind, and an enormous confirmation bias, because on the days when she was expecting the post to be occupied she looked harder at it.
And there is a mechanism problem that she thinks is fatal and that nobody in Porthallow has ever engaged with.
A cormorant does not care about boats.
They are not a food source, they are not a threat, and the fleet at Porthallow is eleven small crabbers that go out at dawn and come back when they are done.

A bird sitting on a post at the end of a wall is sitting there because it is a good post with a good view of the channel and it needs to dry, and it leaves when it is dry, and how long that takes depends on wind and sun and how long it has been in the water.
There is also no reason to think it is one bird.

Merryn has tagged enough of them to know how much they move; the post at Porthallow is a good post and there are several hundred cormorants working that stretch of coast, and the idea that the same individual has been on that pole since her grandmother was a girl is not defensible for a second.
The days a boat is late are days with weather in them.
Weather is also what keeps a cormorant on a post.
A wet bird in still cold air takes a long time to dry.
A wet bird in a breeze is off in twenty minutes.
So the confound is not incidental — it is the strongest single predictor of both variables, and any correlation between late boats and occupied posts falls straight out of it with nothing left over.
That is the whole of it.
She has said it in exactly those words to her uncle, at a table, at nineteen, and her uncle said, "Right," and did not argue, and she has never once managed to make it stick.
The *Marged Ann* went out at ten past six with two aboard and did not come back.
Merryn was fourteen.
It was a flat grey day with no weather in it whatsoever, which matters, and the other ten boats were in by half past two.
She has checked the record.
Wind at the Lizard that afternoon was force two to three, visibility good, sea slight.
It is the single data point in the whole of her life that her own explanation does not cover, and she has been extremely careful never to build anything on it.
By four the harbour knew.

By five the coastguard had it and there was a lifeboat out of Falmouth and two of the crabbers had gone back out, and by seven it was dark and there was a helicopter working the ground west of the Manacles.
Merryn was at her grandmother's, which is where the family goes.
There is a particular thing that happens in a village on an evening like that and it is not what people imagine.
Nobody stood on the wall.
Nobody wailed.
Merryn's cousin, who was seventeen, did the sandwiches.
That is what he did for eleven hours: he made sandwiches for people who were not eating, and put them on the table, and took them away, and made more, and nobody told him to and nobody stopped him.
Merryn has thought about that as much as she has thought about the bird.
What there was, for eleven hours, was a kitchen with too many people in it and a great deal of tea and long stretches of ordinary conversation that stopped every time a phone went.
At about nine her grandmother got up and went to the window and stood there for a while.
She was seventy-eight and she had buried a brother off that coast in 1969 and she had not said a word for two hours.
Merryn asked her what she was doing.

Her grandmother said: "She's on the post." And Merryn, who had done fifty-eight days with a notebook two years earlier and knew exactly what she thought about all of it, went and stood at that window and looked down the harbour at a post in the dark with a bird-shaped thing on it and did not say one word about confirmation bias.
They found the *Marged Ann* at twenty to two in the morning, eleven miles south-south-west, with a fouled prop and a dead radio and two extremely cold and extremely embarrassed men aboard.
The prop had picked up a length of somebody else's rope, which happens perhaps twice a year in that fleet and is normally a nuisance and an hour with a knife.
The radio had failed for a reason that was never satisfactorily established and that one of the two men was extremely defensive about for the next decade.
Nobody was hurt.
The post was empty at first light.
Merryn has never known whether it was empty at three in the morning or at six, because by the time the boats came in past the wall she was asleep on a sofa with her boots on.
She is thirty-one.
She has a doctorate.

Her work is on cormorant foraging in the Western Approaches and she has, at the last count, put satellite tags on ninety-one birds, and there is nothing in the literature or in her own data that supports a single thing her grandmother said at that window.
She holds both of these positions and has stopped finding it difficult.
It took her about a decade.
At nineteen she thought she had to choose, and chose the first, and was insufferable about it at two Christmases.
The first is that it is a bird on a post.
Everything about that night is explained by an ordinary cormorant doing an ordinary thing at an ordinary time, in front of a family who needed something to look at.

The second is that on the ninth of October her grandmother got up and went to the window at nine o'clock at night and said four words, and every person in that kitchen — eleven of them, including two who had been at sea for forty years and did not believe in anything — stopped talking and looked, and then went back to the tea.
And that whatever that was, it held that room together for another five hours.
Merryn goes home about four times a year.
Her grandmother died in 2021.
She always looks at the post.
She has never seen a bird on it in the dark and she has been checking for seventeen years, which she is aware is exactly the kind of statement that a person makes when they have already decided.
Her uncle is seventy-one and still goes out, in the same boat, with a radio that works and a second radio in a bag.
She asked him once, at about twenty-five, when she was full of the tags and the data and the Western Approaches, whether he actually believed any of it about the post.
He thought about it for a good while, which he does.

Then he said that when he was a boy his own grandmother had told him the same thing, and that he had gone out for forty years knowing that if he was late there would be a bird on that post and somebody in a kitchen looking at it, and that he had never once needed to work out whether it was true.
"It's not about the bird," he said.
"It's that somebody's counting."
Nobody looks at a weathervane, and that is the entire reason this took two hundred years to notice.
A weathervane is designed to turn.
That is its only function.

It sits on a spindle on a church tower and it turns to face the wind, and if you looked up at it at four o'clock and again at six and it was pointing somewhere else, you would think nothing at all, because that is what it is for.
Femke has tried this on people and it works every time.
She asks them which way the vane on their own church was pointing this morning.
Nobody has ever known.
She asks whether they would notice if it turned while they were watching and they all say yes, and then she asks when they last watched one, and there is a pause.
A weathervane is the most public instrument in a Dutch town and it is the one nobody reads, precisely because everybody has known since they were four exactly what it does.
The cockerel on the Grote Kerk at Nieuwe Sluis is copper, about ninety centimetres from beak to tail, and it went up in 1791 with the tower.

It has been down three times: in 1893 for the spindle, in 1946 for war damage that was not to the cockerel itself but to the mounting, and in 2011 for conservation, when a man from Utrecht took it away for four months and came back with it and a report that is in the church office and that Femke has read.
The report says it is an ordinary copper vane of its period, well made, with a bearing that has been replaced twice, and that it turns freely and is correctly balanced.
Femke's family have been in that town since before the tower.

Her great-grandfather was a wheelwright and her grandfather was a wheelwright until there was no such job and then he was in a factory at Zwolle, and the family has lived in three houses on the same street since 1880 and there is nothing remarkable about that in the Netherlands.
The workshop is a hairdresser's now.

The yard behind it, where the whole of this starts, is a car park with four spaces, and Femke has stood in it and worked out roughly where a man would have been standing in November 1951 to have that view of the tower over the roofline, and it is between the second and third space.
What is in her family, and what Femke did not know about until she was twelve, is the book.
It is a school exercise book with a marbled cover and it is in a drawer, and it has been added to by four people, and the first entry is in November 1951 in her great-grandfather's handwriting.
Each entry is a date, a time, and two compass bearings.
The first bearing is where it was.
The second is where it went to.
That is all.

There is no commentary in the first two hundred entries and no explanation anywhere in the book of what it is for, because the man who started it knew what it was for and assumed that anybody holding it would too.
The reason there is a book at all is a Thursday in November 1951.

Her great-grandfather was in the yard behind the workshop at about half past three in the afternoon, and it was flat calm — properly flat, the kind of still that happens over that country in November when a high sits on it, with smoke going straight up from every chimney in the town.
And the cockerel turned.
He watched it go, in still air, through about a hundred and thirty degrees, from south-west round to north-north-west, taking perhaps forty seconds, and stop.
Forty seconds is the detail that Femke keeps coming back to.
A vane in a gust snaps round.
It goes in a second or two and it overshoots and comes back and hunts about before it settles, because it is a plate on a spindle being hit by moving air.
Forty seconds, smoothly, through a hundred and thirty degrees, with no overshoot and no hunting, is not what a plate on a spindle does when it is hit by anything.
It is what a plate on a spindle does when it is turned.
He went and got two men from the workshop and one of them was the sexton and they stood in the street and looked at it for a quarter of an hour, and nothing else happened.
There was no wind that afternoon or that evening.
Smoke went straight up until dark.

The sexton's name was Aalders and he had the keys and he went up the tower that evening and came down and said that the mechanism was as it always was, which is written into entry two in a different hand.
The wind came in from the north-north-west at about eleven the following morning and blew hard for two days.

That is entry one and it is written in a wheelwright's hand with the time to the nearest quarter hour and both bearings estimated by eye, and underneath it, in the same ink, is the sentence that made Femke sit down on the floor of her grandmother's spare room: *Others have said this.
Nobody writes it down.*
There are eleven hundred entries in that book.
Not eleven hundred turns.

That is a distinction her great-aunt was firm about and that Femke has kept: an entry is an observation, and about a hundred and forty of them record the vane doing nothing on a day when somebody expected it to do something, which is exactly the sort of entry that a person keeping a record to prove a point would leave out.

Her great-grandfather kept it from 1951 until 1974, and then her grandfather until 2003, and then her great-aunt, who was the one who actually understood what she was doing, until 2019, and then nobody, and then Femke.
There is a gap.

Between the November of 2019 and the March that Femke was twelve there are no entries, because her great-aunt died in the October and the book went into a drawer in a spare room with a quantity of other paper and nobody thought about it.
Femke found it looking for something else.
Her grandmother said, when asked, "Oh, Truus's book," in the voice of somebody identifying a lampshade.
The pattern is not subtle and it does not need statistics to see, although Femke has done the statistics.
Her great-aunt did not do statistics and did not need to.

She had read the book front to back perhaps thirty times and she could tell you, without looking, that the winter ones were good and the summer ones were rubbish and that anything under about eight hours tended to come to nothing.
All three of those held up when Femke put it in a spreadsheet, which she has always thought is the more interesting result.
The cockerel turns to a new bearing while the wind is still doing something else, and the wind arrives on that bearing somewhere between four and forty hours later, and the median is nineteen.
It does not do this every time.
About a third of the entries are marked with a small cross, which was her great-aunt's notation for *nothing followed*, and Femke has worked out that the crosses cluster in summer.
It is much better in winter.
It is best of all in the ten days either side of a deep low coming in off the Atlantic, which is the situation that matters in a town four metres below sea level behind a dyke.
Which is either the most significant thing in the book or the most obvious.

Winter storms in the Netherlands come from a small number of directions in a small number of situations, and a vane that turned at random would look good in winter for no reason at all, and Femke has spent a good deal of time trying to work out how to separate those two and has not managed it.
The thing her great-aunt did, which nobody before her had done, was to start writing down the wind that actually arrived — bearing and force and time — in a second column.
Which is why the book is not a curiosity.

It is a hundred and eleven pages of paired observations, and Femke had it digitised at nineteen, and it is now in a spreadsheet with eleven hundred rows, and she has done what you do with eleven hundred rows.
The entry that matters is not from 1951.
It is from the thirty-first of January 1953, at eleven in the morning, in her great-grandfather's hand, and it reads: *N by NW, hard round, held.
Told Bakker, told de Vries, told the sexton.
Bakker moved his beasts.* The North Sea flood came that night.
Femke is not going to make more of that entry than it will carry and she has thought about how to put this for a long time.
Nieuwe Sluis is not one of the places where the dyke went.
The water came into that town to about knee height in the low streets and went down in three days and the losses were livestock and furniture.
Nobody there was hurt.
The places where it was catastrophic were in Zeeland and South Holland and there was nothing any weathervane could have done about any of it.

What the entry says is that on the morning of the thirty-first of January 1953, a wheelwright looked at a copper bird, and wrote down a bearing, and went and told three men, and one of them moved his cattle to the high field and the other two did not.
That is the whole of it.
Two cows and a horse.
Femke has been to the church at Nieuwe Sluis on the thirty-first of January four times now, at eleven in the morning, and stood on the corner by the bakery and looked up.
She does not know what she is doing and she does not do it for a reason she can give.
Bakker has been dead since 1988 and there is nobody in that town who knows the entry exists apart from her mother, who is not interested.
Femke is twenty-four and she works for the water board, which was not a coincidence.
She keeps the book.
There are nineteen entries in her handwriting and the most recent is from the fourteenth of March and it has a cross beside it.

She has shown the spreadsheet to two colleagues who model surge, both of whom found it interesting and neither of whom could do anything with it, because the honest position is that eleven hundred bearings estimated by eye from a street over seventy years is not an instrument, and because the modern forecast is better than nineteen hours and is right far more often than two thirds of the time.
She writes in it anyway, at the kitchen table, in the same book, under her great-aunt's last entry.

And about four times a winter she goes out into the street at some point in the afternoon and stands on the corner by the bakery and looks up at a copper cockerel on a tower, in the way that nobody in that town has done since her great-aunt died — which is to say deliberately, for a minute at a time, on purpose, at a thing that is designed to turn.
She has seen it move twice.
The first was in the January she was nineteen and it was in a gust and it snapped round and hunted about and settled, which is what a vane does, and she wrote nothing.

The second was on the fourth of December 2024 at about twenty past two in the afternoon, in still air, and it went through perhaps eighty degrees in something over half a minute, smoothly, and stopped.
She stood on that corner for a further eleven minutes and then went home and got the book out and wrote the date and the time and two bearings under her great-aunt's hand.
The wind came in on the bearing she had written at about six the following morning, which is sixteen hours, which is inside the median.
That entry has no cross beside it.
It also has no note, and no underline, and no exclamation mark, because there is a way that book is written and Femke is the fifth person to write in it.
The gorge at Ōnuki is about sixty metres across and about forty deep and the river at the bottom of it is small and extremely loud.
There was a bridge.
It was a suspension footbridge with wooden decking and two steel cables and it was built in 1961 to replace an older one, and it went in a typhoon in September 1998, and nobody was on it.
It went at about two in the morning and the first anybody knew was that a man on the near side got up at six and looked out and there was nothing there.
Haruto has seen four photographs of it.

Two are family snapshots taken from the near anchors with somebody standing on the deck, one is from a newspaper in 1961 with about thirty people on it for the opening, and one is from the prefectural records and shows the cable anchorage in a way that has since turned out to be extremely useful to him.
The anchors are still there.
Two concrete blocks on each side, waist high, with the cable stubs cut off flush, and Haruto has sat on the near ones many times.

Somebody cut the cables flush in about 2000 because children were swinging on the stubs, and there is a photograph of that being done and the man with the angle grinder is Haruto's father, aged twenty-six, which is a fact Haruto did not learn until he was nineteen and which reorganised a certain amount of how he thought about his father.
The road round is eleven kilometres and takes twenty-five minutes and it is a perfectly good road and there is a bus twice a day.
Twenty-five minutes to go sixty metres.
That is the whole geography of the place and everybody in that valley can say the numbers without thinking, and they say them cheerfully, and there is nothing in the tone that suggests a grievance.

Nobody rebuilt the bridge because there were nine households on the far side in 1998 and there are two now, and a footbridge over a gorge costs what a footbridge over a gorge costs, and every single person in that valley agrees that the decision was correct and can tell you exactly who made it and in what year.
The estimate in 2001 was a number that Haruto's father can still quote and that was, in the terms of that village, unarguable.
It was put to a meeting.
The meeting agreed.
The minutes are two pages and there is no dissent recorded and Haruto has read them.
There are photographs of that meeting and his grandmother is in the second row.
And on one night in the middle of June, the fireflies do the line of it.

Haruto's grandmother had described it to him for years before he saw it and her description was, he thinks, better than the thing, in the way that descriptions of things by people who love them usually are.

What it actually is: on one night — never more than two, usually one, between about the eighth and the twentieth of June depending on the season — the *genji-botaru* over that gorge concentrate along a line.
Not a solid line.
It is not a rope of light and anybody expecting that is going to be disappointed and Haruto has watched several visitors be disappointed.
It is a band, perhaps four metres deep, running from the near anchors to the far anchors, sixty metres, in the dark, at about the height the decking used to be.

There are maybe two or three hundred insects in it, flashing in the slow synchronising way that the Genji firefly does, and it holds for about ninety minutes from a quarter past eight and then it is over.
The synchronising is worth a word because it is the part that does not photograph.

Genji fireflies in a group settle into rhythm — not perfectly and not all at once, but over a few minutes a group will drift into flashing together, and the interval in that part of Japan is about two seconds.
So what you are watching is not two hundred lights.
It is a band sixty metres long that goes on and off, slowly, with stragglers, for an hour and a half.
You can see the far side lit.
That is the part that catches people.

The far anchors are sixty metres away and there is no light in that valley at all after eight, and for ninety minutes on one night a year there is enough of a glow at the far end that you can make out the concrete.
The rest of the gorge has fireflies too.
That is important and it is the thing everybody leaves out.
There are fireflies up and down that river for two kilometres and the whole gorge is full of them all through June.
Haruto has walked that river at night in June perhaps forty times and there are good stretches and thin stretches and the good ones move about between years depending on what the water has done.
The line is a concentration, not an exclusion.
And the concentration is real and it is on the line of a bridge that has not existed since 1998, and Haruto has photographed it four times with a long exposure and the shape is a shape.
He has also, at nineteen, done the thing that ought to have been done first, which was to go up and down the gorge on the same night and look for other bands.
There are none.

The rest of the gorge that night is fireflies in the ordinary distribution — low, near the water, in the vegetation, scattered over about thirty vertical metres — and there is one band, in one place, at one height, for ninety minutes.
He got the reason from a woman at the prefectural university when he was fifteen, in an email, and she was extremely patient and gave him more of her time than he deserved.
Genji fireflies need clean flowing water for the larvae and a particular kind of bank for the pupae, and the adults gather over water and drift on the air.
And the air in a gorge is not uniform.

Warm air comes off the rock faces where the sun has been on them and cold air sits over the water, and where those two meet you get a layer — a horizontal boundary, running the length of the gorge, that stays put on a still evening and that anything light enough will accumulate at.

She sent him a paper about aerial plankton at inversion boundaries, which he did not understand at fifteen and read again at twenty-two and did understand, and which is not about fireflies at all and is the most useful thing anybody has ever sent him.
There is such a layer in the gorge at Ōnuki.
It is at about thirty metres below the rim, plus or minus a few, on a still June night.
Which is about where the decking was.

Because the decking was there for the same reason: a bridge over a gorge goes at the height where the two banks can be got to sensibly, and that height was chosen by an engineer in 1961 for reasons of rock and cost that have nothing whatever to do with fireflies and everything to do with the shape of the gorge.
The gorge produced both.
The bridge and the line of light are two answers to the same question about a piece of rock.
Haruto thinks that is a much better fact than a ghost bridge and he has never once got that across to anybody.

He tried it on a group of visitors from Nagoya in 2021 who had come specifically for it and who had driven four hours, and he watched their faces do the thing faces do, and afterwards one of them thanked him politely for the explanation in a tone that meant it had been taken away rather than given.
He has stopped explaining it at the gorge.
He explains it afterwards, in the car park, if anybody asks, and about one in eleven does.
His grandmother crossed that bridge twice a day for thirty-one years.

She lived on the far side until 1998 and worked at the school on the near side, and she went over at ten past seven in the morning and back at about six, and it took four minutes and she did it in every kind of weather including, on two occasions she would talk about, snow that came over her boots.
Twice a day, thirty-one years, about two hundred and twenty days a year.
Haruto did that arithmetic at thirteen and got something over thirteen thousand crossings, and asked her, and she said that sounded about right and that it had never once occurred to her to count.
She moved to the near side in the November of 1998 because there was no bridge and because she was fifty-nine and the road is eleven kilometres.
She has lived four hundred metres from where she grew up for twenty-seven years.
Haruto took her to the gorge on the June he was twelve, which was the first year she had asked, and it took them a long time to get down the path.
They sat on the near anchors from about eight.
The line came up at twenty past and it was, he thinks, roughly a two-hundred-insect year, which is average, and his grandmother did not say anything for ninety minutes.
He was twelve and he spent most of that ninety minutes looking at her rather than at the gorge, which he does not regret.
Afterwards, on the path, going extremely slowly, she said one thing about it, and it was not what he expected and it is why he has told this story perhaps eleven times in his life.
She said: "It's the wrong height." He said it looked right to him.

And his grandmother said that the decking had been about two metres lower than that, and that she had crossed it twice a day for thirty-one years and had looked at that water from it about twenty thousand times, and that she knew exactly how far down it was, and that the light was too high.
Haruto went back the following year with a tape and a laser measure that he borrowed and did not really know how to use.
The band that year was centred about thirty-one metres below the rim.

The anchors, from which the cables sagged, are at twenty-eight, and a suspension bridge deck hangs below its anchors by an amount that depends on the sag, and Haruto has an old photograph and has done the trigonometry twice and gets somewhere between thirty-two and thirty-four.
So she was right.
It is about two metres high.
He has never told her.

She is eighty-six and she goes down there most years and it takes two of them to get her back up the path, and she sits on the anchors for ninety minutes and says nothing, and Haruto sits next to her and looks at a line of light two metres above a bridge that fell down before he was born.
He has thought about telling her about eleven times and has got as far as the sentence twice.
What stops him is not that it would upset her.
She is not a woman who gets upset by a measurement and she would very likely be pleased to be right.
What stops him is that she said it once, on a path, in the dark, in a tone he has never heard her use about anything else, and she has not mentioned it in fourteen years.
She has sat on those anchors every June since and looked at that line and said nothing at all about the height.
Haruto thinks she is not looking at the fireflies.
He thinks she has been looking, every June since 2011, at a strip of air two metres below them, and that she does not require his tape measure to know where it is.
The list is kept in the back of the visitors' book at the homestay in Rumbak and it is not official and nobody is in charge of it.
It has sixty-one names on it and it goes back to 1994.
Each line is a name, a date, a place on the mountain, and, in a column somebody added in about 2003, either a tick or a cross.
The cross means there is no photograph.
There are sixty-one crosses.
The column was added by a Dutch woman in 2003 who was staying three weeks and who had been a librarian, and who could not bear a list without a field in it.
She ticked nothing and crossed everything and drew a line under it and wrote *as of 14/3/03*, and everybody since has just carried on down the page.
Dolma's mother runs the homestay and Dolma has read that list since she was about six, in the way children read the same page of a book a hundred times, and she can recite the first eleven entries.
Entry one is a Czech climber, the nineteenth of October 1994, *above the second bridge*.
Entry two is a woman from Manali, the following March.
Entry three and entry four are the same person on two different days in 1996, which is the only time that has happened and which everybody in Rumbak has an opinion about.
The valley gets snow leopards.

Everybody in Ladakh knows this and it is not a secret and it is a large part of the local economy in winter: people come from a very long way to sit in the cold and look at a slope through a spotting scope, and the guides are extremely good, and a reasonable proportion of them go home having seen one.
Dolma grew up inside that industry and is not sentimental about it.

It has paid for the homestay, her uncle's vehicle, and about a third of her schooling, and the animal that pays for all of it is one that everybody in the valley used to shoot for taking goats, within living memory, and which several old men in Rumbak will discuss with visitors and several will not.
Those sightings are not on the list.
The list is for one animal.

She has a mark — a break in the ring pattern on the left flank, low down, shaped like a comma — and she is enormous, and she has been seen sixty-one times in thirty-one years by people who mostly did not know they were seeing anything unusual until they came down and described her and somebody asked about the flank.
Thirty-one years is longer than a snow leopard lives.
They go about twelve in the wild and perhaps twenty in a zoo, and Dolma has known this since she was nine and has never had any use for it.

The valley's position, which is her uncle's and which she thinks is right, is that there have been two or three of them with the same mark and that the mark runs in a line, and that this is the least interesting problem in the whole business.
And nobody has photographed her.
Dolma would like to be extremely careful here because this is where the story usually goes wrong.
There are photographs.

Sixty-one of them, more or less; some people took several and four people took none because they had no camera, which reduces the actual number and which is the first thing anybody serious asks about.
The photographs are of an empty slope.
Not blurred.
Not obscured.

There is a well-focused, correctly exposed photograph of a scree slope with rock and snow on it and nothing else, taken by a person who was at that moment looking at a snow leopard through the viewfinder, at a distance which in eleven of the sixty-one cases was under a hundred metres.
Dolma has seen forty of those photographs.
Her mother has a folder.
The folder is a plastic wallet and about half of what is in it are prints that people posted back afterwards from Prague and Melbourne and Bengaluru, sometimes years later, sometimes with a letter.
The letters are the part Dolma reads.

There are eleven of them and they are all essentially the same letter, written by eleven strangers who did not know each other, and the sentence that appears in nine of them in some form is: *I know how this sounds.* The explanations offered, in the order she has heard them most often: That people are mistaken, and there was never anything there.
This one is strong.
Human beings are appallingly bad at this and a rock in the right light on a Ladakhi slope has fooled every guide in that valley including her uncle.
That the animal moved.
Also strong.
A snow leopard can be gone in under two seconds and there is a well-known effect where the eye holds an image the camera did not get.
Dolma has watched this happen to a client.
A German man in 2023, at four hundred metres, with a two-thousand-euro lens and a tripod, who took eleven frames of a slope and was completely certain for about ninety seconds that he had it.
He had the frames on the back of the camera within a minute and there was nothing in them and he was, to his enormous credit, delighted rather than upset.
That animal was not the one with the comma.
It was an ordinary young male that half the valley saw that week.
That the camera was pointed somewhere else.
Strongest of all, and it accounts for a great many of the sixty-one, and Dolma's uncle believes this one and says so.

He is a guide of twenty-two years and he has put more people onto snow leopards than anybody in that valley and he will tell you, without any impatience at all, that a person who has just seen one is the least reliable witness on earth about where their own hands were.
And a fourth, which nobody in Rumbak says out loud to visitors and which everybody in Rumbak says to each other, which is that she is not photographable, and which Dolma is not going to defend.

She saw her on the fourteenth of February when she was fourteen, at about ten past four in the afternoon, on the slope above the second bridge, at a distance she paced afterwards at a hundred and sixty metres.
She was alone, which is not allowed and which she is not going to pretend was an accident.
The rule at Rumbak is that nobody under sixteen goes above the second bridge on their own in winter, and it is a good rule and Dolma enforces it now on other people's children with a straight face.
There was a scope at the homestay and a group had gone up the other side that morning and Dolma had a phone and about forty minutes of light.
The animal came out from behind a spur, moving left to right, not hurrying.
There was no wind and there was that particular Ladakhi February light in the last hour, which is flat and blue and which makes the scree look like something poured.

Dolma has told this part perhaps twenty times and she always says the same three things, because they are the three things that were actually in her head and she has never been able to improve on them.
The first is that she was much bigger than the photographs of other ones.
The second is that the tail is not an exaggeration; it is nearly as long as the animal and it was carried in a curve and it is the only part that moved much.
And the third is that she stopped, and turned her head, and looked down the slope at Dolma for a period that Dolma has never been able to estimate.
The comma was on the left flank, low down.
Dolma had not been looking for it and did not go hunting for it.
It was simply there, the way a thing is there, on an animal a hundred and sixty metres away in good light.
Dolma had the phone in her hand the whole time.
She did not take it.
She had it up.

She wants that in, because the version where she never thought of it is a nicer story and is not true: she got the phone up, and she had the animal in the frame, and her thumb was where her thumb goes.

And she stood there for what she later worked out was somewhere between three and five minutes with a phone up and her thumb where her thumb goes, and did not press it, and then the animal went over the ridge.
She checked the phone on the way down.
There was nothing on it.
She checked it again at the homestay and again that night, in case she had taken one without knowing, which people do.
Nothing.
The last photograph on that phone is from the eleventh of February and it is of a dog.
She has never been able to explain why, and she has stopped trying, and she has come to think that the trying was the only part that was doing any harm.

What she says now, at twenty-six, when people push her on it — and they do push, because she is the sixty-second name on that list and because she is the only one of the sixty-two who was holding a working camera and had a clean shot and knew exactly what she was looking at — is this.
Everybody in that valley knows what a snow leopard looks like.
There are ninety thousand photographs.
There is footage.
There are documentaries with music on them and there is a poster of one in the school at Leh and there is a photograph of a snow leopard on the side of a bus.
There were, at ten past four on the fourteenth of February, two things on that mountain: an animal, and a girl looking at it.
And the moment she pressed it there would have been three, and the third would have been the one everybody afterwards was actually going to be looking at.
And she had about four minutes.
Her mother wrote her name in the book that evening and put a cross in the second column, and said nothing about the phone, and has never asked about it in twelve years.
Dolma is twenty-six and she is a guide in the winter, which is what she was always going to be, and she takes people up onto the slope above the second bridge about forty times a season.
She has seen her twice more.
Both times with clients, both times with four cameras going, both times a cross in the book.
She has been asked, by three different film crews, whether she would take them to where she goes.
The second crew offered her a fee that was more than the homestay makes in a February.
She says yes, every time, and takes them, and they get very good footage of a valley that has snow leopards in it, and they go home, and Dolma writes nothing in the book.

The third crew, in 2024, had a young sound recordist who sat with Dolma on the slope for two hours on the last morning and did not ask her anything at all about the list, having plainly been told not to.
Somewhere in the second hour he said that he had been doing this for six years and had never once watched anything without a machine running.
Dolma said that she had a good place about forty minutes up and that there was no signal in it and that the light would be gone by five.
They went.
Nothing happened; it was a slope with choughs on it and a great deal of wind.
They came down in the dark and he thanked her in a way that she has thought about since, and the crew went to Leh in the morning.
She is aware that this is not a story about a snow leopard.
She has decided that this is the point.
